title: fix(schema): ModelAlias empty scoped model alias target is silently ignored instead of erroring
body:
## Summary

In `ModelAlias.resolveRef` (`packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts`), a **scoped model alias whose target is the empty string is silently ignored**: resolution proceeds exactly as if the alias did not exist, so a mistyped/emptied config entry silently does nothing instead of erroring like every other invalid alias target.

## Evidence (verified on main `d0ba1110fb`, the #410 merge)

The two scoped-model lookups guard on truthiness, so an empty-string target never reaches any validation:

- `packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts` — orig-provider scoped lookup: `const origScopedAlias = aliases.models?.[origScopedKey]; if (origScopedAlias) { … }`
- `packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts` — resolved-provider scoped lookup: `const scopedAlias = aliases.models?.[scopedKey]; if (scopedAlias) { … }`

Probe (bun, importing `packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts` directly):

```
resolve({ models: { "openai/pro": "" } }, "openai/pro")
  => "openai/pro"            // alias silently dropped, input returned unchanged

resolve({ providers: { ds: "deepseek" }, models: { "ds/pro": "" } }, "ds/pro")
  => "deepseek/pro"          // provider alias applied, empty model alias silently dropped
```

Contrast with the sibling alias kinds, which were fixed to validate with an explicit undefined check:

- Provider aliases use `if (providerAlias !== undefined && …)` and throw `Invalid model reference` for an empty target (#407/#410).
- Variant alias targets that are empty throw (#406/#410).
- Even a **global** model alias with an empty target throws (indirectly, when the settled ref has no `/`), though its message names the input rather than the target.

Only the scoped model path swallows the empty target completely.

## Why it matters

Alias config is user-authored. An entry like `"openai/pro": ""` (emptied while editing, a templating mistake, a generated config bug) currently fails silently: the model the user believes is remapped is not, and there is no error anywhere to chase. Every neighbouring alias kind treats the same mistake as an `Invalid model reference` error.

## Acceptance criteria

- `resolve` (and `resolveRef`) throws `Invalid model reference: <input>` when a scoped model alias that matches the input has an empty-string target — for both scoped lookups (original provider name and provider-alias-resolved name).
- Existing behaviour for non-empty scoped targets is unchanged (`packages/core/test/model-alias.test.ts` tests 4, 5 and 13 still pass).
- New tests in `packages/core/test/model-alias.test.ts` cover the empty scoped target under both the original and the resolved provider name.
- Related nicety (optional): the global empty-target error message could name the alias target rather than only the input.

Single-repo: the `ModelAlias` resolver lives only in developing-today/opencode (`packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts`).

title: fix(schema): ModelAlias whitespace-only alias targets yield blank provider/model/variant segments instead of erroring
body:
## Summary

In `ModelAlias.resolveRef` (`packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts`), alias targets are validated only against the empty string, `/` and `#`. A **whitespace-only (or whitespace-padded) target segment passes every check** and becomes the provider, model or variant of the resolved ref — producing refs whose segments are blank spaces, which the no-alias parser rejects for the equivalent input.

## Evidence (verified on main `d0ba1110fb`, the #410 merge)

Probe (bun, importing `packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts` directly):

```
resolve({ providers: { x: " " } }, "x/model")                 => " /model"              // provider is a single space
resolve({ models: { "openai/pro": " " } }, "openai/pro")      => "openai/ "             // model is a single space
resolve({ models: { "openai/pro": "  " } }, "openai/pro")     => "openai/  "            // model is two spaces
resolve({ models: { bad: "openai/ " } }, "bad")               => "openai/ "             // global target, model is a space
resolve({ models: { bad: " /gpt-4o" } }, "bad")               => " /gpt-4o"             // global target, provider is a space
resolve({ variants: { hi: " " } }, "openai/gpt-4o#hi")        => "openai/gpt-4o# "      // variant is a single space
resolve({ variants: { hi: "\t" } }, "openai/gpt-4o#hi")       => "openai/gpt-4o#\t"     // variant is a tab
resolve({ models: { bad: "openai/gpt-4o " } }, "bad")         => "openai/gpt-4o "       // trailing space kept in model id
```

Why it happens:

- The initial `input` is trimmed (`const trimmed = input.trim()`), but alias targets substituted into `current` mid-loop are never trimmed or re-checked for whitespace.
- Provider-alias validation (Rule 2) rejects only `!providerAlias || includes("/") || includes("#")` — `" "` passes.
- Variant validation after `resolveVariant` rejects only `!finalVariant || includes("#")` — `" "` / `"\t"` pass.
- The settled-ref check rejects only `slashIdx <= 0 || slashIdx === settledBase.length - 1` — a model consisting solely of spaces has non-zero length, so it passes.

Contrast with the no-alias path: `resolve(undefined, "openai/ ")` throws (the input trim turns it into `openai/`), and `resolve(undefined, " /gpt-4o")` throws (trimmed to `/gpt-4o`). The alias path is therefore more permissive than the plain parser for the same final ref — the same class of divergence closed for empty/`#` targets in #398, #406 and #407.

## Why it matters

Alias config is user-authored; stray whitespace from editing or generated config currently produces a resolved ref with blank segments that downstream model lookup cannot match, surfacing as a confusing "model unavailable"-style failure far from the config mistake instead of an `Invalid model reference` error at resolution time.

## Acceptance criteria

- An alias target segment (provider name, model name, or variant name) that is whitespace-only, or that carries leading/trailing whitespace, causes `resolve`/`resolveRef` to throw `Invalid model reference` — for provider aliases, global and scoped model aliases, and variant aliases alike.
- Refs whose segments are already well-formed are unchanged (`packages/core/test/model-alias.test.ts` existing tests all still pass).
- New tests in `packages/core/test/model-alias.test.ts` cover at least: whitespace-only provider target, whitespace-only scoped model target, whitespace-only variant target.

Related but distinct: #411 (empty scoped model alias target silently ignored — the truthiness-guard counterpart of this validation gap).

Single-repo: the `ModelAlias` resolver lives only in developing-today/opencode (`packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts`).

title: fix(schema): ModelAlias alias lookups match Object.prototype members — toString/constructor names crash the #410/#413 validation with TypeError
body:
## Summary

In `ModelAlias.resolveRef` (`packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts`), alias lookups read inherited `Object.prototype` members as if they were configured aliases. A model, provider, or variant name that happens to equal a prototype member (`toString`, `constructor`, `hasOwnProperty`, `valueOf`, `__proto__`) therefore produces a non-string "target", and the validation added in PRs #410 and #413 crashes with a `TypeError` instead of resolving normally or throwing `Invalid model reference`.

This is visible in the #410/#413 diffs themselves: both PRs changed/introduced guards that assume a lookup returns `string | undefined` —

- PR #413 (commit `837c4e0e1dfb`, merge `0fec462129`): the three model-alias lookups at `model-alias.ts:83` (global), `:109` (scoped under original provider) and `:143` (scoped under resolved provider) now check `!== undefined` and assign the value to `current`.
- PR #410 (commit `e1caf59543f5`, merge `d0ba1110fb`): the provider-alias lookup at `model-alias.ts:132` checks `!== undefined` and then calls `providerAlias.includes(...)`; the variant caller at `model-alias.ts:194` calls `finalVariant.includes("#")` on the value returned by `resolveVariant`, whose bare-key lookup at `model-alias.ts:240` uses the `in` operator (`if (variant in variantAliases)`), which also matches inherited members.

Plain-object alias maps (object literals in tests, and the records produced by config decoding in `packages/core/src/config/normalize.ts`) inherit from `Object.prototype`, so `aliases.models["toString"]`, `aliases.providers["toString"]` and `"toString" in aliases.variants` are all truthy/defined even when the user never configured such an alias.

## Evidence (verified on current main `0fec462129`, the #413 merge)

Probe (bun, importing `packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts` directly):

```
resolve({ models: { other: "openai/gpt-4o" } }, "toString")
  THROWS TypeError: current.indexOf is not a function
resolve({ models: { other: "openai/gpt-4o" } }, "constructor")
  THROWS TypeError: current.indexOf is not a function
resolve({ models: { other: "openai/gpt-4o" } }, "hasOwnProperty")
  THROWS TypeError: current.indexOf is not a function
resolve({ providers: { other: "openai" } }, "toString/model")
  THROWS TypeError: providerAlias.includes is not a function
resolve({ providers: { other: "openai" } }, "constructor/model")
  THROWS TypeError: providerAlias.includes is not a function
resolve({ variants: { hi: "high" } }, "openai/gpt-4o#toString")
  THROWS TypeError: finalVariant.includes is not a function
resolve({ variants: { hi: "high" } }, "openai/gpt-4o#constructor")
  THROWS TypeError: finalVariant.includes is not a function
resolve({ variants: { hi: "high" } }, "openai/gpt-4o#__proto__")
  THROWS TypeError: finalVariant.includes is not a function
```

Contrast with the no-alias path, which handles the same names cleanly:

```
resolve(undefined, "openai/gpt-4o#toString")  => "openai/gpt-4o#toString"   // real variant passes through
resolve(undefined, "toString")               THROWS Error: Invalid model reference: toString
```

So with any alias map configured, a bare model named `toString`, a provider named `toString`, or a variant named `toString`/`constructor`/`__proto__` crashes the resolver with a `TypeError`, where the no-alias parser either passes the name through or raises the documented `Invalid model reference` error. Callers in `ModelResolver` and the session runner catch all errors, so in those paths the crash is silently swallowed and alias resolution is abandoned for that request; direct callers (e.g. `packages/cli/src/session-target.ts`) get an unexplained `TypeError`.

Distinct from #412 (whitespace-only alias targets): that issue is about configured string targets; this one is about lookups returning inherited non-string values for names that were never configured at all.

## Why it matters

Alias resolution sits on the model-selection path for every configured deployment. Names colliding with `Object.prototype` members are not exotic in generated or user-authored config (a variant literally named e.g. `constructor` is legal input to the no-alias parser today), and the failure mode — a `TypeError` from inside validation code, or silently skipped alias resolution where callers catch-all — is far from the actual cause. The #410/#413 hardening made the resolver stricter for configured targets; the lookups themselves should be own-property lookups so unconfigured names behave exactly as they do with no aliases.

Single-repo: the `ModelAlias` resolver lives only in developing-today/opencode (`packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts`).

## Acceptance criteria

- Alias lookups in `resolveRef`/`resolveVariant` only match own properties of the alias maps (e.g. `Object.hasOwn` guards or `typeof === "string"` checks): `toString`, `constructor`, `hasOwnProperty`, `valueOf`, and `__proto__` as a model, provider, or bare variant name behave exactly as they do on the no-alias path (pass through where the plain parser passes them through, `Invalid model reference` where it rejects) — never a `TypeError`.
- A genuinely configured alias whose key is one of those names and whose target is a string still resolves (own-property check, not a blocklist).
- New tests in `packages/core/test/model-alias.test.ts` cover at least: bare model `toString` with a models map present, provider `toString/model` with a providers map present, and variant `openai/gpt-4o#toString` with a variants map present.
- Existing model-alias tests (24/24 on main `0fec462129`) all still pass.

title: fix(schema): ModelAlias bare scoped alias target is misrouted when its variant contains a / — slash test looks past the #
body:
## Problem

`ModelAlias` scoped model-alias targets in the bare form (`newModel#variant`) are misrouted when the variant itself contains a `/`. Both scoped-alias branches decide "is this target a `provider/model` form or a bare model form?" by testing `target.includes("/")` on the **whole target string, including the part after `#`** — so a slash that belongs to the variant flips the branch, the target is taken verbatim as a provider/model ref, and resolution then fails because the part before `#` has no slash.

## Evidence (verified on main `c79bf55a8e`, Bun probe against `packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts`)

`packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts:113` (original-provider scoped branch) and `:153` (resolved-provider scoped branch, Rule 3) both read:

```ts
if (scopedAlias.includes("/")) {
  current = scopedAlias
} else {
  // hash-split bare form: `${provider}/${scopedModel}#${scopedVar}`
}
```

Probe results:

| Case | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `models: {"openai/old": "new#va/r"}`, input `openai/old` | **throws** `Invalid model reference after alias resolution: new` |
| `providers: {ds: "openai"}, models: {"openai/old": "new#va/r"}`, input `ds/old` (Rule 3 branch) | **throws** the same |
| Control — same target with a slash-free variant, `"new#fast"` | resolves to `openai/new#fast` |
| Control — the intended final ref given directly, `openai/new#va/r` (no aliases) | resolves fine, variant `va/r` |
| Control — slash-form target with the same variant, `"other/new#va/r"` | resolves to `other/new#va/r` |

So the bare scoped form is the only one that breaks, and only because the discriminator looks past the `#`. Variants containing `/` are otherwise accepted everywhere in this resolver (the no-alias parser and the alias path both pass them through).

## Why it matters

A scoped alias is the documented way to rename one model under one provider while giving it a default variant. A variant name containing `/` (namespaced effort/variant names occur in the wild) silently turns a valid config into a hard `Invalid model reference` error whose message (`...after alias resolution: new`) points at the model name and gives no hint the variant's slash caused it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `resolve({models: {"openai/old": "new#va/r"}}, "openai/old")` returns `openai/new#va/r` (both the original-provider branch at :113 and the resolved-provider branch at :153).
- [ ] The form discriminator tests the slash only in the part of the target before `#`.
- [ ] Existing behaviour is unchanged for slash-form targets, bare targets with slash-free variants, and all currently rejected targets (empty, padded, second-`#`).
- [ ] New tests in `packages/core/test/model-alias.test.ts` cover the slash-in-variant bare scoped target through both scoped branches; the existing model-alias suite still passes.

Suggested fix: in both branches, compute the discriminator from the pre-`#` segment, e.g. `const hash = target.indexOf("#"); const base = hash === -1 ? target : target.slice(0, hash); if (base.includes("/")) { ... }` — the hash-split else-branch already handles the variant correctly once it is reached.

title: fix(core): settings.baseURL is ignored for opencode-go and its instances
body:
`providers.opencode-go.settings.baseURL` has no effect: requests still go to opencode.ai. The same happens for an `instanceOf: "opencode-go"` copy, so a Go account can't be pointed at a proxy or a local recorder.

```jsonc
"providers": { "opencode-go": { "settings": { "baseURL": "http://127.0.0.1:18998/go-2/v1" } } }
```

Import a key credential for `opencode-go`, then run `opencode run -m opencode-go/glm-5.3 "say hi"`.

title: fix(schema): ModelAlias input reference segments are never checked for padding — padded provider/model/variant resolve into refs that can never match
body:
## Problem

`ModelAlias.resolveRef` rejects alias *targets* whose provider/model/variant segments carry leading or trailing whitespace (`hasPaddedSegment`, added for #411/#412), but it never applies the same check to the *input reference itself*. A user-typed or config-supplied reference with padded segments resolves "successfully" into a `ResolvedRef` whose `providerID`, `id`, or `variant` contains spaces — values that can never match a real provider, model, or variant, so the failure surfaces later and further from the cause instead of as the invalid-reference error every other malformed shape gets.

## Evidence (verified 2026-10-25 on main df5fc16d47)

File: `packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts`

- `resolveRef` (line 47) trims only the outer ends of the whole input string; nothing validates the individual segments after the `/` and `#` splits.
- The settled result is built at lines 191-197 from `settledBase`/`settledVariant` with only a slash-position check — padded segments pass straight into `finalProvider` / `finalModel` / `finalVariant`.
- `parseRefString` (line 277, the no-alias path) likewise checks only emptiness and `#` placement, so padded segments are accepted there too.
- By contrast, alias targets are rejected for exactly this shape at lines 84, 110, and 151 via `hasPaddedSegment` (line 266), and provider alias targets at lines ~140-147.
- Callers pass raw strings straight in with no segment trimming upstream: `packages/core/src/config/normalize.ts:604,816` (config model strings), `packages/core/src/session/runner/model.ts:109`, `packages/core/src/model-resolver.ts:609`, `packages/cli/src/session-target.ts:97` (CLI value).

Reproduction (Bun probe importing `packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts`, main df5fc16d47):

| Aliases | Input | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `{ models: { zzz: "a/b" } }` | `openai /gpt-4o` | OK — `{ providerID: "openai ", id: "gpt-4o", ref: "openai /gpt-4o" }` |
| `{ models: { zzz: "a/b" } }` | `openai/ gpt-4o` | OK — `{ providerID: "openai", id: " gpt-4o" }` |
| `{ models: { zzz: "a/b" } }` | `openai/gpt-4o# fast` | OK — `{ variant: " fast", ref: "openai/gpt-4o# fast" }` |
| `undefined` (no-alias path) | `openai /gpt-4o` | OK — `{ providerID: "openai " }` via `parseRefString` |
| `undefined` (no-alias path) | `openai/gpt-4o# fast` | OK — `{ variant: " fast" }` via `parseRefString` |

Control: the same padding inside an alias *target* — `{ models: { x: "openai/gpt# fast" } }`, input `x` — throws `Invalid model reference: x` today.

## Why it matters

The input is the most common place padding appears (a stray space in a config value or CLI argument). Today it produces a canonical-looking ref with invisible spaces that no provider lookup will ever match, so the user gets a "model not found"-style failure with no hint that whitespace is the cause. The resolver already decided this shape is invalid for targets; the input deserves the same treatment for consistency.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An input reference whose provider, model, or variant segment has leading/trailing whitespace throws the same invalid-reference error as a padded alias target, on both the alias path and the `parseRefString` (no-alias) path.
- [ ] Whole-input leading/trailing whitespace keeps working (it is trimmed today, line 47).
- [ ] New tests in `packages/core/test/model-alias.test.ts` cover padded provider, model, and variant segments in the input, with and without aliases configured; all existing model-alias tests still pass.
- [ ] Dedup checked 2026-10-25: #411/#412 covered padded/whitespace *alias targets* only; no open or recently closed issue tracks padding in the input reference itself.

Single-repo: `ModelAlias` lives only in this repo's schema/core packages.

title: fix(schema): ModelAlias accepts refs with empty segments — openai//gpt and openai/gpt/ resolve to model IDs that can never exist
body:
## Problem

`ModelAlias.resolveRef` and `parseRefString` accept model references with empty segments — a doubled slash (`openai//gpt`) or a model ID ending in a slash (`openai/gpt/`). The resolved `id` then starts or ends with `/` (`"/gpt"`, `"gpt/"`, or even just `"/"`), which is not a model ID any provider carries, yet resolution reports success and hands the malformed ref downstream instead of throwing the invalid-reference error. Model IDs legitimately contain single slashes (nested IDs), so the gap is specifically *empty* segments, not slashes in general.

## Evidence (verified 2026-10-25 on main df5fc16d47)

File: `packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts`

- The settled-result check (line 191) rejects only a slash at position 0 or at the very end of the whole base string (`slashIdx <= 0 || slashIdx === settledBase.length - 1`). It never inspects the model portion for empty segments, so `openai//gpt` (first slash mid-string) and `openai/gpt/` (first slash mid-string) both pass, and lines 195-196 slice out `finalModel` values of `"/gpt"` and `"gpt/"`.
- `parseRefString` (line 277, the no-alias path) checks only that `id` is non-empty (line ~285); `"/gpt"` and `"gpt/"` are non-empty, so both pass there too.
- The whole-string edge cases *are* caught — alias targets `"/gpt"` and `"openai/"` throw `Invalid model reference after alias resolution` — which shows the intent to reject empty provider/model parts; the check just doesn't extend to empty segments inside or at the end of the model part.

Reproduction (Bun probe importing `packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts`, main df5fc16d47):

| Aliases | Input | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `{ models: { x: "openai//gpt" } }` | `x` | OK — `{ providerID: "openai", id: "/gpt", ref: "openai//gpt" }` |
| `undefined` (no-alias path) | `openai//gpt` | OK — `{ providerID: "openai", id: "/gpt" }` |
| `undefined` (no-alias path) | `openai/gpt/` | OK — `{ providerID: "openai", id: "gpt/" }` |
| `{ models: { x: "a//" } }` | `x` | OK — `{ providerID: "a", id: "/", ref: "a//" }` |

Controls that already throw today: alias targets `"/gpt"` and `"openai/"` (whole-string edges), and input `openai/` on the alias path.

## Why it matters

A doubled slash is an easy typo in a config model string or a hand-built ref, and a trailing slash is a common copy/paste artifact. Today both sail through the one component whose job is to canonicalize and validate refs, producing an `id` that can never match a provider model — the failure then appears as a generic model-not-found far from the typo, in both the alias and no-alias paths.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A reference with an empty segment — `//` anywhere in the base, or a model portion ending in `/` — throws the invalid-reference error, on both the alias path and the `parseRefString` (no-alias) path.
- [ ] Legitimate nested model IDs with single slashes (e.g. `openrouter/anthropic/claude-sonnet-4`) still resolve unchanged.
- [ ] New tests in `packages/core/test/model-alias.test.ts` cover the doubled-slash and trailing-slash shapes via direct input and via a model alias target; all existing model-alias tests still pass.
- [ ] Dedup checked 2026-10-25: `gh search issues` for "double slash", "empty segment", and "segments" returns no matching issue, open or closed; the #398-#422 series covered `#` shapes, padding, prototype keys, and slash-in-variant routing, not empty segments.

Single-repo: `ModelAlias` lives only in this repo's schema/core packages.

title: OpenAI-compatible completions door for external harnesses (OpenClaw direct to OpenCode)
body:
## Problem

OpenClaw (external agent harness) currently reaches fleet route models through a standalone proxy (code-repo `opencode-route-proxy`, :18750) that re-implements route/provider resolution outside OpenCode — including provider endpoint resolution, which it gets wrong for credential-backed providers (developing-today/code#4444: the GPT pair resolved to the PAYG platform door instead of the credential-backed Codex backend).

Ruling (Drew, 2026-11-02): OpenClaw should talk directly to OpenCode. The standalone re-implementation is the architectural mistake.

## What exists

`POST /api/experimental/generate` (Generate.Service) already runs one stateless generation through the server's own ModelResolver + LLM layer — route models resolve in-process, no session is stored. But it accepts only a single `prompt` string and returns only text: it cannot serve an external harness that speaks the OpenAI chat-completions wire format (message history, tools, streaming).

## Proposal

Add an OpenAI-compatible completions door to the server, backed by the same in-process machinery:

- `POST /v1/chat/completions` — accepts the OpenAI payload (`model` = a route ref such as `opencode-route/workhorse` or a bare route id, `messages`, `tools`, `tool_choice`, `stream`), resolves the model through ModelResolver (in-process model_routes/provider_routes resolution + provider layer), runs one provider completion via the LLM client, and returns the OpenAI wire shape (JSON, or SSE chunks terminated by `[DONE]` when streaming). No session is created or stored (a fresh attribution id is minted per call, as Generate does).
- `GET /v1/models` — the route models the door serves.
- Server auth applies as for every other route (no new unauthenticated surface).

Consumers: OpenClaw repoints its `opencode-route` provider from :18750 to this door once deployed; the standalone proxy then has no remaining production consumer and can be retired (tracked from the code repo side).

## Acceptance

- Tests: wire-shape tests for non-streaming + streaming completions and the models list, with the completion service faked (pattern: packages/server/test/generate.test.ts).
- A route model that resolves to a plan-backed leaf completes through the fork's own provider wiring (the case the standalone proxy could never serve).

## Door

## Hard constraint (§9.4 — read before scheduling work)
The hosted CommandCode API rejects the current plan; the CLI is the ONLY working route. Backend retirement for this door is blocked on a plan/API change, not on façade work. This issue is therefore FRONT-only: callers repoint to the façade for shape/selection, while the provider backend continues to reach the CLI — explicitly, not by accident. (Note: Command Code is currently DISABLED in the deployed fleet config by Drew, 2026-10-31 — verify live state before assuming any caller exists.)

## Work

2. Parity: chat non-stream + stream against door vs façade, including the ACP-session history behaviour — callers relying on resident-thread history must send full history or use responses chains (§9.2 documented change).
3. Repoint front callers; live-verify; close the front only if the backend face is re-homed explicitly (façade → provider → CLI path named in this issue). If the provider remains disabled fleet-wide, record that the door's remaining value is the disabled provider's backend and schedule accordingly — do not strand it silently.

## Acceptance criteria

title: fix(providers): cloudflare-ai-gateway credential fails upstream auth (code 10000), blocking clef classifications
body:
## Defect

Every Clef classification request currently fails at the Cloudflare upstream with an authentication error, on BOTH the (now retired) standalone door and the server facade — the failure is in the shared credential, not in either front.

Live evidence (2026-11-04, after the #1627 facade redeploy): the recorded clef classifier probe (the exact body in `packages/core/test/facade-parity.test.ts`) sent to `POST http://127.0.0.1:13420/v1/systemone` on the deployed +63c50ee server and to the then-still-running door at `:18742` returned **byte-identical** responses:

```
HTTP 401
{"error":"Cloudflare Workers AI Clef execution failed","details":{"result":null,"success":false,"errors":[{"code":10000,"message":"Authentication error"}],"messages":[]}}
```

The facade side ledgered the attempt (`route_attempt` id 232756, provider `cloudflare-ai-gateway`, model `@cf/cloudflare/clef-flash`, session_id NULL, outcome failure). The same envelope was already observed in the #1638 scratch proof, so the condition predates the facade migration; the migration is behaviour-preserving through it (parity proven), but no classification can complete until the credential is repaired.

## Scope

- Identify which credential the `cloudflare-ai-gateway` route presents upstream (server credential store entry + the Cloudflare env top-up the wrapper performs) and why Cloudflare rejects it with code 10000 (expired/revoked token, wrong account/gateway pairing, or a token minted for a different surface).
- Repair or re-mint it through the normal credential path (never in repo files), then prove one real classification end-to-end: the recorded probe against the facade returns the typed probability answer shape (cf. the 2026-11-02 live door capture in the parity test) instead of the 401 envelope.
- Note in the fix evidence whether the OpenChamber Jev classifier (the consumer, repointed to the facade under #1410) resumes classifying unaided.

Filed from the #1146 sequence: #1410's repoint + door retirement completed behind this defect; this issue is the remaining blocker for actual classification traffic.

title: codex-proxy follow-up from PR #431: single-source the agy-proxy, clef-proxy and antigravity-ls-proxy ports too
body:
## Finding

PR #431 single-sources the codex-proxy port (18744) and explicitly leaves the same pattern in the sibling proxies as a follow-up — its body and commit message both say: "Follow-up (not in this change): agy-proxy (18743) and clef-proxy have the same two-copies pattern." No issue was ever filed for it (issue searches for `agy-proxy`, `CODEX_PROXY_PORT`, "proxy port" and "codex-proxy" return no tracking issue). This issue files that promised follow-up, and adds a third instance the PR didn't mention.

## Evidence (all on current main, verified 2026-10-20)

- **agy-proxy (18743)** — three copies, identical to the codex case PR #431 fixed:
  - `.opencode/opencode.jsonc:1850`: `"baseURL": "http://127.0.0.1:18743/v1"` (antigravity-agy provider)
  - `home/common/default.nix:483`: `"AGY_PROXY_PORT=18743"` in the agy-proxy systemd user service
  - `bin/agy-proxy.mjs:7`: fallback `process.env.AGY_PROXY_PORT || '18743'`
- **antigravity-ls-proxy (18745)** — same three copies, not mentioned in PR #431:
  - `.opencode/opencode.jsonc:1932`: `"baseURL": "http://127.0.0.1:18745/v1"` (antigravity-ls provider)
  - `home/common/default.nix:529`: `"ANTIGRAVITY_LS_PROXY_PORT=18745"` in the service
  - `bin/antigravity-ls-proxy.mjs:7`: fallback `process.env.ANTIGRAVITY_LS_PROXY_PORT || '18745'`
- **clef-proxy (18742)** — two copies (no opencode.jsonc consumer; its models go through the Cloudflare gateway, so the copies are the service env and the script fallback):
  - `home/common/default.nix:460`: `"CLEF_PROXY_PORT=18742"`
  - `bin/clef-proxy.mjs:7`: fallback `process.env.CLEF_PROXY_PORT || '18742'`

For comparison, the pattern PR #431 removed for codex was: `home/common/default.nix:506` `"CODEX_PROXY_PORT=18744"` + `.opencode/opencode.jsonc:2668` hardcoded baseURL.

## Why it matters

These are the same silent-drift failure PR #431 fixed for codex: change or collide one copy and the provider dies with an error that looks like a network/auth problem. Leaving them untracked guarantees the pattern is rediscovered per-proxy, one incident at a time.

## Acceptance criteria

- Each proxy's port is defined once (in the `home/common/default.nix` let block, alongside `codexProxyPort`) and flows to its systemd service environment, the shell session variables, and — for agy and antigravity-ls — the opencode.jsonc baseURL, following the PR #431 pattern.
- Any `{env:...}` baseURL introduced by this work handles the variable-unset case consistently with however the CODEX_PROXY_PORT unset case is resolved (the scripts' built-in fallbacks and the client config must not be able to disagree).
- A grep for the literal ports `18742`/`18743`/`18745` in `.opencode/opencode.jsonc` and the service `Environment` lists in `home/common/default.nix` returns no remaining hardcoded copies (script fallbacks may keep the literal as the documented default).

title: sync-models user service fails from Nix store layout: resolves opencode config to /nix/.opencode/opencode.jsonc
body:
## Symptom

The `sync-models` systemd **user service** on amd (Framework laptop) fails on every run. Latest journal evidence (2026-10-22 00:44:49 CDT, `journalctl --user -u sync-models`):

```
[sync-models] Discovered 22 models from Antigravity Language Server
[sync-models] Discovering Codex models...
[sync-models] Discovered 9 models from Codex cache
[sync-models] Error: /nix/.opencode/opencode.jsonc does not exist!
sync-models.service: Main process exited, code=exited, status=1/FAILURE
```

Discovery works fine — the failure is purely in resolving the config file the script syncs models into.

## Root cause

`bin/sync-models.mjs` resolves the config relative to its own location:

```js
const ROOT_DIR = path.resolve(import.meta.dirname, '..');
const OPENCODE_CONFIG_PATH = path.join(ROOT_DIR, '.opencode/opencode.jsonc');
```

That assumption holds in a repo checkout (`<repo>/bin` → `<repo>/.opencode/opencode.jsonc`). But the home-manager unit (`home/common/default.nix`, `systemd.user.services.sync-models`) runs the file from the Nix store: `node ${../../bin/sync-models.mjs}` interpolates to a lone store file (`/nix/store/<hash>-sync-models.mjs`), so `import.meta.dirname` is `/nix/store`, `ROOT_DIR` becomes `/nix`, and the script looks for `/nix/.opencode/opencode.jsonc` — which never exists.

(`POLICY_PATH` has the same store-layout problem, but its loader already tolerates a missing file and falls back to empty defaults, so it degrades silently instead of failing.)

## Fix

Resolve the config path in this order:

1. `$OPENCODE_CONFIG_PATH` env override, if set.
2. The repo-local `.opencode/opencode.jsonc` when it exists (in-checkout runs keep today's behavior).
3. The deployed user config `~/.config/opencode/opencode.jsonc` — the file the service actually maintains, and the same file the `opencode-config-normalize` path unit already watches.

## Acceptance

- Installed (store-layout) run no longer dies at the config-exists check; it targets `~/.config/opencode/opencode.jsonc`.
- In-repo run behavior unchanged.
- Verified by a dry-run from a store-like layout (script copied alone into a bare directory) passing the config resolution step.

title: id(ssh): PR #594 never enters the alternate screen during a session — its leave path sends the ENTER sequence and ALT_SCREEN_LEAVE is never used
body:
## Finding

PR #594 (OPEN, head `090c356b52a9e1c852692785cee2d0af3e03eef1`) claims to enter the alternate screen on raw SSH shell start and leave it on every exit path (#545), but the enter sequence is never written to the channel while a session runs, and the leave path sends the **enter** sequence again. #545 is not actually fixed by the PR as written.

## Evidence (`pkgs/id/src/world_ssh.rs` on the PR head)

- `:48-50` defines both sequences:
  - `ALT_SCREEN_ENTER = "\x1b[?1049h"`
  - `ALT_SCREEN_LEAVE = "\x1b[?1049l"`
- `:318-320` stores the **enter** string in the session state: `let alt_screen = if !login.command_mode { Some(ALT_SCREEN_ENTER.to_owned()) } else { None };`
- The only place that stored string is ever written to the channel is `leave_alt_screen()` at `:464-475`, after `run_session` ends:

  ```rust
  let Some(sequence) = self.alt_screen.take() else { return; };
  let text = match self.last_error.take() {
      Some(error) => format!("{sequence}\r\n{error}\r\n"),
      None => sequence,
  };
  let _ = self.handle.data(self.channel, text).await;
  ```

  So at exit the terminal receives `\x1b[?1049h` (enter) — the opposite of leaving — immediately before the channel closes.
- `ALT_SCREEN_LEAVE` has no other reference in the file (grep over the full file at the head SHA, cross-checked via `gh pr diff`, `gh api contents` at the head SHA, and a local checkout). Nothing else in the crate emits `1049` either, so no other code path enters the buffer on the session's behalf.
- The PR's own test (`a_raw_shell_enters_and_leaves_the_alternate_screen`, `:1590`) only waits for the enter bytes to arrive before dropping the channel; it never asserts that the leave sequence (`1049l`) is ever sent, so it cannot catch this.

## Why it matters

- Raw sessions keep repainting into scrollback for the whole session — exactly the #545 complaint.
- On exit the terminal is told to *enter* the alternate screen right before disconnect; the "re-send the last error after leaving, so a refused join stays readable in scrollback" mechanism is prefixed with the enter sequence instead of the leave sequence, so the error lands on the alternate screen and disappears — the opposite of the PR's stated goal.

## Acceptance criteria

- A raw (non-command-mode) session writes `\x1b[?1049h` to the channel before the first session frame.
- Every exit path (normal quit, refused join, errored session) writes `\x1b[?1049l`, and the stored last error, when present, is written *after* the leave sequence.
- `ALT_SCREEN_LEAVE` is actually used (no dead constant), and a test asserts both the enter-at-start and leave-at-exit byte sequences on a live session, not just the enter bytes.
- Command mode still never emits either sequence.

## Verification note (added after filing, same run)

The PR head was built and its own test run in a scratch worktree (`cargo test --features ssh,sandbox --lib world_ssh::tests::a_raw_shell_enters_and_leaves_the_alternate_screen`):

- rustc itself warns: ``constant `ALT_SCREEN_LEAVE` is never used`` (world_ssh.rs:50) and ``constant `INPUT_DROP_NOTICE_BYTES` is never used`` (world_ssh.rs:52) — compiler confirmation that both constants are dead.
- The test **passes in 1.08s** — which is consistent with the bug, not against it: the test password's join is refused (compare `a_wrong_password_is_refused_inside_the_shell`), `run_session` ends, and after `REFUSED_SHELL_DELAY` (exactly 1s) `leave_alt_screen()` fires and sends the stored **enter** sequence plus the error, then closes the channel. The test loop sees the enter bytes — arriving at teardown, from the leave path — and passes. It never observes a leave sequence, and a live, accepted session receives no enter sequence from this code at all (grep over the whole repo at the head SHA finds no other `1049` emitter outside lockfiles/corpus data).

title: id(ssh): PR #594's dropped-input notice can never fire in-session — the shell reads a snapshot taken before the queue exists, and the handler's counter is never read again
body:
## Finding

PR #594 (OPEN, head `090c356b52a9e1c852692785cee2d0af3e03eef1`) claims dropped SSH input is "no longer silent" (#549): the shell should show the viewer a notice before the next frame. As wired, the notice can never fire for drops that happen during a session — the only counter the shell reads is a snapshot taken before the input queue exists, when its value is necessarily 0. Only the `tracing::warn!` log line works.

## Evidence (`pkgs/id/src/world_ssh.rs` on the PR head)

- The russh `data()` handler (`:363-388`) counts refused bytes on the **handler** struct: `self.dropped_input += data.len();` on `TrySendError::Full`. It also early-returns when `self.input` is `None` (`:368-370`), and `self.input` is only set inside `shell_request` — so no drop can ever be counted before the shell opens.
- `shell_request` constructs `SshIo` with a **copy**: `dropped_input: self.dropped_input` (`:344`) — at that moment necessarily 0, per the point above.
- After that, nothing ever updates `SshIo.dropped_input`. `note_dropped_input()` (`:455-460`), called at the top of `send()`, reads only the `SshIo` copy, which stays 0 for the life of the session, so `dropped_input_notice()` always returns `None` and `pending_notice` is never set. Drops that happen under load mid-session increment the handler's counter, which is never read again (grep over the full file at the head SHA: the handler counter is written at `:379`/logged at `:383` and read only at the `:344` snapshot).
- Related dead wiring in the same diff: `INPUT_DROP_NOTICE_BYTES: usize = 1024` (`:52`, "Input bytes dropped before the session tells the viewer about it") is defined and never referenced; `dropped_input_notice()` fires at `bytes > 0` instead, so the intended thresholding was never connected either.

## Why it matters

#549's user-visible half — a viewer whose keystrokes are being refused under load is told so — silently does nothing, while the PR description and its unit test (`dropped_input_notice_counts_and_quiet_zero`, which only exercises the pure formatting helper) make it look delivered. The first sign in production would be the same "my input vanished" reports #549 was filed for.

## Acceptance criteria

- The drop count is shared between the russh handler and the session I/O (e.g. an `Arc<AtomicUsize>` or an equivalent channel), so bytes refused after the shell opens reach the shell.
- A test that actually fills the input queue during a live session (or drives the shared counter the same way the handler does) observes the `[-- input dropped: N bytes ... --]` notice on the channel before the next frame.
- The notice threshold is one coherent rule: either `INPUT_DROP_NOTICE_BYTES` is used as documented or the constant is removed.
- The counter resets only after the notice has actually been handed to the viewer, so drops are neither double-counted nor lost between frames.

title: lab-ops-hub: container validator returns C0 controls, space and DEL verbatim outside the host — fetcher raises InvalidURL on URLs both validators accept (PR #612 residual)
body:
## Problem

PR #612 (fixing #611) made the container validator (`pkgs/lab-ops-hub/container/app.py`, `validate_crawl_url`) strip ASCII tab/LF/CR before judging, so the returned URL no longer carries those three controls. The rest of the C0 range (U+0000–U+0008, U+000B, U+000C, U+000E–U+001F), plus space and DEL, are still returned **verbatim** everywhere outside the host, and the container fetcher then chokes on them:

- WHATWG URL parsing (the Worker's `validateCrawlUrl` in `src/lib.ts`, via `new URL`) **trims** leading/trailing C0-control-or-space from the input and **percent-encodes** C0 controls, space and DEL inside the path/query/fragment. It returns a clean serialized URL.
- The container validator accepts the same spellings (its host checks never see path/query characters, and `urlparse` tolerates the leading forms for judging) but returns the raw string. `_fetch_crawl` hands it to urllib/`http.client`, which raises `InvalidURL` ("URL can't contain control characters") for controls/space/DEL in the request target, or `URLError` ("unknown url type") for a leading C0 the parser doesn't strip — so `do_POST` surfaces a 502 for a URL both validators accepted, instead of the crawl result the Worker path produces.

This is the same judge-vs-fetch family as #611/#577: the validator certifies one string and the fetcher is handed another, unusable one. It is acceptance-side only — no verdict divergence and no SSRF direction: blocked hosts wrapped in these controls are still refused by both validators (verified in the battery below).

## Evidence (reproduced on current main d93f430b, merge of PR #612, 2026-10-22)

Differential battery through both real validators (container `validate_crawl_url` vs Worker `validateCrawlUrl` under Bun): every C0 control U+0000–U+0020 plus U+007F in 9 positions (path mid/end, query mid/end, fragment, leading, trailing, leading-on-private, host-end) = 306 cases, plus tab/CR/LF inserted at every position of 20 base URLs = 2,323 cases. **Verdicts agree on all 2,629 cases** (tab/CR/LF parity from #612 confirmed, including slash-run and split-private forms). The **returned URL** diverges in 216 of the 306 C0 cases, e.g.:

```
'http://example.com/pa\x00th'   container returns 'http://example.com/pa\x00th'   Worker returns 'http://example.com/pa%00th'
'http://example.com/pa th'      container returns 'http://example.com/pa th'      Worker returns 'http://example.com/pa%20th'
'http://example.com/?q=a\x7fb'  container returns 'http://example.com/?q=a\x7fb'  Worker returns 'http://example.com/?q=a%7Fb'
'\x00http://example.com/'       container returns '\x00http://example.com/'       Worker returns 'http://example.com/'
'http://example.com/\x00'       container returns 'http://example.com/\x00'       Worker returns 'http://example.com/'
```

Fetcher consequence, verified with the container's own `_fetch_crawl` against a local HTTP server (host swapped to the test server, control positions preserved):

```
'http://<srv>/pa\x00th'   -> InvalidURL: URL can't contain control characters. '/pa\x00th'
'http://<srv>/pa\x01th'   -> InvalidURL (same)
'http://<srv>/pa th'      -> InvalidURL (same, found ' ')
'http://<srv>/pa\x7fth'   -> InvalidURL (same)
'http://<srv>/?q=a\x00b'  -> InvalidURL (same)
'\x00http://<srv>/'       -> URLError: unknown url type
'\x01http://<srv>/'       -> URLError: unknown url type
'http://<srv>/\x00'       -> InvalidURL (same)
```

(In `do_POST` these exceptions land in the outer handler and become a 502, per #572's plumbing — a crawl failure, not a result.)

Pre-existing returned-URL differences that are **not** part of this finding (both fetch fine): the container returns the original IDN spelling (`http://münchen.de/` vs the Worker's punycode form) and keeps an explicit default port (`:80`), by design in the existing code comments.

## Why it matters

`validate_crawl_url`'s contract is judge-what-you-fetch, and #612 just extended that contract to the full URL string for tab/CR/LF. Any crawl target whose path or query carries a raw control, space or DEL — pasted URLs, redirect `Location`s built from user data (the redirect handler validates through the same function), generated links — is accepted by the container validator and then fails the fetch with a 502, while the Worker fallback fetches the WHATWG-normalized form successfully. The two crawlers disagree on the outcome for a class of otherwise-legitimate public URLs.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] For every input both validators accept, the URL `validate_crawl_url` returns contains no raw C0 control (U+0000–U+001F), space, or DEL outside the host — it is either normalized the way WHATWG serializes it (leading/trailing C0/space trimmed; path/query/fragment controls, space and DEL percent-encoded) or the spelling is refused up front with a clear error. Either resolution is acceptable; silently returning a fetcher-breaking string is not.
- [ ] Verdict parity is preserved: spellings refused today (blocked hosts wrapped in these characters, controls inside the host) stay refused, and no currently-accepted public target changes verdict except as needed for the bullet above.
- [ ] Python tests pin the headline cases (path-mid NUL/space/DEL, query-mid NUL, leading NUL, trailing NUL) against the chosen behavior, and the TS suite pins the Worker's returned form for the same inputs.
- [ ] A differential run over the C0 battery (U+0000–U+0020 + U+007F × path/query/fragment/leading/trailing positions) shows verdict parity and no raw-control returned URLs from the container validator.

title: lab-ops-hub: container validator returns WHATWG-encodable ASCII punctuation verbatim outside the host — path/query/fragment/userinfo " < > ^ ` { } go on the request line raw while the Worker fetches the encoded form
body:
## Summary

The container validator's returned-URL encoder (`_encode_url_component`, `pkgs/lab-ops-hub/container/app.py:663`) claims in its comment to encode "the way WHATWG's URL serializer encodes the userinfo, path, query and fragment components", but it only encodes non-ASCII characters (#615) and C0 controls / space / DEL (#614). The ASCII punctuation in WHATWG's per-component percent-encode sets passes through verbatim, so for URLs both validators accept, the container fetches a different (raw) spelling than the Worker fetches (its encoded form).

## Evidence (verified 2026-10-22, current main 23eefe17)

`validate_crawl_url` (Python) vs `new URL(...).toString()` (the Worker's serializer, Node 24):

| Input | Container returns | Worker returns |
|---|---|---|
| `http://example.com/a"b` | `http://example.com/a"b` | `http://example.com/a%22b` |
| `http://example.com/a<b>c` | `http://example.com/a<b>c` | `http://example.com/a%3Cb%3Ec` |
| `http://example.com/a` + backtick + `b` | raw backtick | `a%60b` |
| `http://example.com/a{b}c` | `http://example.com/a{b}c` | `http://example.com/a%7Bb%7Dc` |
| `http://example.com/a^b` | `http://example.com/a^b` | `http://example.com/a%5Eb` |
| `http://example.com/?q=a"b<c` | raw | `?q=a%22b%3Cc` |
| `http://example.com/#a"b<c>` + backtick + `d` | raw | `#a%22b%3Cc%3E%60d` |
| `http://us"er@example.com/` | `http://us"er@example.com/` | `http://us%22er@example.com/` |

A per-character probe of the WHATWG serializer gives the exact sets (on top of the already-encoded non-ASCII / C0 / space / DEL):

- **path**: `"` `<` `>` `^` `` ` `` `{` `}`
- **query**: `"` `<` `>` (note: backtick, `^`, `{`, `}` stay raw in query)
- **fragment**: `"` `<` `>` `` ` ``
- **userinfo**: `"` `;` `<` `=` `>` `@` `[` `]` `^` `` ` `` `{` `|` `}` (the delimiter characters `/ : ? # \` never survive urlparse into the userinfo, so they need no arm)

The sets are per-component: a single shared set would over-encode the query (e.g. a raw backtick in a query is exactly what the Worker fetches) and under-encode the userinfo.

## Why it matters

- The URL `validate_crawl_url` returns is the URL the fetcher fetches (`container/app.py:785`, `urllib.request.Request`). Raw `"`, `<`, `>` etc. go onto the request line unencoded: `http.client` only rejects C0/space/DEL (`_contains_disallowed_url_pchar_re`), so these sail through to the origin, where servers and intermediaries commonly reject a raw `"`/`<`/`>` in the request target with 400 — or parse it differently — while the Worker fetches the encoded form of the same validated URL successfully. Same validated target, different crawl outcome per backend: the #614/#615 divergence class, one character class later.
- The comment on `_encode_url_component` overstates what the function does, which is how this residual stayed invisible through two fixes in this exact spot.

## Acceptance criteria

- `_url_with_encoded_components` percent-encodes the per-component WHATWG sets above in userinfo, path, query and fragment, in addition to the existing non-ASCII / C0 / space / DEL encoding; existing `%XX` sequences are never double-encoded.
- The query component is NOT encoded with the path set (backtick / `^` / `{` / `}` in a query stay raw, matching the Worker byte-for-byte).
- New tests in `test/test_container_validate.py` pin the table above (path, query, fragment, userinfo arms), and the existing differential/parity tests still pass.
- Python suite (`test_container_validate.py`) and TS suite (`lib.test.ts`) both green.

## Suggested fix

Give `_encode_url_component` a per-component extra-set parameter (path / query / fragment / userinfo sets as probed above) and pass the matching set from each call site in `_url_with_encoded_components`; update the function's comment to name the sets it implements.

title: lab-ops-hub: container validator's #577 backslash normalization overreaches into query and fragment — WHATWG keeps \ as data there, so ?q=a\b is fetched as ?q=a/b
body:
## Summary

The container validator's backslash normalization (#577, `pkgs/lab-ops-hub/container/app.py` in `validate_crawl_url`) replaces **every** `\` in the whole input with `/` for http/https URLs. WHATWG treats a backslash as a path delimiter only in the scheme/authority/path portion of a special-scheme URL — in the **query** and **fragment** it is ordinary data and is kept verbatim. The container therefore judges and returns a different URL than the Worker for any spelling with a backslash after the `?` or `#`.

## Evidence (verified 2026-10-22, current main)

`validate_crawl_url` (Python) vs `new URL(...).toString()` (the Worker's serializer):

| Input | Container returns | Worker returns |
|---|---|---|
| `http://example.com/?q=a\b` | `http://example.com/?q=a/b` | `http://example.com/?q=a\b` |
| `http://example.com/#a\b` | `http://example.com/#a/b` | `http://example.com/#a\b` |
| `https://example.com/?q=a\b\c#x\y` | `https://example.com/?q=a/b/c#x/y` | `https://example.com/?q=a\b\c#x\y` |
| `http://example.com/a\b` | `http://example.com/a/b` | `http://example.com/a/b` (path arm agrees — control) |

Found by the 470-case ASCII differential run for #618; this was the only remaining returned-URL mismatch class outside structural-delimiter spellings.

## Why it matters

- The query is sent to the origin: `?q=a\b` and `?q=a/b` are different queries and can name different resources (search terms, signed parameters, Windows-style path parameters). The container crawls a URL the Worker would not, for a target both validators accepted — the same judged-vs-fetched divergence class as #577 itself, in the opposite direction: #577's fix overreaches past the components where the backslash is structural.
- The fragment arm changes the returned/recorded URL identity even though fragments are not fetched.

## Acceptance criteria

- The `\` → `/` replacement applies only up to the first `?` or `#` (the scheme/authority/path portion); backslashes in the query and fragment pass through verbatim, matching the Worker byte-for-byte.
- The #577 authority spellings still normalize and are still judged on the normalized host (`http://127.0.0.1\@example.com/` refused as loopback, `http://example.com\@127.0.0.1/` judged as example.com), and the existing backslash tests pass unchanged.
- New tests pin the query and fragment spellings in the table above.
- Python suite (`test_container_validate.py`) and TS suite (`lib.test.ts`) both green.

## Suggested fix

Split the input at the first `?`/`#` before the replacement and rejoin afterwards — or scope the existing `raw.replace("\\", "/")` to the head segment — taking care that a `\` inside the authority is still replaced even when a `?` appears later in the same spelling (it does: the head segment includes the full authority and path).

title: lab-ops-hub: container fetcher cannot fetch any URL with userinfo — urllib resolves 'user@host' as the hostname, so every userinfo target both validators accept 502s in the container (PR #616/#619 residual)
body:
## Finding

The container crawler cannot fetch **any** URL that carries userinfo — not just the non-ASCII or punctuation spellings PRs #616/#619 fixed the encoding for, but plain ASCII `http://user@example.com/` and `http://user:pass@example.com/`.

Both validators accept userinfo targets and `validate_crawl_url` now carefully percent-encodes the userinfo on the returned URL (#615/#618). But `_fetch_crawl` (`pkgs/lab-ops-hub/container/app.py`, `def _fetch_crawl` ~line 827) hands that returned URL straight to `urllib.request`. urllib never strips userinfo from the netloc: `Request.host` keeps the whole `user@host` / `user:pass@host` string, `http.client` is constructed with it as the hostname, and `getaddrinfo` fails on it. The result is a `URLError` before any request is sent, `do_POST` surfaces it as a 502, and the Worker fallback — whose WHATWG `fetch` converts userinfo to an `Authorization: Basic` header and fetches the target fine — crawls it instead. This is the same accept/502/fallback divergence class as #572/#615/#614/#618, except it covers the entire userinfo component rather than one character set.

## Evidence

- PR #616 (commit `3201b886`, fixes #615) encoded non-ASCII in the userinfo on the returned URL so "the URL the fetcher fetches" would work; its fetcher end-to-end test (`test_fetches_percent_encoded_non_ascii_targets`) covers only a path/query spelling — no fetcher test in #616, #617 or #619 ever fetches a userinfo URL.
- PR #619 (commit `fea31bbe`, fixes #618) extended the userinfo encoding (`_encode_userinfo`, ~line 724; `_url_with_encoded_components`, ~line 739) and pinned the returned forms in `test_ascii_punctuation_percent_encoded_per_component` — again validation-only, no fetch of a userinfo target.
- Reproduced on current main `07a16b76` with the app's own `_fetch_crawl` against a local HTTP server (proxy env unset), on both Python 3.12.3 and Python 3.13.14 (the container image uses nixpkgs `pkgs.python3`):
  - control `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/x` → 200, request received, no `Authorization` header.
  - `http://user@127.0.0.1:<port>/x` → `URLError: <urlopen error [Errno -2] Name or service not known>`; no request reaches the server.
  - `http://user:pa%3Ass@127.0.0.1:<port>/x` (the #619 returned form) → same `URLError`.
  - `http://caf%C3%A9@127.0.0.1:<port>/x` (the #615 returned form) → same `URLError`.
- `validate_crawl_url` on the same main returns `http://user@example.com/`, `http://user:pass@example.com/` and `http://caf%C3%A9@example.com/` as accepted crawl targets, and the Worker validator (`src/lib.ts` `validateCrawlUrl`, run under Bun) accepts the same spellings — so both validators agree the target is crawlable while the container fetcher can never fetch it.
- Related returned-form detail from the same differential (517-case battery, container validator vs Node `new URL`): for an empty password (`http://user:@example.com/`) the Worker returns `http://user@example.com/` and for a bare `@` (`http://@example.com/`) it returns `http://example.com/`, while the container returns both spellings verbatim. A fetcher fix that strips userinfo and only sends credentials that are actually present resolves these too; they are noted here, not filed separately.

## Why it matters

Any crawl target with credentials in the URL — a documented, validator-accepted spelling the last three PRs in this area explicitly polished — silently fails in the container and is re-crawled by the Worker fallback, recording the wrong source and masking the failure as a generic 502. The encoding work in #616/#619 cannot take effect for the userinfo component until the fetcher can fetch a userinfo URL at all.

## Acceptance criteria

- `_fetch_crawl` successfully fetches a validated URL with userinfo (plain, password-bearing, and percent-encoded forms) end-to-end against a local test server, sending the credentials as an `Authorization: Basic` header built from the percent-decoded username/password, matching WHATWG `fetch` behaviour; no credentials header is sent when the userinfo is empty (`http://@host/`).
- Redirect targets carrying userinfo (validated by `_ValidatingRedirectHandler`) fetch the same way.
- New fetcher tests cover userinfo spellings end-to-end (mirroring the existing path/query fetcher tests for #615/#614), and ablation shows they fail on the pre-fix fetcher.
- A container-vs-Worker differential over userinfo spellings (plain ASCII, non-ASCII, ASCII punctuation, empty user/password) shows the container fetching the same target the Worker fetches, with the existing Python (47) and TS suites still passing.

title: lab-ops-hub: container validator returns dot segments, host case and default ports un-normalized — fetcher requests a different path than the Worker
body:
## Finding

The container validator returns the crawl target without the WHATWG
normalizations the Worker validator applies, so for the same accepted
target the two crawlers record — and fetch — different URLs:

1. **Dot segments are never resolved.** Literal `.` / `..` segments and
   their percent-encoded spellings (`%2e`, `.%2e`, `%2e.`, `%2e%2e`, any
   case) are returned verbatim by the container and sent verbatim on the
   wire by its fetcher. The Worker resolves them per the WHATWG URL path
   rules before fetching.
2. **Host case is preserved.** The Worker lowercases the host in the
   returned URL; the container returns `EXAMPLE.COM` as spelled.
3. **Default ports are preserved**, including leading-zero spellings:
   the Worker drops `:80` / `:443` (and `:080` / `:0080`); the container
   returns them verbatim.

`validate_crawl_url` (`pkgs/lab-ops-hub/container/app.py:77`, returns at
:399 and :439) returns `_url_with_encoded_components(raw …)` — the raw
spelling with only the character-encoding fixes of #614/#615/#618. No
step resolves path segments, lowercases the host, or drops a default
port. The Worker validator (`pkgs/lab-ops-hub/src/lib.ts:130`) returns
`u.toString()` (:182, :188), the fully WHATWG-normalized form.

## Evidence

Verified this run on main `00bb59d5` (lab-ops-hub at `07a16b76`),
driving both real validators (Python `validate_crawl_url`; Worker's
`validateCrawlUrl` under Bun):

| Input | Container returns | Worker returns |
|---|---|---|
| `http://example.com/a/../b` | `http://example.com/a/../b` | `http://example.com/b` |
| `http://example.com/a/./b` | `http://example.com/a/./b` | `http://example.com/a/b` |
| `http://example.com/%2e%2e/admin` | `http://example.com/%2e%2e/admin` | `http://example.com/admin` |
| `http://example.com/a/%2e%2e/b` | `http://example.com/a/%2e%2e/b` | `http://example.com/b` |
| `http://example.com/%2e/%2e/x` | `http://example.com/%2e/%2e/x` | `http://example.com/x` |
| `http://example.com/a/%2E/b` | `http://example.com/a/%2E/b` | `http://example.com/a/b` |
| `HTTP://EXAMPLE.COM/Path` | `http://EXAMPLE.COM/Path` | `http://example.com/Path` |
| `http://example.com:80/x` | `http://example.com:80/x` | `http://example.com/x` |
| `https://example.com:443/x` | `https://example.com:443/x` | `https://example.com/x` |
| `http://example.com:080/x` | `http://example.com:080/x` | `http://example.com/x` |
| `http://user:pass@EXAMPLE.com:80/` | `http://user:pass@EXAMPLE.com:80/` | `http://user:pass@example.com/` |

Fetcher consequence, reproduced with the app's own `_fetch_crawl`
(`app.py:827`) against a local HTTP server (proxy env unset): for
`http://127.0.0.1:<port>/a/../b` the server receives the request target
`/a/../b` verbatim, and for `/%2e%2e/admin` it receives `/%2e%2e/admin`
verbatim. The Worker's WHATWG `fetch` requests `/b` and `/admin`. An
origin (or any proxy/WAF in front of it) that routes on the raw request
target therefore serves the container a different resource than the
Worker for the same validated target, and `%2e%2e` spellings are the
classic path-confusion form when one layer resolves them and another
does not. Redirect targets inherit the divergence: the container's
`_ValidatingRedirectHandler` validates the raw `Location` value and
fetches the container's returned form.

Verdicts agree throughout (every spelling above is accepted by both
validators, and blocked-host controls — `LOCALHOST`, `127.0.0.1:080` —
are refused by both): this is a fetched-URL identity divergence, not an
accept/refuse one. Minor opposite-direction note from the same battery:
empty query/fragment markers — the Worker keeps a trailing `?` / `#`
(`http://example.com/x?`), the container drops them; folding that into
the same normalization pass settles it either way.

Dedup: searches for "dot segment", "default port", "lowercase host"
and "%2e" return no issue covering this; the closed #614/#615/#618
series covers character *encoding* on the returned URL only. The
validator pair exists only in this repo (grep of the
opencode/openchamber/nix clones is empty).

## Why it matters

The container and the Worker fallback are supposed to crawl the same
target; the last several fixes in this area (#577/#586/#611/#614/#615/
#618) each aligned one piece of the returned URL so "the URL the
fetcher fetches" is the URL the Worker fetches. Path identity is the
remaining piece: today a target spelled with dot segments — including
the percent-encoded traversal spelling — is fetched as two different
paths depending on which crawler serves it, so crawl results (status,
body, recorded URL) differ by crawler for reasons invisible to callers.

## Acceptance criteria

- `validate_crawl_url` returns the WHATWG-normalized form for the
  battery above: dot segments (literal and `%2e` spellings, any case,
  including a trailing dot segment's trailing-slash semantics) resolved,
  host lowercased, and the scheme's default port dropped (including
  leading-zero spellings); non-default ports, empty path segments
  (`//`), query and fragment are preserved as WHATWG preserves them.
- A fetcher end-to-end test shows the container requesting the resolved
  path (`/b`, `/admin`) for dot-segment targets, matching the Worker.
- A container-vs-Worker differential over the battery (plus the
  existing validator batteries) shows byte-identical returned URLs,
  with the existing Python and TS suites still passing.
- Care with ordering: normalization must not double-decode
  percent-encodings the #529/#615/#618 steps produced (e.g. a literal
  `%252e` segment is data, not a dot segment).

title: lab-ops-hub: container validator returns IP literals un-canonicalized — inet_aton spellings and expanded IPv6 kept verbatim, Worker returns the canonical address
body:
## Finding

The container validator judges IP-literal hosts correctly (the
inet_aton spellings of private addresses are refused, #468/#502), but
it returns accepted IP literals in the spelling the caller typed,
while the Worker validator returns the canonical form. For the same
accepted target the two crawlers therefore record — and hand to their
fetchers and logs — different URL strings:

- IPv4 short / integer / hex / octal spellings are returned verbatim:
  `1.2.3`, `1.2.256`, `134744072`, `0x8080808`, `010.0.0.010`,
  `8.8.2056`, `8.16777215`, `1.2.3.04`, `0x8.0x8.0x8.0x8`.
- IPv6 literals are returned un-compressed and un-lowercased:
  `[2001:4860:4860:0000:0000:0000:0000:8888]`.

`validate_crawl_url` (`pkgs/lab-ops-hub/container/app.py:78`) parses
the literal for judging (`ipaddress.ip_address` / `_inet_aton_ipv4`,
app.py:364-366) but its success returns (app.py:440-442, and the
DNS-name return at :400-402) hand back
`_url_with_encoded_components(raw)` — the raw spelling — unless the
host was percent-decoded. The Worker validator
(`pkgs/lab-ops-hub/src/lib.ts:130`) returns `u.toString()`, the
WHATWG-canonical form (canonical dotted quad; compressed lowercase
IPv6).

This is the IP-literal remainder of the returned-form divergence:
#633 covers dot segments, host case and default ports in the returned
URL, but not the IP-literal spellings themselves; #468/#502 fixed
which addresses are *judged* private, not the form that is returned.

## Evidence

Verified this run on main `5a84351c`, driving both real validators
(Python `validate_crawl_url`; Worker's `validateCrawlUrl` under Bun).
Allow/refuse agreed on every probe (all private inet_aton spellings
refused by both); only the returned form differs:

| Input | Container returns | Worker returns |
|---|---|---|
| `http://1.2.3/` | `http://1.2.3/` | `http://1.2.0.3/` |
| `http://1.2.256/` | `http://1.2.256/` | `http://1.2.1.0/` |
| `http://134744072/` | `http://134744072/` | `http://8.8.8.8/` |
| `http://0x8080808/` | `http://0x8080808/` | `http://8.8.8.8/` |
| `http://010.0.0.010/` | `http://010.0.0.010/` | `http://8.0.0.8/` |
| `http://8.8.2056/` | `http://8.8.2056/` | `http://8.8.8.8/` |
| `http://8.16777215/` | `http://8.16777215/` | `http://8.255.255.255/` |
| `http://1.2.3.04/` | `http://1.2.3.04/` | `http://1.2.3.4/` |
| `http://0x8.0x8.0x8.0x8/` | `http://0x8.0x8.0x8.0x8/` | `http://8.8.8.8/` |
| `http://[2001:4860:4860:0000:0000:0000:0000:8888]/` | verbatim | `http://[2001:4860:4860::8888]/` |

Fetcher-side, the container's resolver does reach the same address
(`socket.getaddrinfo`: `1.2.256` → `1.2.1.0`, `134744072` → `8.8.8.8`,
`8.8.2056` → `8.8.8.8`), so this is not an SSRF bypass. The harm is
the standing one for this validator pair: the judged, recorded and
fetched spellings diverge between the two crawlers. Anything keyed on
the URL string (crawl history, dedup, audit logs, a downstream
consumer that parses the returned URL with a strict dotted-quad
parser instead of inet_aton semantics) sees `134744072` where the
Worker recorded `8.8.8.8` — a host string that was never the judged
canonical address.

## Suggested fix

In the IP-literal success path of `validate_crawl_url`, return the
URL with the host replaced by the canonical form of the address that
was judged — `str(ip)` for IPv4, `[compressed-lowercase]` for IPv6 —
via the existing `_url_with_host` helper (app.py:674), the same way
the percent-decoded path already substitutes the judged host.
DNS-name returns are out of scope (host case there is #633).

## Acceptance criteria

- For every accepted IP-literal input, the container validator
  returns the same URL string as the Worker's `validateCrawlUrl`,
  including the table above.
- Allow/refuse verdicts are unchanged on the full existing probe
  corpus (private inet_aton spellings still refused).
- New cases in `pkgs/lab-ops-hub/test/test_container_validate.py`
  pin the canonical returns; the Python suite passes and the TS
  suite is untouched.

title: lab-ops-hub: container validator returns empty path, empty port and empty userinfo un-normalized — recorded URL differs from the Worker
body:
## Finding

The container validator returns three spellings without the WHATWG normalizations the Worker validator applies, so for the same accepted target the two crawlers record different URLs:

1. **Empty path gets no `/`.** `http://example.com` and `http://example.com:8080` are returned with an empty path; the Worker returns `http://example.com/` / `http://example.com:8080/`.
2. **An empty port keeps its colon.** `http://example.com:/path` is returned verbatim; the Worker drops the empty port and returns `http://example.com/path`.
3. **An empty userinfo keeps its `@`.** `http://@example.com/` is returned verbatim; the Worker serialises the empty userinfo away and returns `http://example.com/`. (The fetcher already treats a bare `@` as carrying no credentials — `_split_userinfo`, `app.py` — so this arm is purely about the returned/recorded form.)

`validate_crawl_url` (`pkgs/lab-ops-hub/container/app.py`) returns `_url_with_encoded_components(raw …)` — the caller's spelling with only the character-encoding fixes. No step supplies the `/` for an empty path, drops an empty port, or drops an empty userinfo. The Worker validator (`pkgs/lab-ops-hub/src/lib.ts:130`) returns `u.toString()`, the fully WHATWG-normalised form. `urlparse(...).geturl()` also drops empty `?`/`#` markers the Worker preserves (`http://example.com/path?` → container `…/path`, Worker `…/path?`) — same root cause, lower stakes; fixing it is optional but should be decided explicitly.

This is distinct from #633 (dot segments, host case, default ports): an empty port is not a default port, and none of #633's three arms touches the empty path or empty userinfo.

## Evidence

Verified this run on current main, driving both real validators (Python `validate_crawl_url`; Worker's `validateCrawlUrl` under Bun):

| Input | Container returns | Worker returns |
|---|---|---|
| `http://example.com` | `http://example.com` | `http://example.com/` |
| `https://example.com` | `https://example.com` | `https://example.com/` |
| `http://example.com:8080` | `http://example.com:8080` | `http://example.com:8080/` |
| `http://example.com:/path` | `http://example.com:/path` | `http://example.com/path` |
| `http://@example.com/` | `http://@example.com/` | `http://example.com/` |
| `http://example.com/path?` | `http://example.com/path` | `http://example.com/path?` |
| `http://example.com/path#` | `http://example.com/path` | `http://example.com/path#` |

Controls that already agree: `//double//slash`, `%41%42`, `%zz`, `:0/`, `;params`, non-empty userinfo.

## Why it matters

The validated URL is the crawl record: the two crawlers keying the same target under different spellings (`http://example.com` vs `http://example.com/`) defeats cross-crawler dedup/comparison, and an empty-port colon is a spelling no other URL parser in the pipeline produces.

## Acceptance criteria

- `validate_crawl_url` returns the WHATWG form for the cases above: `/` supplied for an empty path, empty port colon dropped, empty userinfo `@` dropped.
- A differential test against the Worker validator covers these spellings (plus a decision, recorded in the test or PR, on the empty `?`/`#` markers).
- Existing container validator tests stay green; no change to which targets are accepted or refused.

title: lab-ops-hub: container validator drops the DNS root dot only for the percent-encoded spelling — returned URL differs from the Worker and from its own literal-dot form
body:
## Finding

For a host with a trailing DNS root dot, the container validator returns a different URL depending on how the dot was spelled, and the percent-encoded spelling disagrees with the Worker validator:

| Input | Container returns | Worker returns |
|---|---|---|
| `http://example.com./` | `http://example.com./` | `http://example.com./` |
| `http://example.com./path` | `http://example.com./path` | `http://example.com./path` |
| `http://example.com%2e/` | `http://example.com/` | `http://example.com./` |
| `http://example.com%2E/` | `http://example.com/` | `http://example.com./` |
| `http://sub.example.com%2e/` | `http://sub.example.com/` | `http://sub.example.com./` |
| `http://example.com%2e/path` | `http://example.com/path` | `http://example.com./path` |

Verified this run on current main (e810ca8d), driving both real validators: Python `validate_crawl_url` (`pkgs/lab-ops-hub/container/app.py`) and the Worker `validateCrawlUrl` (`pkgs/lab-ops-hub/src/lib.ts`) under Bun. Acceptance agrees everywhere probed (both refuse `http://localhost%2e/`, both accept the public forms) — only the returned/recorded form diverges.

## Root cause

`container/app.py:250-251` strips a single trailing root dot from the judged host (`host = host[:-1]`, #466) — correct for judging. But the percent-decoded return path (`container/app.py`, the `_url_with_host(u, host) if percent_decoded else raw` call in `validate_crawl_url`, ~line 402) rebuilds the returned URL from that stripped host, so the dot is lost. The literal-dot spelling takes the `raw` path and keeps its dot. The Worker strips the dot only for its checks (`src/lib.ts:145-146`) but returns `u.toString()`, and WHATWG host parsing decodes `%2e` to `.` and serialises the root dot back — so the Worker returns the dotted form for both spellings.

## Why it matters

The validated URL is the crawl record and the fetched URL: the same target is recorded as `http://example.com/` by the container (percent-encoded input) but `http://example.com./` by the Worker and by the container itself (literal input), defeating cross-crawler dedup/comparison for root-dot spellings — the same class of divergence #633/#639 addressed for dot segments, ports and empty components. (Fetching is unaffected in practice: a root-dot host resolves identically.)

## Acceptance criteria

- One canonical returned form for the root-dot host, identical for the literal and percent-encoded spellings and matching the Worker (or the Worker changed too, with the decision recorded — the two validators must agree).
- A differential test against the Worker validator covers `example.com.`, `example.com%2e`, `example.com%2E` and a subdomain form, with and without a path.
- No change to which targets are accepted or refused (`localhost%2e` stays refused, `example.com..` stays refused); existing container and Worker validator tests stay green.

## Suggested fix

In the percent-decoded return path, re-attach the root dot that judging stripped (track whether the decoded host ended in `.` before the strip at app.py:250 and append it to the host passed to `_url_with_host`), or record the pre-strip decoded host for the return form while judging the stripped one.

title: lab-ops-hub: container validator keeps the password colon when the password is empty (user:@ / :@) — returned URL differs from the Worker
body:
## Problem

The container validator (`pkgs/lab-ops-hub/container/app.py`, `validate_crawl_url`) returns a URL whose userinfo keeps the password colon when the password is empty, while the Worker validator (`pkgs/lab-ops-hub/src/lib.ts`, WHATWG `URL`) serialises that colon away:

| Input | Container returns | Worker returns |
|---|---|---|
| `http://user:@example.com/` | `http://user:@example.com/` | `http://user@example.com/` |
| `http://:@example.com/` | `http://:@example.com/` | `http://example.com/` |
| `http://:@example.com:80/` | `http://:@example.com/` | `http://example.com/` |

Verified this run on main `93065f0d` by driving both real validators over a 357-URL differential matrix plus a focused 23-URL probe; these were the only userinfo divergences. Controls that already agree and must not change: `http://:pass@example.com/` (kept), `http://::@example.com/` -> `http://:%3A@example.com/` (the colon is password *data*), `http://user::@example.com/` -> `http://user:%3A@example.com/`, `http://user:pass@example.com/` (kept), and the bare empty userinfo `http://@example.com/` (already dropped, #639).

## Root cause

WHATWG serialises userinfo from the parsed username/password: the `:` separator is emitted only when the password is non-empty, and the whole `@` is dropped when both are empty. The container instead round-trips the raw userinfo string:

- `_encode_userinfo` (app.py ~line 895) re-adds `":"` whenever a separator was present in the raw spelling (`if sep:`), regardless of whether the password is empty.
- `_url_with_encoded_components` (app.py ~line 909) decides whether to keep the `@` on the *raw* userinfo's truthiness (`if userinfo`), so `":"` — a non-empty string with two empty components — survives as `:@` even once the encoded form is empty.
- `_normalize_validated_url` has the same raw-truthiness shape, though the final encoded-components rebuild is what reaches the caller.

#639 fixed exactly this class for the *empty userinfo* spelling (`@` with nothing before it) but missed the colon-bearing spellings, because `:` and `user:` are non-empty strings.

## Why it matters

The URL `validate_crawl_url` returns is the URL that is recorded and fetched (the module's standing #633/#639 contract: both crawlers record — and fetch — the same URL for the same target). Fetch *behaviour* already agrees — `_split_userinfo` (app.py ~line 979) treats `:@` as carrying no credentials and `user:@` exactly as `user@` — so this is a returned-form divergence only: the same crawl target is recorded under two different URL strings depending on which crawler ran, defeating dedup/logging comparisons between the container and Worker paths.

## Acceptance criteria

- `validate_crawl_url("http://user:@example.com/")` returns `http://user@example.com/` and `validate_crawl_url("http://:@example.com/")` returns `http://example.com/`, matching the Worker byte for byte (including with a default/non-default port present).
- The controls above are unchanged: `:pass@`, `::@` -> `:%3A@`, `user::@` -> `user:%3A@`, `user:pass@`, and bare `@`.
- New cases in `pkgs/lab-ops-hub/test/test_container_validate.py` pin the returned form for the empty-password spellings (the existing tests assert acceptance only); Python suite and the TS suite (`test/lib.test.ts`) pass.
- A differential run of both validators over userinfo spellings shows no remaining userinfo divergences.
