title: lab-ops-hub: container validator returns UTS-46 ignored codepoints in the host it judged without them — returned URL differs from the Worker, and U+180E cannot be IDNA-encoded at fetch time
body:
## Problem

The container validator (`pkgs/lab-ops-hub/container/app.py`, `validate_crawl_url`) judges a host in its UTS-46-mapped form — the `_UTS46_IGNORED` codepoints (app.py lines 55-58: U+00AD, U+034F, U+180E, U+200B, U+FEFF, U+2060-U+2064, ...) are deleted before the checks (line 221, #526) — but it returns the *raw* host spelling with those codepoints still in it. The Worker validator (`pkgs/lab-ops-hub/src/lib.ts`) returns the host with them deleted, because WHATWG domain-to-ASCII deletes them in `u.hostname` itself:

| Input host | Container returns | Worker returns |
|---|---|---|
| `http://exa\u200bmple.com/` (U+200B) | `http://exa\u200bmple.com/` | `http://example.com/` |
| `http://exa\u00admple.com/` (U+00AD) | raw soft hyphen kept | `http://example.com/` |
| `http://exa\u180emple.com/` (U+180E) | raw U+180E kept | `http://example.com/` |
| `http://exa\u2060mple.com/` (U+2060) | raw U+2060 kept | `http://example.com/` |
| `http://exa\ufeffmple.com/` (U+FEFF) | raw U+FEFF kept | `http://example.com/` |
| `http://example.com\u200b/` (trailing label) | raw U+200B kept | `http://example.com/` |

Verified this run on main `93065f0d` by driving both real validators over a focused probe set. Acceptance/refusal verdicts agree everywhere (blocked spellings stay blocked: `http://local\u200bhost/` and `http://127\u200b.0.0.1/` are refused by both, judged on the mapped form). Only the returned form diverges. The existing test (test_container_validate.py ~line 669) pins only that these hosts are *accepted* — it never asserts the returned string.

## Why it matters

1. **Recorded-URL divergence** — the standing #633/#639 contract is that both crawlers record and fetch the same URL for the same target; here the container records a host string the Worker never produces.
2. **One arm can fail at fetch time.** The fetcher resolves the returned host via IDNA. Python's own IDNA codec maps most of these codepoints away (`"exa\u200bmple.com".encode("idna") == b"example.com"`, likewise U+00AD/U+2060/U+FEFF), so those spellings happen to fetch the judged host — but it refuses U+180E outright: `"exa\u180emple.com".encode("idna")` raises `UnicodeError: Invalid character '\u180e'`. So a target both validators accept, and the Worker fetches as `example.com`, carries a returned host the container's IDNA resolution path cannot encode. (Probed directly against the codec this run; the exact fetch-time failure mode — resolver error vs 502 — is for the fixer to confirm end-to-end.)

## Why this is filed-only (design note for the fixer)

The obvious fix — return the mapped host — is *not* a free choice here: `_url_with_encoded_components` deliberately leaves the host untouched ("judged in mapped form, fetched via IDNA", #615), because for ordinary IDN hosts the raw spelling is the intended fetch form (e.g. `münchen.de` is fetched as the Unicode spelling and encoded by the resolver). The ignored-codepoint case is narrower — the mapped form differs from the raw form *only by deletion of codepoints that are never part of any label* — but the fixer should decide explicitly whether to:

- (a) delete exactly the `_UTS46_IGNORED` codepoints from the returned host (leaving every other IDN spelling untouched), or
- (b) return the fully mapped host whenever the mapping changed anything, and revisit #615's rationale, or
- (c) refuse U+180E-class spellings the local IDNA codec cannot encode, documenting the Worker divergence.

Option (a) looks smallest and matches the Worker byte for byte on every probed spelling, but the choice interacts with open #588 (UTS-46 label validity) and should be made once, not by accident.

## Acceptance criteria

- For every codepoint in `_UTS46_IGNORED`, `validate_crawl_url` on a public host containing it returns the same URL string the Worker returns (host with the codepoint deleted), OR the issue is closed with a documented, tested decision for option (c) above.
- Blocked-host judgement is unchanged: `local\u200bhost`, `127\u200b.0.0.1` and friends stay refused; ordinary IDN hosts (`münchen.de`, `ｅｘａｍｐｌｅ.com`) return exactly what they return today.
- Tests in `test_container_validate.py` pin the *returned form* (not just acceptance) for the ignored-codepoint hosts, including U+180E; Python and TS suites pass.
- A differential run of both validators over ignored-codepoint spellings (interior and trailing, single and multiple labels) shows no remaining divergences in verdict or returned form.

title: lab-ops-hub: container validator appends the empty-query marker after the fragment — path?#frag returns as path#frag?, differing from the Worker
body:
## Finding

PR #648 (https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/648, commit `7bd77d0937`, merged as `93065f0d`) added `_empty_query_fragment_markers` to preserve the empty `?` / `#` markers WHATWG keeps (#639), but it re-attaches the markers as a **suffix after `geturl()`** at every rebuild site. When the query is empty and the fragment is non-empty, the `?` therefore lands *after* the fragment instead of before the `#`:

| Input | Container returns (current `main`) | Worker / WHATWG `URL` returns |
|---|---|---|
| `http://example.com/path?#frag` | `http://example.com/path#frag?` | `http://example.com/path?#frag` |
| `http://example.com?#frag` | `http://example.com/#frag?` | `http://example.com/?#frag` |
| `http://example.com/a?#b?c` | `http://example.com/a#b?c?` | `http://example.com/a?#b?c` |
| `http://%65xample.com/path?#frag` | `http://example.com/path#frag?` | `http://example.com/path?#frag` |
| `http://8%2e8%2e8%2e8/path?#frag` | `http://8.8.8.8/path#frag?` | `http://8.8.8.8/path?#frag` |

Verified on current `main` by running `validate_crawl_url` from `pkgs/lab-ops-hub/container/app.py` (extracted fresh via `gh api ...?ref=main`) against the table above, cross-checked against Node's WHATWG `URL` serializer (the Worker's reference). The percent-decoded-host and canonical-IP rebuilds are affected too, because all three rebuild sites share the suffix pattern.

## Evidence

- `pkgs/lab-ops-hub/container/app.py:784-798` — `_empty_query_fragment_markers()` returns the markers as an unordered suffix string (`"?"` computed from the pre-`#` spelling, `"#"` if the fragment is empty).
- `pkgs/lab-ops-hub/container/app.py:860` — `_normalize_validated_url`: `...geturl() + _empty_query_fragment_markers(url)`.
- `pkgs/lab-ops-hub/container/app.py:937` — `_url_with_encoded_components`: same `geturl() + markers` suffix.
- `pkgs/lab-ops-hub/container/app.py:737-741` — `_url_with_host`: same suffix on all three return arms.
- `geturl()` rebuilds a non-empty fragment as `#frag` at the end of the string, so a suffixed `?` is parsed back as fragment data, not as the query marker.
- PR #648's test battery covered `path?#` (both markers empty — suffix order happens to be correct), `path?x#` (non-empty query), and `#frag?notquery` (`?` as fragment data), but not the empty-query + non-empty-fragment combination. Its 43,200-spelling differential evidently did not include that tail either.
- PR #653 (open, fixes #651) stacks on this code and does not touch the marker logic, so it carries the same defect.

## Why it matters

This is exactly the class of divergence #639 set out to eliminate: the two crawlers record different URLs for the same accepted target. Worse than a dropped marker, the returned URL is a *different* URL — the fragment is corrupted (`frag?` instead of `frag`) and the present-but-empty query becomes absent — so anything keying on the recorded URL (dedup, redirect handling, downstream fetch of the recorded form) sees a different target than the one that was judged and that the Worker records.

## Acceptance criteria

- `validate_crawl_url` returns the WHATWG form for empty-query + non-empty-fragment spellings, e.g. `http://example.com/path?#frag` → `http://example.com/path?#frag`, including through the percent-decoded-host and canonical-IP rebuild paths.
- The empty-fragment marker case stays correct (`path?#`, `path#`, `path?x#` unchanged) and a `?` inside the fragment stays data (`#frag?notquery` unchanged).
- New regression tests pin the `?#<non-empty fragment>` combination in the Python suite (and the TS suite if the Worker pin is extended); the differential probe set includes empty-query × non-empty-fragment tails.
- Existing Python / TS validator suites still pass; no verdict (accept/refuse) changes.

title: lab-ops-hub: container validator resolves a trailing '..;' / '.;' segment as a dot segment — bare-semicolon params tail is lost, returned path differs from the Worker
body:
## Summary

The container validator (`pkgs/lab-ops-hub/container/app.py`) resolves a trailing dot segment followed by a **bare semicolon** (`..;`, `.;`, `%2e;`, `%2e%2e;`) as if it were a plain dot segment, and returns a different path than the Worker returns for the same target. WHATWG treats `..;` as an ordinary path segment (the semicolon is data), so the Worker keeps it; the container drops the segment entirely (and, for `..;`, pops the previous segment too), so the two crawlers record — and fetch — different URLs.

## Evidence (verified on main `3ac2e9ee`, driving the real Python validator vs Node's WHATWG `URL`)

| Input | Container returns | Worker (WHATWG) returns |
|---|---|---|
| `http://example.com/..;` | `http://example.com/` | `http://example.com/..;` |
| `http://example.com/.;` | `http://example.com/` | `http://example.com/.;` |
| `http://example.com/foo/..;` | `http://example.com/` | `http://example.com/foo/..;` |
| `http://example.com/a/.;` | `http://example.com/a/` | `http://example.com/a/.;` |
| `http://example.com/a/b/..;` | `http://example.com/a/` | `http://example.com/a/b/..;` |
| `http://example.com/%2e;` | `http://example.com/` | `http://example.com/%2e;` |
| `http://example.com/%2e%2e;` | `http://example.com/` | `http://example.com/%2e%2e;` |
| `http://example.com/..;?q` | `http://example.com/?q` | `http://example.com/..;?q` |

Controls that already agree (non-empty params are handled): `http://example.com/..;foo`, `http://example.com/foo/.;x`, `http://example.com/a/..;foo` all return unchanged in both.

## Root cause

`urlparse` splits the last path segment at the first `;` into `path` + `params`. For a bare trailing `;` the params are the **empty string**:

```
urlparse("http://example.com/..;")  -> path="/..", params=""
urlparse("http://example.com/..;foo") -> path="/..", params="foo"
```

- `_normalize_validated_url` (app.py:849) rejoins only when params is truthy: `full_path = u.path + (f";{u.params}" if u.params else "")` — so the `;` is lost exactly when params is empty, and `_resolve_dot_segments` then treats the rejoined `/..` / `/.` / `/%2e` as a dot segment. The comment at app.py:816-820 documents the rejoin intent ("a trailing `..;foo` is data, not a double-dot segment") but the empty-params arm defeats it. The existing tests at app.py:979-980 / the test suite cover only `..;foo` spellings.
- `_url_with_encoded_components` (app.py:~942) has the same loss independently: it rebuilds from `u.path` + `u.params`, so even a correctly normalized `/..;` would come back as `/..`.

## Why it matters

The URL `validate_crawl_url` returns is the URL the fetcher fetches. A target whose last segment is `..;` / `.;` (a legitimate, if unusual, path spelling) is fetched by the container at the collapsed path — a different resource than the Worker fetches and than was judged — the same returned-form divergence class as #633/#639, in the one params arm those fixes missed.

## Acceptance criteria

- `validate_crawl_url` returns the WHATWG form for the table above (segments `..;`, `.;`, `%2e;`, `%2e%2e;` preserved verbatim, including before `?`/`#`).
- The fix covers both rebuild sites (`_normalize_validated_url` and `_url_with_encoded_components`); one clean way is to take the full path (including the `;params` tail) from `urlsplit`, which never splits params, instead of rejoining `urlparse`'s split.
- New regression tests in `pkgs/lab-ops-hub/test/test_container_validate.py` pin the bare-`;` spellings alongside the existing `..;foo` controls; existing suite stays green.
- No change to acceptance/refusal verdicts — returned form only.

title: lab-ops-hub: literal U+3002/U+FF0E/U+FF61 root-dot spellings still return the fullwidth form from the container validator (PR #657 remainder)
body:
## Finding

PR #657 fixed #647 for **percent-encoded** root-dot spellings, but the same divergence survives for the **literal** UTS-46 label-separator spellings of the root dot: U+3002 (。), U+FF0E (．) and U+FF61 (｡) written as literal characters in the URL.

`validate_crawl_url` in `pkgs/lab-ops-hub/container/app.py` judges the UTS-46-mapped host (the translate at app.py:~221 maps all three characters to `.`), and PR #657's `has_root_dot` (app.py:254) is computed on that mapped host — but the re-attach at app.py:411-415 only runs on the `percent_decoded` branch. The non-percent branch returns `raw`, so a literal separator spelling comes back with the fullwidth character still in it.

## Evidence (verified on current main f1a8abf0, merge of PR #657)

Running the real `validate_crawl_url` from `pkgs/lab-ops-hub/container/app.py` (Python suite: 58/58 pass):

| Input | Container (current main) | Worker / WHATWG |
|---|---|---|
| `http://example.com。/` (literal U+3002) | `http://example.com。/` | `http://example.com./` |
| `http://example.com．/` (literal U+FF0E) | `http://example.com．/` | `http://example.com./` |
| `http://example.com｡/` (literal U+FF61) | `http://example.com｡/` | `http://example.com./` |
| `http://example.com%E3%80%82/` (percent U+3002) | `http://example.com./` | `http://example.com./` |
| `http://example.com。:8080/` | `http://example.com。:8080/` | `http://example.com.:8080/` |
| `http://user@example.com｡/` | `http://user@example.com｡/` | `http://user@example.com./` |

Verdicts are correct in all these cases — judging uses the mapped host (`http://localhost。/` and `http://127.0.0.1。/` are refused, as are their percent spellings). Only the returned form diverges.

## Why it matters

The returned URL is the crawl record and the fetched URL. This is exactly the #647 harm PR #657 set out to fix — "the same target was recorded under two different URLs depending on spelling, defeating cross-crawler dedup/comparison" — surviving for the literal spellings of the same three characters. The percent-encoded spelling of U+3002 and the literal spelling of U+3002 are the same host character arriving two ways; the validator now returns two different URLs for them, and the literal form also disagrees with the Worker validator, whose WHATWG parser serialises the mapped `.` form.

Related context (fixer may scope to the root dot or address it together): the same raw-return path also leaves *interior* literal separators unmapped (`http://example。com/` returns the literal `。` form; the Worker returns `http://example.com/`). The root-dot cases above are the ones inside PR #657's stated scope.

## Acceptance criteria

- `validate_crawl_url` returns the ASCII dotted form for literal U+3002 / U+FF0E / U+FF61 root-dot spellings, byte-identical to their percent-encoded spellings and to the Worker's `validateCrawlUrl` (path, port, userinfo and `?#` marker variants included).
- Verdicts unchanged: dotted spellings of blocked targets (`localhost。`, `127.0.0.1。`) stay refused; a second separator still counts as an empty label and is refused.
- New tests mirror the #647 battery in `test/test_container_validate.py` for the literal spellings (and a TS pin in `test/lib.test.ts` if the Worker side needs one — it already returns the dotted form).
- A differential run against the real Worker validator over literal + percent spellings of all three separator characters shows zero diffs.

Found by the pr-diff-review job reviewing PR #657 (commit 5b115fa98845a5582c241812de7f354fede05cb1, merge f1a8abf0c4da2fee9b28c42805ecfc6b62340acb). Deduped against open/closed issues: #647 (closed) covered only the percent-encoded spellings; the literal-spelling return form appears in no open or closed issue (#654 is the separate empty-query-marker defect).

title: muse-proxy: MUSE_PROXY_PORT parsed with bare parseInt — the one bin proxy that skips the strict parseProxyPort helper (#483)
body:
## Finding

`bin/muse-proxy.mjs:26` is the only proxy in `bin/` that does not parse its listen port through the shared strict helper:

```js
const PORT = parseInt(process.env.MUSE_PROXY_PORT || '18747', 10);
```

Every sibling uses `parseProxyPort` from `bin/proxy-port.mjs` — codex-proxy.mjs:10, clef-proxy.mjs:8, agy-proxy.mjs:10, antigravity-ls-proxy.mjs:10, design-code-proxy.mjs:6/:9/:10 (7 sites). The helper's header (proxy-port.mjs:1-8, from #483) states the rule and the exact failure modes a bare `parseInt` causes:

> A bare parseInt is not a validator: 'abc' becomes NaN (an opaque ERR_SOCKET_BAD_PORT crash at listen time), '18744abc' and '18744.9' silently become 18744, and '0x4a38' becomes 0, which binds a random ephemeral port while every client keeps dialling the configured one. Every proxy parses its *_PROXY_PORT through here instead, so a bad value fails at startup with the env var and its value named.

muse-proxy was added after that rule (it mirrors codex-proxy per its header comment) and never adopted the helper — and the guard that should have caught it doesn't see it: `bin/proxy-port.test.mjs`'s test "all seven parse sites in the five proxies use the shared helper" enumerates only the five older proxies, so muse-proxy is in neither its import/`parseInt` checks nor the site count.

## Verified on current main (f1a8abf0)

Live repro, `MUSE_PROXY_PORT=<value> node bin/muse-proxy.mjs`:

- `18747abc` → silently binds 18747 (trailing junk ignored; `parseProxyPortValue` rejects this spelling)
- `99999` → crashes with an unhandled `RangeError [ERR_SOCKET_BAD_PORT]` stack from `node:net`, naming neither the env var nor its value
- `abc` → same opaque crash (`Received type number (NaN)`)
- `0x4a38` → binds port **0** — a random ephemeral port — and logs `listening on http://127.0.0.1:0`, while clients keep dialling 18747

With the helper, each of these exits 1 at startup with `MUSE_PROXY_PORT="<value>" is not a valid port (expected an integer 1-65535)`.

## Why it matters

This is the exact silent-misconfiguration class #483/#494 fixed for the other five proxies: a typo'd `MUSE_PROXY_PORT` in a service environment either crashes opaquely or — worse, for `0x…`/0 spellings — starts "successfully" on a random port while every configured client dials the dead one. The proxy family is meant to be uniform here; one member quietly opting out is how the bug class comes back.

## Acceptance criteria

- `bin/muse-proxy.mjs` imports `parseProxyPort` from `./proxy-port.mjs` and parses its port as `parseProxyPort('MUSE_PROXY_PORT', 18747)`; no bare `parseInt(process.env.…PROXY_PORT…)` remains in the file.
- Bad spellings (`abc`, `99999`, `18747abc`, `18747.9`, `0x4a38`, `0`, `-1`) exit 1 at startup with the error naming `MUSE_PROXY_PORT` and the offending value; unset/empty still defaults to 18747 and a valid value binds exactly that port (existing `bin/muse-proxy.test.mjs` suite stays green).
- The guard test in `bin/proxy-port.test.mjs` covers muse-proxy: it joins the enumerated proxy list (import + no-bare-parseInt assertions) and the parse-site count goes from seven to eight. If muse-proxy is not launched from `home/common/default.nix` the way the other five are, the home-manager test's file list should be evaluated separately rather than silently extended.
- Cross-repo: muse-proxy exists only in this repo (no `MUSE_PROXY_PORT`/`muse-proxy` copy in developing-today/opencode, developing-today/openchamber, or dezren39/nix — grep-verified at filing), so this is a single-repo fix, not a cross-repo set.

title: lab-ops-hub: container validator returns the raw fullwidth/compatibility-mapped host spelling — Worker returns the UTS-46-mapped form it judged
body:
## Summary

The Lab Ops Hub container validator judges a host in its UTS-46/NFKC-mapped form but, for a host whose mapping is a compatibility mapping to ordinary ASCII letters/digits (e.g. fullwidth Latin), returns the caller's raw spelling — while the Worker validator returns the mapped form it judged. The two validators therefore hand back different URLs for the same input, and the URL the container records and fetches is not the spelling it judged.

## Evidence (verified this run on current main `6da91105`, driving both real validators)

`pkgs/lab-ops-hub/container/app.py`:

- Line 229: judging uses the mapped host — `host = unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", host).lower()` (plus the separator translation at :230 and ignored-codepoint deletion at :231). The security checks do see through the spelling: fullwidth `ｌｏｃａｌｈｏｓｔ` is refused as local host localhost, and the fullwidth-digit IPv4 spelling is refused as 127.0.0.1.
- Lines 426–431 (public-DNS return path): the URL is rebuilt from the judged host only `if percent_decoded or has_literal_separator` — otherwise `raw` is returned unchanged. A fullwidth-letter host is neither, so the raw spelling survives.

Probe results:

```
container (Python)  validate_crawl_url("http://ｅｘａｍｐｌｅ.com/")      -> "http://ｅｘａｍｐｌｅ.com/"   (raw fullwidth returned)
container (Python)  validate_crawl_url("http://ＥＸＡＭＰＬＥ.com/")      -> "http://ＥＸＡＭＰＬＥ.com/"
container (Python)  validate_crawl_url("http://ｇｐｔ２.example.com/")   -> "http://ｇｐｔ２.example.com/"
Worker    (TS)      validateCrawlUrl("http://ｅｘａｍｐｌｅ.com/")        -> "http://example.com/"     (mapped form returned)
```

## Why it matters

The validated URL is the artifact both crawlers fetch, log, and compare; the container/Worker pair is maintained to return one canonical spelling for one input (the same principle behind #637's canonical IP-literal return, #652's ignored-codepoint return, and #660's separator return — #660's rebuild triggers only on `has_literal_separator`, so compatibility-mapped letters were left behind). Here the container fetches a URL whose host is only converted to the judged name implicitly, by the fetcher's stdlib IDNA-2003 nameprep — a different mapping table from the UTS-46 mapping the validator judged with, so for spellings where the two tables disagree the fetched host need not be the judged host. Returning the judged form removes the second, unjudged mapping from the path.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `validate_crawl_url("http://ｅｘａｍｐｌｅ.com/")` returns `http://example.com/` — in general, whenever the judged (mapped) host differs from the caller's host spelling, the returned URL carries the judged host, as the percent-decoded (#529) and literal-separator (#660) paths already do.
- [ ] Spellings whose host the mapping does not change return exactly what they return today (no gratuitous rebuilds; existing return-form tests keep passing).
- [ ] New cases pinned in `pkgs/lab-ops-hub/container` Python tests (fullwidth lowercase, fullwidth uppercase, fullwidth digit in a label), and the TS suite still passes unchanged.

## Dedup / scope

Not #652 (UTS-46 *ignored* codepoints deleted from the judged host), not #659 (raw U-label returned for IDN targets vs the Worker's A-label), not #660 (literal separator spellings U+3002/U+FF0E/U+FF61), not #527 (judging of mapped spellings of blocked targets — that side works). This is the return-form remainder for compatibility mappings. Single-repo: the validator pair lives only in this repo's `pkgs/lab-ops-hub` (container + Worker); no copy exists in opencode/openchamber/nix.

title: lab-ops-hub: container validator returns the raw Kelvin-sign (U+212A) host spelling — extraction folds it to 'k' before the #666 mapped-host check can see it
body:
## Summary

PR #666 fixed the container validator returning the raw compatibility-mapped host spelling (#665) by measuring the host before its NFKC step and rebuilding the returned URL when that step changed the spelling. One spelling escapes that measurement entirely: **U+212A KELVIN SIGN**. The container judges `http://K.example.com/` as host `k.example.com` but returns `http://K.example.com/` verbatim, while the Worker validator returns `http://k.example.com/`. The two validators again hand back different URLs for the same input — the exact #665 divergence, for the one character whose fold happens before the new measurement point.

## Evidence (verified on current main `c1524b63`, driving both real validators)

`pkgs/lab-ops-hub/container/app.py`:

- Host extraction folds the character before the #666 measurement exists: `host = (u.hostname or "").lower()` — `urllib`'s `hostname` property already lowercases, and Python's Unicode lowercase mapping for U+212A is ASCII `k`. So the extracted host is `k.example.com` from the start.
- PR #666's `host_before_mapping = host` is captured from that already-folded host, so `host_was_mapped = host != host_before_mapping and host.isascii()` is `False` for a Kelvin-sign host: nothing downstream of extraction changes the spelling, and the public-DNS return path returns `raw` unchanged.
- Judging is unaffected (it sees the folded form): `http://K.localhost/` is refused as local host `k.localhost`. This is purely a return-form divergence.

Probe results:

```
container (Python)  validate_crawl_url("http://K.example.com/")        -> "http://K.example.com/"   (raw returned)
container (Python)  validate_crawl_url("http://K.com/")                -> "http://K.com/"
container (Python)  validate_crawl_url("http://Kexample.com:8080/p")   -> "http://Kexample.com:8080/p"
container (Python)  validate_crawl_url("http://%e2%84%aa.example.com/") -> "http://k.example.com/"   (percent spelling correct)
Worker    (TS)      validateCrawlUrl("http://K.example.com/")          -> "http://k.example.com/"
Worker    (TS)      validateCrawlUrl("http://K.com/")                  -> "http://k.com/"
```

Note the internal inconsistency: the percent-encoded spelling of the same host returns the judged form, the literal spelling does not. A mixed host also works (`http://Kｅ.com/` -> `http://ke.com/` in both), because the fullwidth character triggers the #666 rebuild — only a host whose *sole* fold is the Kelvin sign escapes.

Completeness: a brute-force scan of every Unicode codepoint through the extraction-fold → NFKC pipeline shows U+212A is the **only** character whose lowercase mapping lands on an NFKC-stable ASCII form, i.e. the only spelling this blind spot can ever hide. Every other cased compatibility character either keeps a non-ASCII judged form (the open #659 U-label question) or is changed again by NFKC, which #666's check does see.

## Why it matters

Same principle as #665/#652/#660: the validated URL is the artifact both crawlers fetch, log, and compare, and the pair is maintained to return one canonical spelling for one input. Here the container records and fetches a spelling it never judged — the judged host `k.example.com` exists only inside the validator — and the container/Worker pair disagrees on the return for the same input, so behavior depends on which validator handled the crawl.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `validate_crawl_url("http://K.example.com/")` returns `http://k.example.com/`; in general, a host whose spelling was folded at extraction time (before the NFKC step) also rebuilds the returned URL from the judged host.
- [ ] The percent-encoded and mixed-spelling controls keep their current returns (`%e2%84%aa` -> `k.example.com`, `Kｅ.com` -> `ke.com`), and spellings the pipeline does not change return exactly what they return today.
- [ ] New cases pinned in `pkgs/lab-ops-hub/container` Python tests (Kelvin sign as a full label and inside a label, with a port/path), and the TS suite still passes unchanged.

## Dedup / scope

Not #665 (compatibility mappings visible to the NFKC step — fixed by #666; this fold happens *before* that step, at `urlparse` extraction/lower-casing). Not #652 (UTS-46 *ignored* codepoints deleted by the translate step), not #659 (raw U-label returned for non-ASCII IDN targets — the Kelvin judged form is pure ASCII), not #660 (literal separator spellings). Found by PR-diff review of #666. Single-repo: the validator pair lives only in this repo's `pkgs/lab-ops-hub` (container + Worker); no copy exists in opencode/openchamber/nix.

title: muse-proxy: streaming execution failure is sent as unframed JSON on a 200 SSE response — clients see an empty successful stream
body:
## Finding

`bin/muse-proxy.mjs` sends the streaming response headers (`200` + `Content-Type: text/event-stream`) before the `muse exec` child runs. When the child then fails — non-zero exit with no content, or a non-`completed` terminal state with no content — the close handler's failure branch cannot change the status, and it ends the response with a bare JSON error object:

```js
if (!res.headersSent) {
  res.writeHead(500, { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' });
}
res.end(JSON.stringify({ error: { message: `Muse execution failed: ${detail}` } }));
```

In stream mode `res.headersSent` is always true at that point, so the client receives an SSE response whose body is one unframed JSON line: no `data:` prefix, no error chunk, no `data: [DONE]`. An OpenAI-compatible SSE client parsing `data:` lines sees an empty, apparently successful stream (HTTP 200, zero events) — the failure is silently swallowed. The non-streaming path is correct (500 + JSON error), so the two modes disagree about the same failure.

## Evidence

Reproduced on main `f71a064e` with a stub `muse` on PATH that prints `stub muse: auth expired` to stderr and exits 3 (the stub pattern from `bin/muse-proxy.test.mjs`):

- `POST /v1/chat/completions` with `"stream":true` →
  ```
  HTTP/1.1 200 OK
  Content-Type: text/event-stream; charset=utf-8

  {"error":{"message":"Muse execution failed: stub muse: auth expired"}}
  ```
  (raw JSON body — not SSE-framed, no `[DONE]`)
- Same request without `stream` → `HTTP/1.1 500` with the same JSON error body (correct).

Code: `bin/muse-proxy.mjs` — stream headers are written in the request handler before spawn (`res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'text/event-stream; ...' })`); the failure branch is in the `child.on('close', ...)` handler (`const failed = ...` / `Muse execution failed`). The `child.on('error', ...)` handler has the same shape: with headers already sent it writes nothing, leaving the framing to the close handler.

Single-repo: `bin/muse-proxy.mjs` exists only in this repo. (codex-proxy has no execution-failure detection at all in its close handler — a different gap; this issue is only about muse-proxy's stream framing.)

## Why it matters

Streaming is the default mode for the OpenCode/OpenChamber clients this bridge serves. A muse CLI failure (expired OAuth login, CLI crash, model rejection) currently presents to a streaming client as a successful, empty completion — the hardest failure shape to diagnose, and inconsistent with the proxy's own non-streaming behaviour.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] In stream mode, a failed execution terminates the SSE stream with a framed error the client can surface (e.g. a `data:` chunk carrying the error object) followed by `data: [DONE]`, instead of a bare JSON body.
- [ ] Non-streaming failure behaviour is unchanged (500 + JSON error).
- [ ] A regression test in `bin/muse-proxy.test.mjs` uses a failing stub `muse` (non-zero exit) and pins both modes: stream body is SSE-framed, carries the failure message, and ends with `[DONE]`; non-stream returns 500.
- [ ] Existing muse-proxy tests (terminal-tail reconciliation, #484) still pass.

title: muse-proxy: a run that fails after producing partial output is reported as a successful 'stop' — failure is masked whenever any content exists
body:
## Problem

`bin/muse-proxy.mjs` decides whether a `muse exec` run failed with this predicate (line 439):

```js
const failed = (code !== 0 && fullContent.length === 0) || (terminalState && terminalState !== 'completed' && fullContent.length === 0);
```

Both clauses require `fullContent.length === 0`. So whenever the CLI emitted **any** assistant text before failing, the failure is masked: the proxy returns the partial text as a normal successful completion with `finish_reason: 'stop'`.

## Evidence (verified 2026-10-23 with a stub `muse` on PATH, same harness style as `bin/muse-proxy.test.mjs`)

Case A — terminal event says the run failed, exit code 0:
- stub emits `run.output.delta` `"partial answer"`, then `run.terminal.failed` with `terminal: "failed"`, exit 0.
- Non-stream response: **200**, `message.content: "partial answer"`, `finish_reason: "stop"`.
- Stream response: partial chunk, then a finish chunk with `finish_reason: "stop"` + `[DONE]`. No error anywhere.

Case B — child crashes mid-run, exit code 3:
- stub emits `run.output.delta` `"partial answer"`, writes stderr, exit 3 (no terminal event).
- Both modes: **200 / finish_reason "stop"** with the partial text, exactly as Case A.

The empty-content cases are handled correctly (#670: non-stream 500, stream SSE error frame + `[DONE]`); only the partial-content cases slip through.

## Why it matters

Clients (opencode and any OpenAI-compatible consumer) cannot distinguish a truncated, failed run from a complete answer: they present the partial text as the model's full reply and record the request as successful. A mid-run auth expiry, rate limit, or CLI crash after the first tokens is indistinguishable from success — the worst failure shape for a bridge whose whole job is faithful translation.

## Acceptance criteria

- A run whose terminal state is present and not `completed` is reported as an error regardless of how much content was produced: non-stream → 500 with the `Muse execution failed: …` error body; stream → the already-streamed deltas are followed by the #670 SSE error frame + `[DONE]`, and **no** `finish_reason: 'stop'` chunk is emitted.
- A run with no terminal event and a non-zero exit code is likewise an error even when partial content exists (same surfacing as above).
- A run with terminal state `completed` stays a success even if the exit code is non-zero (the terminal event is authoritative), and all existing behavior for completed runs (tail reconciliation #484, usage accounting) is unchanged.
- New tests in `bin/muse-proxy.test.mjs` cover both cases above in both stream and non-stream modes (stub markers in the style of the existing FAILME/DIVERGE cases), and the existing three tests still pass (`node --test bin/muse-proxy.test.mjs`).

## Suggested fix

Make the terminal state authoritative and drop the content-length gate, e.g.:

```js
const failed = terminalState ? terminalState !== 'completed' : code !== 0;
```

## Related sighting (judge separately)

`bin/agy-proxy.mjs:553` has a similar content-gated check (`code !== 0 && !responseText`). That CLI exposes no authoritative terminal event, so the semantics differ; noted here only so the fixer can decide whether it deserves its own issue — it is not part of this issue's acceptance criteria.

title: muse-proxy: signal-killed runs report 'muse exec exited with code null', and #673's empty-stderr terminal-state fallback is untested
body:
## Finding

PR #673 (fixing #672) reworked `bin/muse-proxy.mjs`'s failure handling so failure is judged by the authoritative terminal state, and — when stderr is empty — the error detail names that terminal state instead of the misleading `muse exec exited with code 0`. The fallback expression it left behind (current `main`, `bin/muse-proxy.mjs:404-409`) has two remaining gaps in the same spot:

```js
const failed = terminalState ? terminalState !== 'completed' : code !== 0;
if (failed) {
  const stderrLine = stderrTail.trim().split('\n').pop();
  const fallback = terminalState && terminalState !== 'completed'
    ? `muse run terminated with state '${terminalState}'`
    : `muse exec exited with code ${code}`;
```

### 1. Signal-killed runs report `muse exec exited with code null`

The close handler is `child.on('close', (code, signal) => …)` (line 367), but `signal` is never used. When the child dies by signal (OOM `SIGKILL`, `SIGTERM`, …), Node reports `code === null`, the run correctly counts as failed (`code !== 0`), but with empty stderr the detail becomes the literal string `muse exec exited with code null` — the same class of misleading detail #673 set out to eliminate for the terminal-state case.

Reproduced on current main (`4a91edc3`, merge of #673) with a stub `muse` that kills itself and prints nothing:

```sh
#!/bin/sh
kill -9 $$
```

- Non-stream: `500 {"error":{"message":"Muse execution failed: muse exec exited with code null"}}`
- Stream: SSE error event with the same `code null` message, then `data: [DONE]`

### 2. The empty-stderr terminal-state fallback added by #673 has no test coverage

Both failure stubs added by #671/#673 emit a stderr line (`stub muse: run failed midway`, `stub muse: crashed midway`), and the #672 test only asserts `/Muse execution failed: stub muse:/` — so the `stderrLine` is always what satisfies the assertion and the new fallback string is never exercised.

Verified by ablation in a scratch copy: reverting **only** the fallback-detail lines to the pre-#673 form (`stderrTail… || \`muse exec exited with code ${code}\``), while keeping #673's failure predicate, still passes the full suite 4/4 (`node --test bin/muse-proxy.test.mjs`). The behaviour itself works today — a stub emitting `run.terminal.failed` with **no** stderr returns `Muse execution failed: muse run terminated with state 'failed'` in both modes — but nothing pins it, so a future refactor can silently regress it back to `exited with code 0`.

## Evidence

- PR #673: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/673 (commit `df1dd2502d98b2a7bf435e7a2789f49965354dbe`, merged in `4a91edc359063734da7d0b8a8dedbd2d49591216`), diff hunk changing the failure predicate and detail fallback in `bin/muse-proxy.mjs`.
- Current main: `bin/muse-proxy.mjs:367` (close handler signature `(code, signal)`), `:404-409` (predicate + fallback quoted above).
- Tests: `bin/muse-proxy.test.mjs` — `FAILPARTIAL`/`CRASHPARTIAL` stubs (lines 32-43) both write to stderr; the #672 test's error assertions (lines 175, 188) match only the stderr text.
- Live repro of both the `code null` message and the working-but-untested terminal-state message, run against current main as described above.

## Why it matters

This proxy is the OpenAI-compatible surface other tools drive `muse exec` through; when a run dies, the error detail is often the *only* diagnostic a client (or a human reading its logs) gets. `exited with code null` sends debugging in the wrong direction (a signal kill — e.g. OOM — looks like a corrupt message), and the one fallback #673 deliberately improved can regress unnoticed because no test reaches it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A run terminated by a signal with empty stderr and no terminal event produces an error detail that names the signal (e.g. `muse exec terminated by signal SIGKILL`) instead of `exited with code null`, in both stream (SSE error frame + `[DONE]`) and non-stream (500) modes.
- [ ] A stub mode that emits a non-`completed` terminal event with **empty** stderr is added to `bin/muse-proxy.test.mjs`, asserting the detail names the terminal state (e.g. `terminated with state 'failed'`) in both modes.
- [ ] A stub mode whose child dies by signal (e.g. `kill -9 $$`) with empty stderr is added, asserting the signal-naming detail in both modes.
- [ ] `node --test bin/muse-proxy.test.mjs` passes, and ablating either fallback branch makes exactly the new assertions fail.

title: codex-proxy: a failed codex run is reported as a successful 'stop' — close handler ignores exit code and signal in both modes
body:
## Finding

`bin/codex-proxy.mjs` never checks whether the spawned `codex exec` child actually succeeded. Its `child.on('close', (code, signal) => ...)` handler (bin/codex-proxy.mjs:401) ignores both `code` and `signal`, does not track stderr (no `stderrTail` — the stderr handler at :395 only logs), and unconditionally reports success: non-stream mode returns HTTP 200 with `finish_reason: "stop"`, and stream mode emits a `finish_reason: "stop"` chunk + `data: [DONE]`.

So a run that fails — auth expired, model rejected, CLI crashed — is indistinguishable from a successful empty (or partial) reply for the identical request.

This is the codex-proxy counterpart of the two defects already fixed in the sibling `bin/muse-proxy.mjs`: #670 (streaming failure invisible to SSE clients) and #672 (failure masked whenever any content exists). The muse-proxy fix judged failure on close and framed stream errors as SSE; codex-proxy has no failure detection at all (noted as "a different gap, not filed" in the #670 run's backlog entry).

## Evidence (reproduced on main d8bfe7c6)

Ran `bin/codex-proxy.mjs` with a stub `codex` at `$HOME/.local/bin/codex` (the proxy's own binary resolution) that reads the prompt from stdin:

- Stub prints `stub codex: auth expired` to stderr and exits 3, no stdout:
  - non-stream: HTTP **200**, `content: ""`, `finish_reason: "stop"`, `completion_tokens: 0`
  - stream: HTTP 200, one chunk with `finish_reason: "stop"`, then `data: [DONE]` — no error anywhere
- Stub emits one `item.completed` agent_message (`partial answer`), prints `stub codex: run failed midway` to stderr, exits 3:
  - non-stream: HTTP **200**, `content: "partial answer"`, `finish_reason: "stop"`
  - stream: content chunk `partial answer`, then a `finish_reason: "stop"` chunk + `[DONE]`
- Stub success case (agent_message + `turn.completed`, exit 0) correctly returns 200 with the full text in both modes.

Dedup: searches for "codex-proxy" across open/closed issues return only #434/#435/#437/#480/#483/#496/#661/#670 — none covers exit-code/failure detection. Cross-repo: `bin/codex-proxy.mjs` exists only in this repo (no copy in developing-today/opencode, developing-today/openchamber, dezren39/nix).

## Why it matters

OpenCode consumes this bridge in streaming mode as a provider. A failed Codex run presented as a clean `stop` with empty or truncated text is worse than an error: downstream code and users treat it as the complete answer, and an auth expiry presents as "the model said nothing" instead of a diagnosable failure.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A child that exits non-zero (or is killed by a signal) is reported as a failure in both modes, regardless of how much content was already produced: non-stream returns HTTP 500 with an `error.message` naming the failure (last stderr line when present, otherwise a fallback naming the signal or exit code — never `code null`/`code -2` style artifacts); stream mode emits a `data:`-framed error event followed by `data: [DONE]` and no chunk claims `finish_reason: "stop"`.
- [ ] Successful runs (exit 0) are unchanged in both modes.
- [ ] A regression test with a stub `codex` (fail-with-no-output and fail-after-partial-output cases, both modes) passes; the existing proxy test suites still pass.

title: agy-proxy: failed agy run reported as successful 'stop' — stream handler never checks the exit code, non-stream masks failure when partial output exists
body:
## Finding

`bin/agy-proxy.mjs` reports a failed `agy` run as a successful completion in most shapes:

- **Stream mode** — the `child.on('close', code => ...)` handler (`bin/agy-proxy.mjs:467`) checks `code` only for the resume-retry case (`code !== 0 && !hasOutput && allowRetry && targetConvId`, :471). Every other non-zero exit falls through to the unconditional success ending at :481-510: a chunk with `finish_reason: 'stop'` plus `data: [DONE]`. The `stderrBuffer` collected at :463-465 is never read anywhere in the stream path, so the failure cause is discarded entirely.
- **Non-stream mode** — the failure branch is gated on empty output (`if (code !== 0 && !responseText)`, :553), so a run that fails after producing a partial response returns HTTP 200 with `finish_reason: 'stop'` and the truncated text. (This is the sighting noted for separate judgement in #672; the stream half above was not covered there or anywhere else.)

This is the agy-proxy counterpart of the defects already fixed in the sibling `bin/muse-proxy.mjs` (#670, #672, #674) and `bin/codex-proxy.mjs` (#676): a failed run presented as a clean `stop`.

## Evidence (reproduced on main `4b85ef69`)

Ran `bin/agy-proxy.mjs` with a stub `agy` at `$HOME/.local/bin/agy` (the proxy's own binary resolution) whose behaviour keys on the requested `--output-format`:

- Stub prints `stub agy: auth expired` to stderr and exits 3, no stdout:
  - stream: HTTP **200**, one chunk with `finish_reason: "stop"`, then `data: [DONE]` — no error anywhere
  - non-stream: HTTP **502** `{"error":"agy process exited with non-zero code","code":3,"stderr":"stub agy: auth expired"}` (correct — the control case)
- Stub emits one `step_update` text delta (`partial answer`) / `{"response":"partial answer"}`, prints `stub agy: run failed midway` to stderr, exits 3:
  - stream: HTTP 200, content chunk `partial answer`, then a `finish_reason: "stop"` chunk + `[DONE]`
  - non-stream: HTTP **200**, `content: "partial answer"`, `finish_reason: "stop"`
- Stub success case (delta + `result` event / `{"response":"full answer"}`, exit 0) correctly returns 200 with the full text and `stop` in both modes.

Dedup: searches for "agy-proxy" / "agy" across open and closed issues return only #434/#435/#437/#483/#661/#672 — #672 notes the non-stream gate at :553 as "judge separately" and explicitly excludes it from its acceptance criteria; none covers the stream handler or failure detection in this proxy. Cross-repo: `bin/agy-proxy.mjs` exists only in this repo (no copy in developing-today/opencode, developing-today/openchamber, dezren39/nix).

## Why it matters

OpenCode consumes this bridge in streaming mode as a provider. A failed agy run (expired auth, CLI crash, model rejection) presented as a clean `stop` with empty or truncated text is worse than an error: downstream code and users treat it as the complete answer, and an auth expiry presents as "the model said nothing" instead of a diagnosable failure. The two modes also disagree with each other — and with the proxy's own correct empty-output non-stream case (502 with stderr).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A child that exits non-zero (or is killed by a signal — `code` is `null` then) is reported as a failure in both modes, regardless of how much content was already produced: non-stream returns an error status (the existing 502 shape, with stderr, is fine) instead of 200/`stop`; stream mode emits a `data:`-framed error event naming the failure (last stderr line when present) followed by `data: [DONE]`, and no chunk claims `finish_reason: "stop"`.
- [ ] The resume-retry behaviour is preserved: a failed resume (`code !== 0`, no output, a conversation was being resumed) still retries once as a fresh conversation before any failure is reported.
- [ ] Successful runs (exit 0) are unchanged in both modes.
- [ ] A regression test with a stub `agy` (fail-with-no-output and fail-after-partial-output cases, both modes — the `bin/codex-proxy.test.mjs` / `bin/muse-proxy.test.mjs` stub pattern; there is currently no `bin/agy-proxy.test.mjs`) passes; the existing proxy test suites still pass.

title: codex-proxy: a turn.failed event with exit 0 is reported as a successful 'stop' — #677 judged failure by exit code only, no terminal-event check
body:
## Finding

PR #677 fixed `bin/codex-proxy.mjs` judging failure **only by the child's exit code** (`code !== 0` in the `close` handler, `bin/codex-proxy.mjs:412` on main `4b85ef69`). But `codex exec --json` also reports failure **in-band**: it emits a `{"type":"turn.failed","error":{"message": …}}` event for a fatal error during a turn, and that event can arrive on a run that **exits 0**. The proxy's event parser (`processJsonLine`, `bin/codex-proxy.mjs:340-380`) handles only `item.completed` and `turn.completed` — `turn.failed` is silently ignored, so an exit-0 failed turn is still reported as a successful `stop`:

- no output before the failure → HTTP 200, empty content, `finish_reason: "stop"` (non-stream) / a bare `stop` chunk + `[DONE]` (stream)
- partial output before the failure → HTTP 200 carrying the truncated text as a clean `stop` (both modes)

That is exactly the masked-failure shape #676 fixed for the exit-code half — and exactly the shape `bin/muse-proxy.mjs` already guards against by judging failure from the run's authoritative terminal event first and the exit code second (`failed = terminalState ? terminalState !== 'completed' : code !== 0`, the #672/#673 pattern PR #677's body says it mirrors). The codex half of that pattern — the event-state half — is missing.

Exit 0 does not rule out a failed turn for codex: other codex providers explicitly check for turn-failure events on exit 0 (e.g. the codex-cli AI SDK provider's exit-code logic: "0 | Success | Check for turn failure events; return results if none", with a dedicated event-based error-detection pass for "failures that may not manifest as non-zero exit codes"), and headless-codex guidance is to fail on a `turn.failed` event rather than trust the exit code. `turn.failed` (`TurnFailedEvent { error }`, "on fatal error during a turn") is part of the documented `codex exec --json` event protocol.

Note on scope: top-level `{"type":"error", …}` events also exist in the protocol, but some are transient reconnect notices; this issue only requires the unambiguous `turn.failed` case. Whether to treat non-reconnect `error` events as failures is a judgement call for the implementer.

## Evidence (reproduced on current main `4b85ef6906a25c1a59694c64986cb17828b6c2b6`)

Ran the real `bin/codex-proxy.mjs` (pristine copy from `origin/main`) with a stub `codex` at `$HOME/.local/bin/codex` (the proxy's own binary resolution):

- Stub prints `{"type":"turn.failed","error":{"message":"stub codex: model overloaded"}}`, exits 0:
  - non-stream → **200**, `content: ""`, `finish_reason: "stop"`
  - stream → **200**, one `finish_reason: "stop"` chunk, then `data: [DONE]` — no error anywhere
- Stub prints an `item.completed` agent_message (`partial answer`), then `{"type":"turn.failed","error":{"message":"stub codex: run failed midway"}}`, exits 0:
  - non-stream → **200**, `content: "partial answer"`, `finish_reason: "stop"`
  - stream → **200**, the `partial answer` chunk, then a `finish_reason: "stop"` chunk + `[DONE]`
- Control ( `item.completed` + `turn.completed`, exit 0) → 200 with the full text and `stop` in both modes, unchanged.
- The existing suites pass on the same main: `node --test bin/codex-proxy.test.mjs bin/muse-proxy.test.mjs` → 10/10 — no existing test emits `turn.failed`.

Source PR: #677 (`fix(codex-proxy): report failed codex runs as errors, not successful stops`, fixes #676, commit `a0a1b077`, merge `4b85ef69`). Its failure predicate is the single line `if (code !== 0)` at `bin/codex-proxy.mjs:412`; nothing in the PR's new `bin/codex-proxy.test.mjs` covers an in-band failure event.

Dedup: searches for `turn.failed` across all issues (open + closed) return nothing; `codex-proxy failed` returns only #676 (closed, the exit-code half), #670 (muse-proxy streaming), #496 and the open #678 (agy-proxy's separate exit-code masking — a different proxy and a different mechanism; this finding is codex-only). The `bin/codex-proxy.mjs` bridge exists only in this repo.

## Why it matters

Clients of the proxy (opencode's codex provider) cannot distinguish a failed codex turn from a successful empty or short answer: a rate-limited, overloaded, or otherwise fatally failed turn presents as a clean `stop`, so callers accept truncated/empty output instead of surfacing an error or retrying — the same silent-corruption failure mode #670/#672/#676 were filed and fixed for.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `bin/codex-proxy.mjs` tracks a `turn.failed` event during the run; on `close`, a run that emitted `turn.failed` is reported as a failure even when the exit code is 0: non-stream returns HTTP 500 with `Codex execution failed: <the turn.failed error message>` (falling back to stderr/signal/exit-code detail when the event carries no message), and stream mode writes a `data:`-framed error event + `data: [DONE]` with no chunk claiming `finish_reason: "stop"` — mirroring the existing #677 error framing.
- [ ] Partial output followed by `turn.failed` + exit 0 is an error in both modes, not a 200 `stop` carrying the truncated text.
- [ ] Successful runs (exit 0, `turn.completed`, no `turn.failed`) are unchanged in both modes.
- [ ] New stub modes in `bin/codex-proxy.test.mjs` pin the no-output and partial-output `turn.failed` + exit-0 shapes in both modes; ablating only the `turn.failed` check fails exactly those new tests, and the full codex-proxy + muse-proxy + proxy-port suites pass.

title: design-code-proxy: quota error in a 200 JSON body hangs the request forever — writeHead precedes the in-body check, so fallback can never fire
body:
## Finding

`bin/design-code-proxy.mjs`'s local-dispatch fallback can never fire for a quota error reported **in the JSON body of an HTTP 200 response**, and the client request **hangs forever** instead.

In `tryTarget` (`bin/design-code-proxy.mjs:213-266` on main `4b85ef69`):

1. The response callback calls `clientRes.writeHead(localRes.statusCode || 200, ...)` at **line 219** — before the body has been read. From that moment `clientRes.headersSent` is `true`.
2. The non-stream body handler (line 254-258) parses the body and, for a quota error, calls `return onFail(new Error('Quota exceeded in JSON body'))`.
3. The primary target's `onFail` wrapper (line 279-280) begins with `if (clientRes.headersSent) return;` — so it silently returns without trying the fallback target and **without ever ending `clientRes`**. The fallback target's own `onFail` (line 284) is guarded the same way, so the hang happens whichever target returns the quota body.

The status-based path works fine because the `429`/`>=500` check (line 213) runs *before* `writeHead` — only the in-body check, which the code explicitly added to catch quota exhaustion, is defeated by the ordering.

## Evidence (reproduced on current main `4b85ef6906a25c1a59694c64986cb17828b6c2b6`)

Ran the real `bin/design-code-proxy.mjs` locally with stub HTTP backends on the Antigravity/Codex ports (`DESIGN_CODE_PROXY_PORT`/`ANTIGRAVITY_LS_PROXY_PORT`/`CODEX_PROXY_PORT` pointed at the stubs), model `design-code-flash`, non-stream:

- Stub primary returns **HTTP 200** with `{"error":{"code":429,"message":"quota stub","type":"insufficient_quota"}}`:
  - `curl --max-time 5` → **timed out after 5002 ms with 0 bytes received** (curl exit 28); the proxy logged only the primary attempt — no "Falling back" line, the fallback stub was never contacted, and the response was never ended. Without a client-side timeout this hangs indefinitely.
- Control — stub primary returns **HTTP 429 status** with an error body:
  - Proxy logged `returned 429`, tried the fallback target, and answered **502 `All design code backends failed: HTTP 429` in under a second** — the intended behaviour the in-body path was written to provide.

## Why it matters

The in-body quota shape is exactly what this branch exists for (backends that report quota exhaustion in a 200 JSON error body). Today, instead of failing over to the fallback model/backend, every such request wedges an open client connection forever — the worst failure mode for a dispatch proxy whose whole job is fallback — and leaks the socket on both sides until the client gives up.

## Suggested fix

For the non-stream path, buffer the body and run the quota check **before** `clientRes.writeHead(...)`; only write the head once the response is known not to be a quota failure (the stream path must keep writing its head up front). Equivalently, restructure so the head is written at the point the body is ended for non-stream responses.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A non-stream request whose primary backend returns HTTP 200 with `{"error":{"code":429,...}}` or `{"error":{"type":"insufficient_quota",...}}` tries the fallback target instead of hanging; if the fallback succeeds, its (model-rewritten) response is returned; if it also fails, the client gets the existing 502 `All design code backends failed` response promptly.
- [ ] The same holds when the *fallback* target returns the in-body quota error: prompt 502, no hang.
- [ ] Unchanged behaviour: HTTP-status 429/5xx fallback, connection-error fallback, successful non-stream responses (status, headers, `model` rewritten to the design model id), and streaming responses.
- [ ] Regression tests cover the in-body quota case (primary and fallback) with stub backends — `bin/design-code-proxy.mjs` currently has no test file; `bin/codex-proxy.test.mjs` / `bin/muse-proxy.test.mjs` show the stub-backend pattern to follow.

Cross-repo check: `design-code-proxy` exists only in this repo (git grep across developing-today/opencode, developing-today/openchamber, dezren39/nix: no copies) — no cross-repo set.

title: design-code-proxy: forwarded Content-Length truncates the re-serialized success body (PR #682)
body:
## Finding

`bin/design-code-proxy.mjs`'s `writeHead()` helper (added by PR #682, fixing #681) forwards the backend's `Content-Length` header verbatim, but the non-stream success path then sends a **different body** than the backend sent: it re-serializes the parsed JSON with the `model` field rewritten and pretty-printing (`JSON.stringify(json, null, 2)`). Whenever the backend sets `Content-Length` — the normal behaviour of a buffered JSON HTTP server — the forwarded length is the length of the backend's original (usually compact) body, so the client reads exactly that many bytes and gets **truncated, unparseable JSON**.

Evidence (PR + current main):

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/682 (1 commit `be7244972df90becc95b70b018ab23489c6f8163`, merge `c6ec7bd623df42909fdfa2225d249b593ad2e44c` = current main)
- `bin/design-code-proxy.mjs:224-231` on main `c6ec7bd6`:

  ```js
  const writeHead = () => {
    if (!clientRes.headersSent) {
      clientRes.writeHead(localRes.statusCode || 200, {
        ...localRes.headers,
        'Access-Control-Allow-Origin': '*'
      });
    }
  };
  ```

  `...localRes.headers` includes the backend's `content-length`.
- `bin/design-code-proxy.mjs:270-272`: `json.model = modelId; writeHead(); clientRes.end(JSON.stringify(json, null, 2));` — the body actually sent is longer than the backend's body in essentially every case (pretty-printing alone guarantees it; the model rewrite usually changes the length too).

## Reproduced on current main (`c6ec7bd6`)

Ran the real `bin/design-code-proxy.mjs` with stub backends (same stub pattern as `bin/design-code-proxy.test.mjs`), except the primary stub sets an explicit `Content-Length` on its compact JSON success body, as a standard HTTP server does:

- Request: non-stream `design-code-flash` chat completion, primary returns 200 with `Content-Length: 191` and a 191-byte compact JSON body.
- Proxy response: status 200, `content-length: 191` forwarded — but the re-serialized pretty body is longer, so the client receives exactly 191 bytes, ending mid-JSON.
- `JSON.parse` of the received body fails: `Expected ',' or '}' after property value in JSON at position 191`.
- Control: the PR's own test suite passes 5/5 on the same main — its stubs never set `Content-Length` (Node then answers chunked), which is why the suite cannot see this. The sibling in-repo proxies (muse/codex/agy) also happen to answer chunked (they set only `Content-Type`), so the default local chain may not trigger it today; any backend that sets `Content-Length` — e.g. the real Antigravity LS backend this proxy fronts, or any Go/Rust/framework server — truncates every successful non-stream response through this proxy.

The streaming path uses the same `writeHead()` spread, so the same mismatch applies in principle there too (each SSE chunk's `model` is rewritten, changing lengths); SSE backends normally answer chunked, so the verified harm is the non-stream path.

## Why it matters

This turns the proxy's success path into corrupted output for a whole class of standards-compliant backends: the client gets a 200 with a syntactically invalid JSON body instead of the completion. It sits in the exact helper PR #682 introduced, and the new test file's stubs mask it by never sending the one header that triggers it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A non-stream success response from a backend that sets `Content-Length` arrives at the client complete and parseable, with `model` rewritten to the design model id (no truncation).
- [ ] The proxy does not forward a stale `Content-Length` for any body it re-serializes (drop the header and let Node frame the response, or set it to the actual sent length); headers for bodies forwarded byte-for-byte (the non-JSON catch branch) stay correct.
- [ ] Regression test: a stub backend that sets an explicit `Content-Length` on its JSON success body, asserting the client receives the full model-rewritten body; the existing 5 tests in `bin/design-code-proxy.test.mjs` still pass.
- [ ] Streaming success behaviour unchanged.

title: antigravity-ls-proxy: reasoning_effort 'default'/'name' resolves to a non-enum model — MODEL_MAP metadata keys pass the family lookup
body:
## Bug

`bin/antigravity-ls-proxy.mjs` — `resolveModelEnum`, step 3 (family-with-effort lookup, lines 138–140):

```js
let effort = (requestedEffort || family.default || 'medium').toLowerCase().trim();
if (!family[effort]) effort = family.default || Object.keys(family)[0];
const enumVal = family[effort];
```

The guard only checks that `family[effort]` is *truthy*. A family entry in `MODEL_MAP` is not just effort → enum: it also carries the metadata keys `default` (an effort name, e.g. `'medium'`) and `name` (a display name, e.g. `'Gemini 3.8 Flash'`). A client that sends either of those strings as `reasoning_effort` / `effort` (both are read from the request body at the chat-completions handler) therefore "resolves" successfully — to a value that is not a model enum at all. That bogus value is then sent to the language server as `model:` in `GetModelResponse` and as `plannerConfig.requestedModel.model` in cascade mode, where it can only fail (or be misinterpreted) server-side, instead of falling back to the family's default effort the way a genuinely unknown effort does.

## Evidence (verified this run)

The function and `MODEL_MAP` were extracted verbatim from current `main` and driven directly:

| request | result `modelEnum` |
|---|---|
| `gemini-3.8-flash`, effort `"default"` | `"medium"` ❌ (an effort name, not an enum) |
| `gemini-3.8-flash`, effort `"name"` | `"Gemini 3.8 Flash"` ❌ (the display name) |
| `gemini-3.1-pro`, effort `"default"` | `"high"` ❌ |
| `gemini-3.8-flash`, effort `"high"` | `"MODEL_PLACEHOLDER_M318"` ✅ |
| `gemini-3.1-pro`, effort `"medium"` (not offered) | `"MODEL_PLACEHOLDER_M37"` ✅ correct default fallback |
| `gemini-3.8-flash`, no effort | `"MODEL_PLACEHOLDER_M319"` ✅ |

So an unrecognized effort falls back correctly, but an effort that happens to collide with a `MODEL_MAP` metadata key slips through with a garbage "enum".

## Why it matters

- The proxy's own contract (step 5 of the same function) is "refuse rather than quietly run a different model than the one asked for" — this path does the opposite: it quietly runs with a non-model value.
- `reasoning_effort` is client-controlled in the OpenAI-shaped API; values like `"default"` are plausible from generic clients/configs. The failure surfaces downstream as an opaque language-server error naming a model the user never asked for, far from the real cause.

## Suggested fix

In step 3, accept an effort only when its mapped value is actually an enum (e.g. a string starting with `MODEL_`, matching every effort value in `MODEL_MAP`); otherwise fall back to `family.default` (and validate that fallback the same way). Equivalently, restrict the accepted effort names to the known effort keys (`low` / `medium` / `high` / `extra-low`) before indexing the family object.

## Acceptance criteria

- `resolveModelEnum('gemini-3.8-flash', 'default')` and `('gemini-3.8-flash', 'name')` return the family's default-effort enum (`MODEL_PLACEHOLDER_M319`), never `"medium"` / `"Gemini 3.8 Flash"`.
- Existing correct behaviour is unchanged: valid efforts resolve to their enums, an unoffered effort (e.g. `medium` on `gemini-3.1-pro`) still falls back to the family default, and unknown models still throw the 400 "Unknown model" error.
- A regression test covers the metadata-key efforts (`default`, `name`) — this proxy currently has no test file, so a black-box test in the style of `bin/muse-proxy.test.mjs` (spawn the proxy against a stub language server via `ANTIGRAVITY_LS_ADDRESS`/`ANTIGRAVITY_CSRF_TOKEN` and capture the `model` the proxy sends) or an equivalent unit test of the resolver is acceptable.

title: clef-proxy: invalid client JSON returns 500 instead of 400 — body parse shares the upstream try/catch, non-JSON upstream is masked, and there are no tests
body:
## Problem

`bin/clef-proxy.mjs` is the only bin proxy whose client-body parse shares one `try/catch` with the upstream call, so a client error is reported as a server error:

- `bin/clef-proxy.mjs:115-157` — `JSON.parse(bodyText)` sits inside the same `try` as the Cloudflare fetch, and the single `catch` at :154-156 always answers `500`.
- Verified live on main (4f905d75): `POST /v1/systemone` with body `not-json{` returns **500** `{"error":"Unexpected token 'o', \"not-json{\" is not valid JSON"}`. Every sibling proxy returns **400** for the same input (e.g. muse-proxy.mjs, codex-proxy.mjs, agy-proxy.mjs, antigravity-ls-proxy.mjs all parse in a dedicated try and answer 400).
- Same catch also swallows upstream-shape errors: if the Cloudflare gateway returns a non-JSON body (e.g. an HTML 502/429 page), `await cfRes.json()` at :142 throws and the client gets a bare 500 with a JSON-parse message, losing the upstream status. If the upstream body parses to `null`, `cfData.success` at :144 throws a TypeError down the same path.

`bin/clef-proxy.mjs` also has no test file at all — every other bin proxy has one (`muse-proxy.test.mjs`, `codex-proxy.test.mjs`, `agy-proxy` via its suite, `design-code-proxy.test.mjs`, `antigravity-ls-proxy.test.mjs`, `proxy-port.test.mjs`).

## Why it matters

Clients (and OpenCode's error handling) treat 400 and 500 differently: a malformed request reported as 500 looks like a proxy outage, invites retries of a request that can never succeed, and hides real upstream failures behind a parse-error message with the wrong status.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `POST /v1/systemone` with a non-JSON body returns 400 (matching the sibling proxies), with the parse error in the body.
- [ ] A non-JSON upstream response does not surface as a client-facing JSON-parse 500; it is reported as an upstream failure preserving the upstream status (or 502).
- [ ] A `null`/non-object upstream JSON body does not throw on `cfData.success`.
- [ ] New `bin/clef-proxy.test.mjs` (run: `node --test bin/clef-proxy.test.mjs`) covers at least: health, invalid JSON → 400, missing token → 401. The 400 test fails on the pre-fix code.

title: id: match_kind is defined four times — CLI, REPL, protocol and a dead helpers copy can silently diverge
body:
## Problem

`match_kind` — the exact/prefix/contains ranking that decides how `find` results are ordered — is defined **four times** in `pkgs/id`, with byte-identical bodies (verified on main `3d7b96a5`):

| # | Location | Visibility | Production caller |
|---|----------|-----------|-------------------|
| 1 | `pkgs/id/src/lib.rs:387` | `pub fn` (crate root, `id::match_kind`) | `pkgs/id/src/commands/find.rs:931,938` (imports `crate::match_kind` at `find.rs:81`) |
| 2 | `pkgs/id/src/helpers.rs:298` | `pub fn` (`id::helpers::match_kind`) | **none found** — only its own unit tests (`helpers.rs:422+`) and doctest (`helpers.rs:287`) reference it |
| 3 | `pkgs/id/src/protocol.rs:525` | private `MetaProtocol::match_kind` | server-side find in the same file (`protocol.rs:685,692`) |
| 4 | `pkgs/id/src/commands/repl.rs:771` | private `Self::match_kind` | REPL find in the same file (`repl.rs:725,732`) |

Each copy also carries its own partially-overlapping test suite (`lib.rs:617+`, `helpers.rs:422+`, `protocol.rs:754+`, plus `find.rs:974+` exercising copy 1). The suites have already drifted in coverage: e.g. the empty-needle and case-sensitivity cases are pinned in different subsets at different sites.

## Why it matters

The same user query is ranked through three different code paths depending on entry point — CLI `find` (copy 1), the server/protocol find (copy 3), and the REPL find (copy 4). Today they agree only because the bodies happen to be identical. Any future fix or ranking change (e.g. word-boundary scoring, case handling, empty-query handling) applied to one copy silently diverges the three surfaces, and the duplicated test suites give false confidence that "the" behaviour is pinned. Copy 2 is additionally a dead public API: it looks like the canonical helper, is documented with a doctest, and is the one a new contributor would most likely edit — to no effect.

## Suggested fix

Pick ONE canonical definition (the crate-root `id::match_kind` in `lib.rs` is the one the CLI already uses; `MatchKind` itself is defined in `protocol.rs:93` and re-exported at `lib.rs:269`), then:

- Delete the `helpers.rs`, `protocol.rs` and `repl.rs` copies; make `protocol.rs` and `repl.rs` call the canonical function.
- Decide explicitly what happens to the public `id::helpers::match_kind` path (remove it, or keep it as a re-export of the canonical fn) and note the choice in the PR.
- Merge the four test suites into one at the canonical site, keeping the union of cases (empty needle/haystack, case sensitivity, unicode, ordering).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Exactly one `fn match_kind` definition remains in `pkgs/id/src/` (`grep -rn "fn match_kind" pkgs/id/src` returns one hit, plus call sites).
- [ ] CLI find, REPL find and protocol find all resolve to that definition.
- [ ] The merged test suite covers every case the four old suites covered (no case silently dropped).
- [ ] `cargo test --no-default-features` (or the id `test-unit` flake check) passes; no behaviour change for any existing test.

title: home: PR #695's dead-env cleanup left two in the same block — file watcher is not actually off (dead DISABLE_FILEWATCHER name) and LSP_TOOL still set
body:
## Finding

PR #695 (merged, merge commit `3d7b96a5cd4d5476942ec5efa6a7df128159e244`, commit `2446d3e999c86c16754bbda901c535b552395154`) dropped three dead OpenCode env vars from `home/common/default.nix`, citing developing-today/opencode#105 and developing-today/opencode#115 — but the same `sessionVariables` block still sets two more names those same issues adjudicated as dead, and one of them carries an active behavioural intent that is silently not happening.

Found by the pr-diff-review job reviewing PR #695; verified against current main of both repos on 2026-10-23 (code `3d7b96a5`, opencode `fe5d6c8e943882a01d7914264b710c7e8ac11b5a`), cross-checked via local clones and `gh api` contents.

## Evidence

### 1. `OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_DISABLE_FILEWATCHER` — the file watcher is NOT off, despite the config saying it is

- `home/common/default.nix:1252-1255` on current main:
  ```
  # File watcher off by default (Drew, 2026-10-20): the working trees
  # are giant, and watching costs more than the live-external-edit
  # awareness it buys. Diffs are git-computed on demand either way.
  OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_DISABLE_FILEWATCHER = "1";
  ```
- Nothing in opencode reads that name: `git grep OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_DISABLE_FILEWATCHER` on opencode main returns only docs rows (`packages/web/.../cli.mdx`), no code reader.
- The actual gate is `packages/cli/src/server-process.ts:146` in opencode:
  ```ts
  filewatcher: !truthy(process.env.OPENCODE_FILEWATCHER_DISABLE ?? process.env.OPENCODE_DISABLE_FILEWATCHER),
  ```
  i.e. the watcher defaults to ON and is disabled only via `OPENCODE_DISABLE_FILEWATCHER` / `OPENCODE_FILEWATCHER_DISABLE`. Neither correct name is set anywhere in this repo (`git grep` on main: no hits).
- This exact dead name was already adjudicated in opencode: #104 ("filewatcher-disable sets a dead env name — OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_DISABLE_FILEWATCHER is read nowhere", CLOSED, fixed there by renaming opencode's own setters to `OPENCODE_DISABLE_FILEWATCHER`), and #115's body calls it out again. PR #695 removed `OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_ICON_DISCOVERY` ~7 lines above this line, in the same block, but left this one.

### 2. `OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_LSP_TOOL` — dead line from the same #105 set PR #695 was cleaning up

- `home/common/default.nix:1240` on current main: `OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_LSP_TOOL = "1";`
- opencode#105 named this variable explicitly as one of its four dead vars ("the LSP-tool gate (`OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_LSP_TOOL`…)"), with `git grep` excluding docs returning zero hits; re-verified this run on opencode main `fe5d6c8e`: zero hits outside `packages/web`. #105 is CLOSED and its English docs row for this variable is gone.
- PR #695's stated four-var list covered three of #105's vars plus #115's icon-discovery var; this one — the fourth #105 var — was not in the list and survives.

## Why it matters

- Item 1 is not cosmetic: the home config's stated intent (Drew, 2026-10-20 — watcher off because the working trees are giant and watching costs more than it buys) is silently not in effect on any machine built from this config. The server spawns with the file watcher on by default.
- Item 2 is the same silent-no-op class PR #695 was created to eliminate; leaving it re-creates the "set but unread" trap for the next reader of this block.
- Cross-repo scope checked: neither dead name is set in developing-today/openchamber or dezren39/nix (`git grep` on their mains: no hits) — this is a code-repo-only setter, so this single issue tracks the whole finding.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `home/common/default.nix` sets `OPENCODE_DISABLE_FILEWATCHER = "1";` (the name `server-process.ts` actually reads) in place of the dead `OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_DISABLE_FILEWATCHER` line, keeping the "file watcher off by default" comment accurate.
- [ ] The `OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_LSP_TOOL = "1";` line is removed (mirroring PR #695's drop decision for its #105 siblings), or a reader is implemented in opencode with a test — dropping is the expected route.
