title: id(web): clearing the world seed field silently installs with seed 0 — empty input passes the Number() guard in both install and compile flows
id(web): Go to Line accepts 0/negatives as line 1, truncates fractions, and silently closes on out-of-range lines
body:
## Problem

The Go to Line dialog in the `pkgs/id` web editor (`pkgs/id/web/src/goto-line.ts`) does not validate the entered line number on Enter. The `<input type="number" min="1">` attributes are never enforced, because the `keydown` handler reads the raw value and acts on it directly — there is no `<form>` / constraint-validation step.

Verified on main `d495a5cd` with a temporary vitest probe driving the real dialog (probe since removed; the three cases below reproduce with the existing `goto-line.test.ts` harness):

1. **Line `0` (and negatives) are treated as line 1 — and create an invalid selection.** `goto-line.ts:88` does `parseInt(dialogInput?.value ?? "", 10)`; the only check is `Number.isNaN`. `getLineStartPos` (`goto-line.ts:36`) returns `0` for any `targetLine <= 1`, so `0` and `-3` both dispatch `TextSelection.create(doc, 0)`. ProseMirror logs `TextSelection endpoint not pointing into a node with inline content (doc)` and the selection lands at doc position `0`, outside the `code_block`. Typing `0` should be rejected, not silently reinterpreted as the top of the file.
2. **Fractional input is silently truncated.** `2.9` moves the cursor to line 2 (doc position `8` in a `first\nsecond\nthird` doc) because `parseInt` drops the fraction. A line number is an integer; `2.9` is invalid input, not line 2.
3. **Out-of-range input closes the dialog with no feedback.** `999` in a 3-line document: `getLineStartPos` returns `null`, nothing moves, and `closeGotoLine()` runs unconditionally (`goto-line.ts:100`) — the dialog disappears and the user cannot tell whether the jump happened, failed, or the line does not exist. The dialog already knows the line count (it renders `Line # (1–N)` and sets `input.max`), but the handler never compares against it.

Existing tests (`pkgs/id/web/src/goto-line.test.ts`) cover only valid inputs (`1`, `2`), Escape, and dialog lifecycle — none of these invalid cases.

## Why it matters

Go to Line is a primary navigation affordance in the editor. Silently treating `0`/negatives as line 1, truncating fractions, and swallowing out-of-range jumps with no feedback makes navigation unpredictable, and the `0` case additionally constructs a selection ProseMirror itself warns is not inside inline content.

## Acceptance criteria

- Entering `0`, a negative number, a fractional number (e.g. `2.9`), a non-numeric value, or a line greater than the document's line count does **not** move the cursor and does **not** silently close-and-forget: the dialog stays open (or reopens/focuses the input) with the invalid value visible/selectable so the user can correct it. A brief inline hint is welcome but not required.
- Valid integers in `[1, lineCount]` keep working exactly as today (line 1 → start of the code block content, line N → start of line N).
- New tests in `goto-line.test.ts` cover at least: `0`, a negative, a fraction, and a value greater than the line count — each asserting the selection did not move and the dialog did not silently succeed.
- The valid-path tests already in `goto-line.test.ts` continue to pass.

## Suggested fix

In the Enter handler, parse strictly (reject anything that is not a base-10 integer string, e.g. via a `Number` + `Number.isInteger` check on the trimmed value rather than bare `parseInt`), compare against `getLineCount(activeView)`, and only dispatch + `closeGotoLine()` on success; on failure, keep the dialog open and select the input text.

Single-repo: `getLineStartPos` / the goto-line dialog exist only in `developing-today/code` (`pkgs/id/web`); no copy exists in opencode, openchamber, or dezren39/nix.

title: id(web): Tab/Shift-Tab on a selection indents/dedents the wrong lines — unselected lines changed, selection's first line skipped
body:
## Summary

`pkgs/id/web/src/indent.ts` — Tab (indent) and Shift-Tab (dedent) with a
multi-line selection indent/dedent the wrong lines: lines outside the
selection are changed, and the line the selection starts in can be skipped.

## Evidence (verified on main `d495a5cd` with a temporary vitest probe driving the real commands; probe removed after the run)

Document `line1\nline2\nline3` in a `code_block` (content positions:
line1 at 1, line2 at 7, line3 at 13):

| Selection | Expected | Actual |
|---|---|---|
| line2 only (7–12) | only `line2` indented | `"  line1\n  line2\n  line3"` — all three lines indented |
| mid-line2 → mid-line3 (9–15) | `line2` + `line3` indented | `"  line1\nline2\n  line3"` — unselected line1 indented, line2 (where the selection starts) NOT indented |
| `a` only (1–2) in `a\nb\nc\nd\ne` | only `a` indented | all five lines indented |
| dedent: line3 only (17–23) in `  line1\n  line2\n  line3` | only `line3` dedented | `"line1\nline2\nline3"` — all three lines dedented |

## Root cause

`indentCommand` (indent.ts:55-58):

```ts
if (lineStart >= from || lineStart === blockStart) {
  if (lineStart <= to + offset) {
```

- `lineStart === blockStart` unconditionally indents the block's first line,
  whatever the selection.
- `lineStart >= from` excludes the line containing `from` whenever the
  selection starts mid-line (its line start is `< from`).
- `lineStart <= to + offset` compares an original-document line start
  against the selection end shifted by the insertions already made, so
  every inserted indent widens the range and pulls in following lines.

`dedentCommand` (indent.ts:107) has the mirror flaw for selections:
`lineStarts.filter((ls) => ls <= to)` has no lower bound, so every line
from the block start up to the selection end is dedented.

The existing test `indents only lines overlapping the selection`
(indent.test.ts) does not catch this: it asserts only that line2 is
indented and line3 is untouched, and its comment even records the
blockStart side effect as expected.

## Why it matters

Tab/Shift-Tab on a selection is a basic editor operation in the id web UI.
Today it silently reformats lines the user never selected — and with a
collaborator-shared document, that churn is broadcast to peers.

## Acceptance criteria

- Indent and dedent with a selection change exactly the lines the
  selection overlaps: the line containing `from` through the line
  containing `to` (state the rule chosen for a selection ending exactly
  at a line start, and pin it in a test).
- The four probe cases above behave as in the Expected column.
- Regression tests cover: selection on a single non-first line,
  selection starting mid-line, selection ending before later lines
  (no offset drift), and the dedent mirror cases.
- The existing indent/dedent tests still pass, updated where they
  encoded the buggy blockStart behaviour; single-cursor Tab/Shift-Tab
  behaviour unchanged.

Single-repo: `git grep indentCommand` in the opencode, openchamber and
nix clones returns nothing — the plugin lives only in pkgs/id/web.

title: id(web): images at the advertised 10 MiB max pass the client check but are rejected by the server's 10 MiB whole-body limit
body:
## Summary

An image at (or just under) the client's advertised 10 MiB maximum passes the
web UI's size check but is rejected by the server, because the client's limit
applies to the **file** while the server's identical 10 MiB limit applies to
the **whole multipart request body**, whose encoding adds overhead the file
budget does not account for.

## Evidence (verified on main `26c54292`, 2026-10-23)

- Client: `pkgs/id/web/src/image-upload.ts:34` — `MAX_IMAGE_SIZE = 10 * 1024 * 1024`;
  paste/drop handlers skip a file only when `file.size > MAX_IMAGE_SIZE`
  (`image-upload.ts:170` and `:198`), so a file of exactly 10 MiB is uploaded.
  The constant is pinned by `image-upload.test.ts:43-49`.
- Server: `pkgs/id/src/web/routes.rs:265` — the whole router is layered with
  `DefaultBodyLimit::max(10 * 1024 * 1024)`. `upload_handler`
  (`routes.rs:1272`) has no size check of its own, so the body limit is the
  only server-side bound and it counts every byte of the multipart envelope.
- Measured with Node's `FormData`/`Request` (the same encoding the browser
  produces) for a file named `photo.png`:
  - file size 10,485,760 → multipart body 10,485,930 bytes (**170 bytes of
    overhead**: boundary, `Content-Disposition` with the filename, part
    `Content-Type`, closing boundary). Over the server limit → rejected.
  - file size 10,485,660 (100 bytes *under* the advertised max) → body
    10,485,830 → still rejected.
  - file size 10,485,560 → body 10,485,730 → accepted.
  So the effective maximum is ≈200 bytes below the advertised one, and it
  shrinks further with longer filenames. The user sees only a generic
  `Upload failed (…)` error from `uploadImageFile` with no hint that a file
  the UI explicitly allowed is "too large".

## Why it matters

The two sides disagree about what the limit measures, so the boundary of the
documented feature is broken in exactly the range a user who checks the limit
will hit: a 10 MiB image (a common phone-photo size class) is promised by the
client and refused by the server. The failure mode is silent/confusing rather
than a clear "image too large" message.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A file of exactly `MAX_IMAGE_SIZE` bytes (10 MiB) with a typical
      filename uploads successfully end to end, **or** the client limit is
      lowered/documented so the largest client-accepted file always fits the
      server body limit (including multipart overhead for long filenames).
- [ ] The server rejects an over-limit file with a clear size-related error
      (not a generic multipart/body error leaking through `upload_handler`).
- [ ] A test pins the relationship between the two limits (e.g. a Rust test
      asserting the upload route's effective body limit exceeds the client
      `MAX_IMAGE_SIZE` plus a multipart-overhead allowance, or a client test
      for the adjusted constant) so the two cannot drift back into conflict.
- [ ] Existing `image-upload` web tests and the Rust web route tests still pass.

Suggested fix direction: raise the body limit for the `/api/upload` route
only (route-scoped `DefaultBodyLimit` above 10 MiB + overhead, e.g. 11 MiB)
and/or add an explicit file-size check in `upload_handler` returning
`413` with a clear message — rather than raising the global router limit,
which also guards `/api/save` and the other POST routes.

title: id(web): Find panel and Go to Line dialog never appear after the editor is recreated — module singletons outlive the editor, destroy helpers have no production caller
body:
## Problem

Find (Ctrl+F / Ctrl+H) and Go to Line (Ctrl+G) silently stop working after the editor is recreated — e.g. after disconnecting from one world/session and opening another file. The shortcuts return `true` but no panel/dialog ever appears in the new editor.

## Root cause (same pattern, both modules)

Both modules keep their DOM in a **module-level singleton** that is created once for the first editor and never invalidated:

- `pkgs/id/web/src/search-panel.ts`: `panelState` (lines 47–54) is module-global. `openPanel` only creates the panel `if (!panelState.panelEl)`, and `panelState.view` / the event handlers captured by `setupPanelEvents` are bound to the **first** view forever.
- `pkgs/id/web/src/goto-line.ts`: `dialogEl` / `dialogInput` (lines 14–16) are module-global. `openGotoLine` only creates the dialog `if (!dialogEl)`. (It does refresh `activeView`, but the dialog element itself stays attached to the old container.)

Both modules export a destroy function (`destroySearchPanel`, `destroyGotoLineDialog`) documented as "Call this when the editor is being destroyed" — but **nothing in production calls either one**. The only callers are the test files' `afterEach`, which is why the existing suites never see the leak. Production teardown (`pkgs/id/web/src/main.ts`, disconnect path, ~line 1287) only calls `this.collab.editor.view.destroy()`.

When the old container is removed from the document, the singleton element is detached with it. The next Ctrl+F / Ctrl+G "opens" the panel by setting `style.display = ""` on the detached node and focusing a detached input — invisible, and for search the handlers still dispatch to the destroyed first view.

## Reproduction (verified this run, on main a8992eb7)

A vitest case mirroring the production lifecycle — create editor 1, open the panel, `view.destroy()` + remove container (**without** calling the destroy helper, exactly as production does), create editor 2, trigger the shortcut — fails for both modules:

- search: second container has no `.search-panel` after Mod-f (`expected null not to be null`)
- goto-line: second container has no `.goto-line-dialog` after Mod-g (same)

Both pass if `destroySearchPanel()` / `destroyGotoLineDialog()` is called between editors, confirming the missing invalidation is the whole defect.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] After an editor is destroyed and a new one created (no manual destroy-helper call in between), Ctrl+F/Ctrl+H shows a working find/replace panel **in the new editor's container**, bound to the new view (typing searches the new document; Enter/replace act on it).
- [ ] Same for Ctrl+G: the Go to Line dialog appears in the new container and jumps in the new document.
- [ ] Regression tests for both modules that recreate the editor **without** calling the destroy helpers (mirroring production teardown) and assert the panel/dialog appears and works in the second editor.
- [ ] Existing search-panel and goto-line suites still pass; typecheck clean.

Suggested fix shapes (either is fine): make `openPanel`/`openGotoLine` self-healing — if the singleton element is detached or belongs to a different container/view, destroy and recreate it bound to the current view — and/or call the destroy helpers from the editor teardown path in `main.ts`. The self-healing form is more robust: it also covers any future recreation path that forgets the teardown call.

Single-repo: no search-panel/goto-line copies exist in developing-today/opencode, developing-today/openchamber, or dezren39/nix (grep-verified this run).

title: id(web): detectLanguage lets a special-name stem override a known extension — justfile.rs highlights as Just, makefile.md as Makefile
body:
## Summary

`detectLanguage` in `pkgs/id/web/src/highlight.ts` checks the file's *stem* against the special-filename table before it ever looks at the extension, so any file whose stem happens to be a special name is highlighted with the wrong language even when its extension unambiguously names another one.

## Evidence (verified on main df383659, temporary vitest probe since removed)

`highlight.ts:133-143` computes `nameWithoutExt` (basename minus its final extension) and returns `FILENAME_TO_LANG[nameWithoutExt]` before the extension lookup at `highlight.ts:158-162`.

Probe results against the real function:

| filename | returned | correct |
|---|---|---|
| `justfile.rs` | `just` | `rust` |
| `makefile.md` | `makefile` | `markdown` |
| `dockerfile.py` | `dockerfile` | `python` |
| `gemfile.json` | `ruby` | `json` |
| `vagrantfile.toml` | `ruby` | `toml` |
| `cmakelists.rs` | `cmake` | `rust` |
| `rakefile.ts` | `ruby` | `typescript` |

Controls that must keep working:

| filename | returned | correct |
|---|---|---|
| `Dockerfile.dev` | `dockerfile` | `dockerfile` (extension unknown) |
| `CMakeLists.txt` | `cmake` | `cmake` (`.txt` has no language) |
| `src/Dockerfile` | `dockerfile` | `dockerfile` (no extension) |

## Why it matters

The editor picks the Shiki grammar solely from this function (filename-detected language, `highlight.ts` `createSyntaxHighlightPlugin`). A mis-detected file is highlighted with a completely unrelated grammar — e.g. documentation about a Makefile (`makefile.md`) or a Rust source file named after the tool it drives (`justfile.rs`). The special-name rule was only ever meant for files that *are* the special file (`Dockerfile`, `Makefile`, `CMakeLists.txt`, `Dockerfile.dev`); it should not override a known extension.

## Acceptance criteria

- When the basename's extension is present in `EXT_TO_LANG`, the extension wins over the stem special-name match (`justfile.rs` → `rust`, `makefile.md` → `markdown`, `gemfile.json` → `json`).
- Special filenames still win when there is no extension (`Dockerfile`, `Gemfile`, `src/Makefile`) or the extension is unknown (`Dockerfile.dev`, `CMakeLists.txt`).
- Dotfile handling (`.env`, `.gitignore`, `.env.local`, …) is unchanged.
- New regression tests in `highlight.test.ts` cover at least the stem-vs-known-extension cases and the unknown-extension controls above; the existing `detectLanguage` suite passes unchanged.

title: id(ssh): PR #720's dropped-input notice still cannot fire in explorer sessions — the shared counter is counted for them but never claimed
body:
## Finding

PR #720 fixes #602 for world shells: the russh `data()` handler and `SshIo` now share one `Arc<AtomicUsize>` dropped-input counter, so bytes refused after the shell opens reach `SshIo::send`, which claims the notice at the documented `INPUT_DROP_NOTICE_BYTES` (1024) threshold.

The same handler and the same input queue also serve the other session type in the same function, and that branch is not wired:

- In `shell_request` on PR #720's head (`c7756f8c`, `pkgs/id/src/world_ssh.rs:319-325`), the `login.explore` branch creates its own `mpsc::channel(INPUT_QUEUE)` (256 frames, `:42` on the head), stores the sender in `self.input`, and spawns `run_explorer(explorer, handle, channel, bytes)` — with no dropped-input counter.
- The non-explorer branch right below it (`:352`) is the only place that clones the shared counter: `dropped_input: Arc::clone(&self.dropped_input)` into `SshIo`.
- The handler (`data()`, `:371`, counting at `:389` via `record_dropped_input`) counts refused bytes on `TrySendError::Full` regardless of which session type owns `self.input` — it cannot distinguish explorer input from world-shell input.
- `run_explorer` (`:1148-1153` on the head) takes only `explorer, handle, channel, bytes`; nothing in its loop ever calls `claim_dropped_input_notice` / `dropped_input_notice`. The only claim site in the file is `SshIo::send` (`:639`).

So for an explorer (`explore:`) session, refused bytes are still counted into a counter nobody reads and logged with `tracing::warn!` only — the viewer is never told their input was dropped. That is the exact silent-drop shape #549 / #602 were filed for, surviving in the second branch of the same `shell_request` after #720 lands. The explorer drains its queue one line at a time and awaits a hub/directory call per submitted line, so a paste/flood arriving while a line executes can fill the 256-frame queue in the same way.

This does not block PR #720: it correctly satisfies #602's acceptance criteria as written (which scope to the world shell / `SshIo`). This issue tracks the residual branch #602 did not name.

## Evidence

- PR: #720 (`fix(id): share the SSH dropped-input counter with the session so the notice can fire`, fixes #602, 1 commit `c7756f8ce520db275e51a5088b40f655068de9b4`, OPEN at filing, 1 file `pkgs/id/src/world_ssh.rs`, +95/-28). Its diff touches the handler counter, `SshIo`, and the two notice tests — no `run_explorer` / explorer-branch hunk.
- Verified on the PR head via `gh api .../contents/pkgs/id/src/world_ssh.rs?ref=c7756f8c`: `grep -n dropped_input` returns the handler, `SshClient`/`SshIo` fields, `record_dropped_input`/`claim_dropped_input_notice`, and the `SshIo::send` claim — no occurrence in the explorer branch or in `run_explorer`.
- Verified on current main (`df383659`, base of #720, local clone == `gh api commits/main`): the pre-fix structure is the same two branches — explorer at `shell_request` spawns `run_explorer` with no counter, world shell copies the (then-`usize`) counter into `SshIo`.
- Cross-repo: `git grep dropped_input_notice` is clean in the opencode, openchamber and nix clones — `pkgs/id` SSH code lives only in this repo.
- Dedup: `gh search issues "dropped input"` returns only #602 (OPEN, world-shell scope); searches for `explorer dropped`, `explorer input`, `run_explorer dropped` and `INPUT_DROP` return nothing. No open or closed issue tracks the explorer branch.

## Why it matters

An explorer user whose keystrokes/paste are refused under load gets the same "my input vanished" experience #549 set out to eliminate, with only a server-side warn log as evidence. Because the counter is now shared and incremented for explorer sessions too, the post-#720 code gives the impression the notice is handled uniformly — a reader of `data()` sees one counter and one notice mechanism, not a per-branch exception.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The explorer branch in `shell_request` passes the shared dropped-input counter (the same `Arc<AtomicUsize>` the handler counts on) into `run_explorer`.
- [ ] `run_explorer` claims the notice with the same helper/threshold as `SshIo::send` (`claim_dropped_input_notice`, `INPUT_DROP_NOTICE_BYTES`) and writes it to the channel before the next explorer output once the threshold is reached; a failed notice write restores the claimed bytes, so drops are neither lost nor double-counted (same reset-only-on-delivery rule as #602).
- [ ] A test drives the shared counter the way the handler does (or fills a live explorer session's input queue) and observes the `[-- input dropped: N bytes ... --]` notice on the explorer channel; below-threshold drops stay quiet and counted.
- [ ] World-shell behaviour from #720 is unchanged: the existing `world_ssh::` suite (incl. `dropped_input_notice_counts_and_quiet_zero` and `dropped_input_notice_follows_the_shared_counter`) still passes.
- [ ] Alternatively, if explorer sessions are deliberately excluded, that decision is recorded in a code comment at the explorer branch / counter definition and on this issue before closing — not left as a silent gap.

title: Close Jules PR #765 as superseded: cursor work already on main, conflicts with #778, and its claimed search-counting change is not in its diff
body:
## Finding (PR diff review, 2026-10-24)

Open draft PR #765 — `⚡ Bolt: ProseMirror widget recycling and search counting optimization` (Jules, head `b9cf7303c`, opened 2026-10-24T15:06:36Z) — duplicates work already on main, conflicts with the sanctioned salvage PR #778, and its body claims a change its diff does not contain. It should be closed as superseded, not merged.

## Evidence

1. **The claimed search-counting change is not in the diff.** The body says it "replaced an O(N) document traversal for counting search matches with an O(1) read from a precomputed set", but the PR touches only two files (`pkgs/id/web/src/cursors.ts` +49/-60, `pkgs/id/web/src/image-upload.ts` +1/-0) and the full 183-line diff contains no search code at all. (The search-counting theme is also the subject of many earlier closed Bolt PRs — #142, #232, #235, #252, #447, #521 — and of open triage issue #310.)
2. **The cursor work is already on main.** Current main (`3184df61`) already has lazy `() => HTMLElement` widget factories and stable state-derived keys in `pkgs/id/web/src/cursors.ts` — e.g. line 655 `key: cursor-own-${ownCursor.clientID}-${ownCursor.color}` is byte-identical to #765's proposed own-cursor key (landed via `09e3cc2b`, the same landing that made Jules PR #753 superseded in #760).
3. **Where #765 differs from main it is weaker.** Main's standalone cursor key (cursors.ts:747) is `cursor-${clientID}-${opacity}-${color}-${connectionState}-${encodeURIComponent(cursor.name)}`; #765's version drops the cursor **name**, the exact weaker-keys flaw #760 cited for not merging #753 (recycled DOM can go stale when only the name changes — cf. #331).
4. **Direct overlap with PR #778.** #765 adds `key: image-upload-${action.id}` to the placeholder `Decoration.widget` call in `pkgs/id/web/src/image-upload.ts`; #778 (the #760 salvage PR, open) adds `key: placeholder-${action.id}` to the same call. Both cannot merge cleanly, and #778 is the tracked salvage vehicle.

## Why it matters

Merging #765 would regress main's cursor keys (dropping `name`), conflict with #778, and deliver none of the search improvement its body advertises. Leaving it open invites exactly the duplicate-Jules pile-up #310 and #760 are trying to clear.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] PR #765 is closed as superseded, with a comment linking this issue, main's cursor landing (`09e3cc2b` / cursors.ts on main), and PR #778 for the image-upload key.
- [ ] No part of #765 is merged unless a specific hunk is shown to be absent from main and stronger than main's version — in which case it is salvaged via #778 or a successor, not by merging #765.
- [ ] The discrepancy between the PR body (search-counting claim) and its diff is noted on the PR so future Bolt runs are not credited with it.

Related: #310, #760, #778, #331. Filed by the pr-diff-review job; this job files only — a sweep does the closing.

title: id(web): Origin check ignores the port — a different localhost port passes as same-origin (CSRF/CSWSH gap in security.rs)
body:
## Problem

The id web UI's Origin check (`pkgs/id/src/web/security.rs`) compares only the **host** of the `Origin` header against the host of the `Host` header — the port is stripped from both sides before comparison, so an origin on a *different port* of the same host passes as "same-origin".

This defeats the layer the module docs say it provides (security.rs:12-15): defeating cross-site request forgery and cross-site WebSocket hijacking for browser requests. An origin is scheme + host + **port**: a page served from `http://localhost:9999` (any other local web app, dev server, or attacker page proxied/served on another local port) is a different origin from the id UI on `http://localhost:3000`, but the guard treats them as the same. WebSocket handshakes carry no CORS preflight, so the Origin check is the only browser-side defence for the `/ws/*` routes when no token is configured (the default loopback setup relies on exactly these host/origin layers).

## Evidence (verified on main `1161bcff`)

- `security.rs:73-83` — `host_only()` strips an optional `:port` (and lower-cases) from a Host/Origin authority: `host_only("localhost:9999") == host_only("localhost:3000") == "localhost"`.
- `security.rs:138-145` — the guard's same-origin test is exactly that comparison:
  ```rust
  let same = origin_authority(origin).is_some_and(|a| host_only(a) == host_only(&host_header));
  ```
  So a request with `Host: localhost:3000` and `Origin: http://localhost:9999` evaluates `same == true` and is **not** refused.
- The existing test `same_origin_is_allowed_cross_origin_is_not` (security.rs:278) only exercises a same-port origin (`http://localhost:3000` vs Host `localhost:3000`) and a different-host origin (`https://evil.example`); no test covers a different-port origin.
- No other layer compensates: `grep -rn Origin pkgs/id/src/web` shows this guard is the only Origin check in the web stack.

Repro (verified by running the guard): a test added to the security tests in a scratch worktree driving `guard` with `Host: localhost:3000` and `Origin: http://localhost:9999`, asserting the *current* behaviour, **passed** on main `1161bcff` — i.e. the different-port origin was answered `200 OK` where a true same-origin check would refuse with `403`. Full run: `cargo test --features web --lib web::security::` → 12 passed, 0 failed (11 pre-existing + the repro case).

## Why it matters

- The loopback default has no token, so layers 2+3 (host allow-list + origin check) are the whole browser-attack defence. Layer 3 currently does not distinguish local origins, which is precisely the neighbour it exists to distinguish: other content reachable in the user's browser on another local port.
- The collab/world WebSocket routes are state-changing and long-lived; a cross-site WebSocket from a different local origin inherits the user's ambient access to the UI.

## Suggested fix

Compare the full authority (host **and** port) for the Origin check, while keeping the host allow-list check host-only as it is today:

- Keep `host_only()` for the allow-list comparison (step 2).
- For step 3, compare a port-preserving normalised authority (lower-cased host, explicit port when present; IPv6 brackets handled like `host_only` does) of `origin_authority(origin)` against the `Host` header authority.
- Decide and document the no-port cases: an Origin with no explicit port vs a Host with an explicit port (e.g. behind a proxy / default-port serving) — treat missing port as the scheme default, or refuse; either is defensible, but it must be a deliberate, tested choice, not an accident of stripping.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Request with `Host: localhost:3000` and `Origin: http://localhost:9999` (and the IPv4/`[::1]` equivalents) is refused with 403.
- [ ] Same-authority origins (same host, same port, any case) still pass; different-host origins still 403; `Origin: null` still refused.
- [ ] New regression tests cover different-port origin refusal and same-port acceptance; existing security tests pass (`cargo test --features web web::security`).
- [ ] Module docs updated so the stated Origin guarantee matches the implemented comparison.

title: id(web): file-list tag pill truncation panics on a multi-byte character straddling byte 256 — templates.rs slices &v[..256] off-boundary
body:
## Problem

The web file list's tag-pill rendering truncates long tag values with a raw byte slice that **panics** when the cut point falls inside a multi-byte UTF-8 character — taking down the file-list request for any file carrying such a tag.

`pkgs/id/src/web/templates.rs:261-265` (`render_file_list`):

```rust
let truncated = if v.len() > crate::tags::TAG_DISPLAY_MAX_BYTES {  // 256
    format!("{}…", &v[..crate::tags::TAG_DISPLAY_MAX_BYTES])
} else {
    v.clone()
};
```

`&v[..256]` panics with `byte index 256 is not a char boundary` whenever byte 256 is mid-character. Tag values are user-controlled (set from the CLI, the bulk-tag UI, or synced from peers) and reach this code via `get_file_list` → `FileInfo.tags` (`routes.rs`), so one crafted/accidental tag value makes `/files` (and the `/api/files` partial) fail for that file list.

## Repro (verified on main `1161bcff`)

Verbatim harness of the two lines above with `v = "a"×255 + "é" + "tail-tail-tail"` (length 269 > 256; `é` occupies bytes 255..257):

```
thread 'main' panicked at trunc.rs:5:38:
end byte index 256 is not a char boundary; it is inside 'é' (bytes 255..257 of string)
```

Any value longer than 256 bytes whose byte-256 offset splits a 2–4-byte character triggers it (e.g. an emoji or CJK character at that offset, or a long CJK/accented value).

## The safe helper already exists in the same crate

`pkgs/id/src/commands/tag.rs:90-100` defines `pub fn truncate_on_char_boundary(s: &str, max: usize) -> String`, which walks back to a char boundary before slicing — and its tests already cover exactly this shape (`tag.rs:407`: a value with `é` straddling the limit). The web template re-implemented the truncation inline and missed the boundary walk.

## Suggested fix

In `templates.rs`, replace the inline slice with the existing helper:

```rust
let truncated = crate::commands::tag::truncate_on_char_boundary(v, crate::tags::TAG_DISPLAY_MAX_BYTES);
```

(`truncate_on_char_boundary` returns the string unchanged when it fits, so the `if` can go.) Add a regression test rendering a file list whose tag value has a multi-byte character straddling byte 256, asserting the pill shows the boundary-truncated value + `…` and nothing panics.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Rendering a file list containing a >256-byte tag value with a multi-byte character straddling byte 256 does not panic and shows the value truncated on a char boundary with `…`.
- [ ] Values ≤256 bytes and pure-ASCII long values render exactly as before.
- [ ] The web template uses the crate's existing `truncate_on_char_boundary` (no second inline implementation).
- [ ] New regression test in the web templates tests; `cargo test --features web` web template tests pass.

title: id(world-doctor): PR #801 — a Warn finding exits nonzero claiming '6 problem(s)', and the ceiling/profile checks are dead from the CLI (inputs hardcoded None)
body:
## Problem

PR #801's new `id world doctor` (F12.16, tracking issue #559) does not behave the way its own severity model and PR description promise, in two independent ways:

### 1. A `Warn` finding exits nonzero, and the error counts every check as a problem

- `pkgs/id/src/world_doctor.rs:24` — `Severity::Warn` is documented as "Something is off but does not stop a world from running."
- `pkgs/id/src/world_doctor.rs:53-57` — `DoctorReport::healthy()` is `all(|f| f.severity == Severity::Ok)`, so a single Warn makes the whole report "unhealthy".
- `pkgs/id/src/commands/world.rs:426-430` (branch `id/phase-12`) — the CLI bails whenever `!report.healthy()`, with `bail!("world doctor found {} problem(s)", report.findings.len())`. `findings.len()` is the total number of checks (always 6), not the number of non-Ok findings.

So the one Warn path that exists today (toolchain: a configured Roc binary that exists but differs from / is not the pinned nightly, `world_doctor.rs` `check_toolchain`) makes `id world doctor` exit nonzero while claiming "found 6 problem(s)" — even when the other five checks are Ok and nothing blocks a world. The PR body says the command "exits nonzero on failure"; Warn is not Fail.

### 2. The ceiling and profile checks can never fire from the CLI

- `pkgs/id/src/commands/world.rs:413-422` — the Doctor handler constructs `DoctorInputs { caps_ceiling: None, profile: None, .. }` unconditionally. There is no flag, env var, or config source that supplies either value.
- `check_ceiling` with `None` always returns Ok ("no capability ceiling (whole catalog)") and `check_profile` with `None` always returns Ok ("no world execution profile (server defaults)").

Both checks are unit-tested in isolation, but through the only user-facing entry point they are dead: a world whose actual ceiling contains `*` or an unknown name, or whose profile has a zero bound, still gets `ok ceiling` / `ok profile` from `id world doctor`. The PR body advertises doctor as checking "the capability ceiling, the execution profile" — from the CLI it checks neither.

## Evidence

- PR #801 (OPEN, branch `id/phase-12`), commits `408e664c3a50`, `0616553c34cd`.
- All file:line references above are on the PR branch as fetched this run (`gh api .../contents/...?ref=id/phase-12`); the code is not on `main` yet, so this is a fix-before-merge finding, not a regression on main.
- No existing issue covers this: #559 is the F12.16 feature tracker PR #801 closes; searches for "doctor warn" / "doctor ceiling profile" found no defect issue.

## Acceptance

- A report whose worst severity is Warn exits 0 (or the severity model / PR description is changed so Warn is explicitly a failure — pick one and make code, docs, and tests agree).
- The failure message counts only non-Ok findings (e.g. "found 1 problem(s)"), not `findings.len()`.
- A test drives the CLI-level report path (not just `check_*` in isolation) with a Warn-only report and asserts the exit behaviour.
- `id world doctor` has a real source for the ceiling and profile it claims to check (flags, env, a live-world query, or local config), OR the two checks are removed from the CLI report and the docs stop claiming them.
- A test shows a bad ceiling / zero-bound profile actually producing a Fail finding through the wired path.

title: id(web): goto-line.test.ts typecheck fails on main — richSchema does not fit helper's narrow rawSchema type, blocks all id PRs
body:
## Problem

`main` (1161bcff) fails the `id` workflow: checks `test-web` and `test-web-typecheck` fail in `pkgs/id/web` typecheck.

Verified from PR #820 run 40140357862 (and main run 40136563100, conclusion failure):

```
src/goto-line.test.ts:354:51 - error TS2345: Argument of type 'Schema<...>' is not assignable to parameter of type 'Schema<"text" | "code_block" | "doc", never>'
src/goto-line.test.ts:394:51 - error TS2345: (same)
Found 2 errors in the same file, starting at: src/goto-line.test.ts:354
error: recipe `test-web-typecheck` failed
```

All other checks in that run passed, including 1633 unit tests and all 374 web unit tests (13 files). This failure blocks every open id PR (#820, #810, #808, #801, …) with an unrelated red `nix flake check`.

## Root cause

The #745 tests added in #746 (44c0cd3a) define a helper in `pkgs/id/web/src/goto-line.test.ts`:

```ts
function createViewFromDoc(
  schema: typeof rawSchema,
  doc: ReturnType<typeof rawSchema.node>,
)
```

`typeof rawSchema` is the narrow `Schema<"text"|"code_block"|"doc", never>` (rawSchema is built from a literal node map). `richSchema` is a generic `Schema` (built via `addListNodes(...)`), so passing `richSchema` at lines 354 and 394 does not typecheck. Line 372 passes `rawSchema` and is fine.

## Fix

Generalise the helper to the base ProseMirror types: `schema: Schema` and `doc: Node` from `prosemirror-model` (the same unparameterised `Schema` type `editor.ts:getSchema` already returns).

## Acceptance

- `bun run typecheck` (tsc --noEmit) in pkgs/id/web passes with no errors in goto-line.test.ts
- goto-line web unit tests still pass
- `nix flake check` test-web / test-web-typecheck go green on the PR

design(aggregator): quota + throughput view — pooled quotas, resets, burn rates, model-choice support
body:
## Design issue — aggregator quota + throughput view

Parent context: the project-management stack design record
(`doc/2026-10-24T11-05-38Z_design_project-management-stack/`) and the
aggregator UI phase (session K, branch `pm/aggregator-ui`). Reference
design (concept only — FSL-1.1-MIT licensed, do NOT vendor its code):
https://github.com/amirfish1/claude-command-center (throughput page +
share card).

### What Drew asked for (2026-10-25)

A view into **all pooled quotas and their resets** plus **throughput**,
so that Muse can quickly answer "what's the quota status" for every
provider and effectively choose the best model/pool for the next piece
of work. A nice GUI should exist, but the priority is machine
analyzability: this view is primarily a data surface for Muse, with
the GUI as a presentation of the same data.

### Required content

Per provider/pool:
- Plan name and pool identity (e.g. OpenCode Go Personal vs Lab are
  separate pools; Antigravity has TWO independent pools — Gemini models
  and the Claude models it supports; Meta Model API is a token quota
  under the Muse Code High Usage subscription).
- Current usage for each window the provider exposes (5-hour, weekly,
  monthly as applicable), % used, and **reset timestamps**.
- State flag: healthy / near limit / walled, with the wall/reset time
  when walled.

Throughput:
- Sessions currently burning, attributed per provider + model.
- Rough token rate per provider (tokens/min over recent windows) and
  cumulative tokens per session — enough to answer "which providers
  are you using at roughly what rate".
- Historical burn per pool between resets, so headroom can be
  projected, not just observed.

Model-choice support:
- Given the fleet burn order (Anthropic pools first, then other plan
  providers, OpenAI last), surface which pool has headroom for a new
  session and which pools are about to reset with unused headroom
  (burn-it-before-reset rule) or are close enough to their limit that
  no second session should start on them.

### Data sources (routes established 2026-10-25)

- Codex/ChatGPT: GET chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex/usage (OAuth).
- OpenCode Go: opencode.ai/zen/go/v1/usage per org.
- CommandCode: api.commandcode.ai/alpha/usage/summary.
- Cline: api.cline.bot/api/v1/users/me/plan/usage-limits.
- DeepSeek: API /user/balance.
- Cloudflare: GraphQL workersInvocationsAdaptive.
- Turso: `turso plan show`.
- Meta Model API: dev.meta.ai Usage page (team quota; key must be the
  team-attached `meta.api-key-funded` — the orphaned key 402s).
- Claude (Anthropic): console only, claude.ai/settings/usage.
- Antigravity: agy `/usage` panel (both pools).
- Open Design: open-design.ai/cloud/dashboard.
- GitHub: REST /users/{user}/settings/billing/usage/summary
  (needs `user` scope; comped minutes net to $0 and do not consume
  the plan).

### Acceptance shape

- One joined, queryable model (projector output / API) that Muse can
  read in one call and answer a full quota question from.
- GUI page rendering the same data (pools, windows, resets,
  throughput) — the CCC-style share card is a nice-to-have on top.
- No estimator for pools already shown in the OpenChamber quota
  picker; log picker values instead (standing rule, 2026-10-24).

Design first: this issue wants a written design (data model, refresh
cadence per source, wall detection) in the stack design record before
implementation.


## Acceptance criteria

- A written design lands in the project-management stack design record: the joined quota/throughput data model, a refresh cadence per data source, and the wall-detection rule per pool.
- The machine-first model answers a full quota question in one call: per pool — plan/pool identity, usage and % used for each exposed window, reset timestamps, and a healthy / near-limit / walled flag with the wall/reset time when walled.
- Throughput is attributed per provider + model: sessions currently burning, rough token rate per provider, cumulative tokens per session, and historical burn per pool between resets.
- Model-choice support is explicit in the output: which pool has headroom for a new session (fleet burn order respected, OpenAI last), which pools are about to reset with unused headroom, and which are too close to their limit for a second session.
- The GUI page renders the same data (pools, windows, resets, throughput); no estimator is built for pools already shown in the OpenChamber quota picker — picker values are logged instead.
- A linked implementation issue (or a tracked item with a named next action) is filed when the design lands, so the design does not sit as finished work.

title: id(web): prosemirror_to_markdown emits img src/alt/title unescaped — quotes truncate values and can inject attributes on reparse
body: ## Problem The reverse conversion in `pkgs/id/src/web/markdown.rs` emits an HTML `` tag by interpolating the image node's `src`/`alt`/`title` values into double-quoted attributes with no escaping at all (markdown.rs:730-754, the `width.is_some() || height.is_some()` branch; there is no escape helper anywhere in markdown.rs). Any value containing a `"` breaks the tag, and the breakage is lossy on the next load: - Node `{src: "x.png", alt: "a \"quoted\" caption", width: 100}` is written to the saved markdown as ``. Re-parsing that tag yields `alt = "a "` — the rest of the caption is silently dropped. - Worse, a value can inject attributes: `alt = "x\" title=\"injected"` is emitted as ``, and the re-parse produces a real `title = "injected"` the document never had. The same applies to `src` and `title` values containing quotes (a crafted `src` can manufacture `alt`/`width` attributes on reparse). Verified this run (2026-10-25) on main `7ce0d74c` with a standalone rustc harness replicating the emission `format!` code and re-parsing with `parse_img_tag`'s verbatim `attr_value` helper: both cases above reproduce exactly as shown. ## Why it matters Image node attributes are strings the node model places no restriction on: alt text comes from markdown image syntax, from uploaded-file names (`result.name` in the web editor), and from collaborating clients' document JSON. Whenever such an image also carries a width or height — exactly the case the HTML-emission branch exists for — saving the document writes a malformed tag, and the next open/save cycle silently truncates the attribute or invents new ones. That is slow-motion document corruption of the same class as #872 (which covers the parse direction of this same tag codec), but a distinct defect with a distinct fix: this one is missing output escaping, not substring matching. ## Suggested fix Escape attribute values on emission: at minimum `"` → `"` (and `&` → `&` first, so existing entities are not double-decoded), for `src`, `alt`, and `title`. Note the interplay with #872: the parser (`parse_img_tag`) does not currently decode entities, so emission and parsing should agree on one convention — if emission escapes, parsing should decode `"`/`&` in values so the round trip is value-preserving. Coordinate the two fixes so the pair forms a consistent codec rather than two half-codecs. ## Acceptance criteria - Round-trip pin: an image node with `alt = "a \"quoted\" caption"` and a width survives ProseMirror → markdown → ProseMirror with the alt value byte-identical. - An alt/title/src value containing `" title="` (or similar) cannot create or alter other attributes on reparse. - Values containing `&` round-trip without double-escaping or entity corruption (state the chosen convention in a test). - Existing image conversion tests in markdown.rs keep passing. Related: #872 (parse direction of the same `` attribute codec). Single-repo: this conversion code exists only in `developing-today/code` (`pkgs/id`).

title: impl(fleet): work-picking jobs consult the orchestrator published priorities before choosing work
body:
# impl(fleet): work-picking jobs consult the orchestrator's published priorities before choosing work

Gap found 2026-10-25: `orchestration.json` (published hourly by the orchestration-pass, contract in #899) is currently read by NO work-picking job — the issue sweeps, the code sweep, and the new-issue creator each pick work from the repo backlogs + GitHub by their own local rules. The priority ladder (today > tomorrow > next 3 days > longer goals > incoming) therefore only binds the orchestrator itself.

Change (small, bodies + one contract note):
- Each work-picking cron body gains a short "consult the orchestrator first" step: read `~/workspace/goals/keep-the-four-repos-healthy/hidden_files/orchestration.json` when fresh (<2h old). Prefer NEEDS ORCHESTRATOR items and today/tomorrow-horizon linedUp tasks in its goals measurement; respect blockedBy — skip an item whose blocker has an active worker and take the next one (that is the behavior Drew specified 2026-10-25).
- Fall back to the job's current picking rules when the file is stale or absent — never block a run on it.
- The orchestrator's published `actions[]` already records its own dispatches; picking jobs add their pick to their existing run logs as today (no new reporting channel).
- Note the contract on #899 so the orchestrator's publisher keeps the fields the pickers depend on (tiers, goals[].linedUp[], blockedBy).

Acceptance: one run each of issue-sweep-rotating and the code sweep shows (in its log) a pick that came from orchestration.json or an explicit "consulted, nothing applicable" line; stale-file fallback exercised once.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Each work-picking cron body (issue sweeps, code sweep, new-issue creator) consults a fresh (<2h old) `orchestration.json` before choosing work, preferring NEEDS ORCHESTRATOR items and today/tomorrow `linedUp` tasks and skipping items whose `blockedBy` has an active worker.
- [ ] A stale or absent `orchestration.json` falls back to the job's existing picking rules and never blocks a run.
- [ ] One run each of issue-sweep-rotating and the code sweep logs either a pick sourced from `orchestration.json` or an explicit "consulted, nothing applicable" line; the stale-file fallback is exercised once.
- [ ] The contract fields the pickers depend on (tiers, `goals[].linedUp[]`, `blockedBy`) are noted on #899.

## Repo-wide PR workflows failing on a diff that cannot affect them — verify pre-existing and repair or re-scope

Observed 2026-10-27 on PR #1447 (queue task 1449 resume, developing-today/code). The PR's diff touched only `pkgs/id/web/src/editor.ts` + `editor.test.ts`, and the designated pkgs/id gate (`id` workflow aggregate `nix flake check`, run 40537332076, incl. web unit/typecheck/lint/fmt) **passed**. These repo-wide workflows were nevertheless red on the PR head:

- `CI` — jobs `web-checks` and `format` failed (run 40537332047)
- `Territory CI` — job `test` failed (run 40537332060)
- `Headless NixOS CI` — job `build` failed (run 40537332087)
- `CI (Beta)` — job `tests` failed (run 40537332174)
- `Metaforge CI` — `NixOS tests` failed (run 40537332196)

Territory (Roc game), Headless NixOS (VM image) and Metaforge cannot be affected by a TypeScript editor-schema change, so at least those are pre-existing or infra failures by construction. The `CI` workflow's `web-checks`/`format` need a determination: same failure on an unrelated PR or on demand, or a genuine second harness for the web tests that disagrees with the nix gate.

Related context: the full/nightly lane also fails daily (see #1078 slice-4 timings: id-e2e-nightly runs 40457980141 / 40449168389 / 40448341046 all failure on 2026-10-27) and #1372/#1374 track two of the VM-test failures. This issue is about the PR-triggered repo-wide set above, which currently trains everyone to ignore red checks on every PR.

## Acceptance criteria

- For each of the five workflows above: a stated verdict (pre-existing failure with the failing job's root cause named, or a real defect this PR class exposes) with run links.
- Each pre-existing failure is either fixed, or the workflow is re-scoped (path filters / required-vs-advisory) so a red check on a PR means something again; the outcome is linked from here.

title: Egress strategy: 2 Gbps home fiber behind Cloudflare/Turso/Tailscale
body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#505 on 2026-10-28 - it was filed in the wrong repo; developing-today/code is its home. Original content follows, verbatim.

---

## Problem

**Bandwidth is the scarce resource, not compute.** The basement fleet has very fast CPUs, ≥3 TB RAM and ~200 TB of disks at near-zero marginal cost — behind exactly **2 Gbps symmetric** of home fiber. Design the egress strategy before anything popular lands on this cluster.

Source: [idea register 2026-10-20](https://github.com/dezren39/hatch-personal/blob/main/workspace/goals/stand-up-lab-cluster-talm-talos-cozystack-postgres-rustfs/files/idea-register-2026-10-20.md) (goal `stand-up-lab-cluster-talm-talos-cozystack-postgres-rustfs`).

## What we know

- One fiber provider (Brightspeed) in his part of Osseo: 2 Gbps up/down. A second line = 4 Gbps total — still small at scale. Cable offers 100 Mbps, more expensive (possible redundancy pickup). TriCounty Communications fiber may reach his part of Osseo → then buy both fibers.
- Hotspot plans and Starlink investigated for emergency backup; Starlink would likely need a business plan for this use.
- Strategy direction (Drew): "tunnel most or much of that to Cloudflare or Turso or anywhere we connect with Tailscale" — shunt bulk traffic to SaaS with cheap or **free egress** (e.g. Cloudflare R2's zero-egress pricing, CF cache/tunnels), compress aggressively, and only cross the home link with what must.
- Budget guardrails: Turso $5 plan and Cloudflare $5 Workers plan in play; free tiers preferred; a $25–$30 Cloudflare plan is possible; **$75 is out**.

## Acceptance / first steps

- [ ] Classify the app's traffic: what can be cached at the edge (CDN), what can live on free-egress object storage (R2), what genuinely must be served from home.
- [ ] Design the tunnel topology: cloudflared from the cluster, Tailscale links, Turso edge replicas — with per-path egress costs written down.

title: P8.1 time & witnesses: witness protocol design (task-09 + owner's 2026-10-28 direction)
body:
## Origin

Design follow-up to #802. Drew's ruling (2026-10-28) reopens P8.1 as a proof of concept (branch A), scoped by the direction below. This issue settles the exact mechanics Drew flagged as 'need to get worked out' before the PoC is built.

## Owner direction (condensed from Drew's 2026-10-28 ruling)

- **Order stays the backbone.** For ~99% of the system's mechanics — merges, code sharing — causal/order validity is all that matters. Provable time must NOT become the backbone of merges; server-side cooperation just uses order.
- **Provable time is still required** for apps that need it — above all multiplayer / no-trust or limited-trust situations with winners and losers.
- **Witness = time oracle.** A witness service records each second: the time plus a value signed with its own secret key — a stream of signed ticks. Every id server could run one, but primarily they would all use the same one: a central witness we operate. Third parties are the product here — almost everyone would use our central/secondary witness servers.
- **Before/after proofs from ticks:** an event carrying a recent witness tick proves it occurred at-or-after that tick; submitting a record to a witness that countersigns it proves it occurred at-or-before that countersigning. Witnesses act as the 'before or current' anchor.
- **Witnesses are graph participants.** Direction of travel is a mostly graph-based model, not just a DAG. A witness can act on a message — judge it valid, sign it, and emit that as its own message in the graph. Candidate checkpoint record: a hash over the concatenation of all graph tips a message contains (to be evaluated, not pre-decided).
- **Untrusted ordering:** in no-trust settings, ordering aids like the bubble-merge concept or a coordinator who determines arrival order; a coordinator can also supply time, or a party can obtain a witnessed 'occurred before T' record for itself.
- **Modes:** timekeeping/witness capability is built into the core app — a dedicated witness-only mode, or witness functions switched on alongside other functions via a flag; if running in server mode it could simply be on. Made available for all operations but only USED by apps that need it.
- **P2P option:** a peer group can run its own witness cluster and accept answers marked valid by a quorum/consensus of its nodes instead of depending on our central server. Their Sybil / Byzantine-generals exposure is their problem; a blockchain is explicitly another day (non-goal here).

## This issue must settle

- Tick format and chaining (per-second signed records; how a tick commits to history; clock-source expectations).
- The two proof constructions (not-before via embedded recent tick; not-after via witness countersignature) and their exact verification rules.
- Witness-as-participant: the witness message type, what 'valid' attests, and whether/how the tip-set hash checkpoint works.
- Modes and flags in the core app (witness-only mode; timekeeping flag; server-mode default).
- Quorum model for P2P witness clusters (threshold semantics; what a client accepts).
- Trust assumptions stated plainly for each deployment shape (central witness vs own cluster).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A design document in `doc/` answering every point above, updating (not replacing) `task-09-time-and-witnesses.md`, with remaining open questions listed explicitly for the owner.
- [ ] The PoC issue (linked from #802) is scoped from the accepted design.

title: mcpx(settings): non-positive durations pass validation, then panic the daemon at time.NewTicker — reapInterval/saveInterval/ssePing accept -5s and 0s
body:
# mcpx(settings): non-positive durations pass validation, then panic the daemon at `time.NewTicker` — reapInterval/saveInterval/ssePing accept `-5s` and `0s`

## Summary

`KindDuration` settings are validated only for parseability, never for sign. Interval settings that are spent directly as `time.NewTicker` periods therefore accept `-5s` and `0s` at every layer (file / env / flag / preset / runtime override), and the daemon later panics with `non-positive interval for NewTicker` — at startup for the reap/save tickers, and on the first SSE events request for the ping ticker. This is the duration sibling of #1697 (byte sizes accept negatives/overflow and panic a `make` cap); that issue's fix does not reach this one, because the values here parse cleanly and overflow nothing.

## Evidence (verified this run, main fbedd805)

Line trace, `pkgs/mcpx`:

- `internal/settings/value.go:499-502` — `Validate`'s `KindDuration` case only checks `time.ParseDuration(raw)` succeeds. `-5s` and `0s` both parse, so both are *valid* settings. `SetRuntime`/`Apply` gate on `Normalize` → `Validate`, so the bad value is admitted at every layer.
- `internal/settings/value.go:317-320` — `Set.Duration()` re-parses with the error discarded and returns the value verbatim.
- Declarations with no floor/positivity constraint: `daemon.reapInterval` (`internal/settings/registry.go:474`, default `30s`), `daemon.saveInterval` (`registry.go:480`, default `5m`), `http.ssePing` (`internal/settings/wire.go:61`).
- Unguarded consumers: `internal/daemon/server.go:539-542` — `Serve()` does `time.NewTicker(s.set.Duration("daemon.reapInterval"))` and the same for `saveInterval`, unconditionally, before the serve loop; `internal/daemon/server.go:1447` — the SSE handler does `time.NewTicker(s.set.Duration("http.ssePing"))`.
- The guarded contrast exists in the same package: `internal/daemon/routes_exec.go:110-114` — `collectArtifacts` substitutes the default when `every <= 0` before calling `NewTicker`. The reap/save/ping sites have no equivalent guard, which is why this stayed hidden.

Laptop probe (real `internal/settings` package; worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-durticker` on the laptop at 541578ae — `internal/settings/value.go` sha256 `c669f256…` and `internal/daemon/server.go` sha256 `a5efbdc6…` are byte-identical to sandbox main fbedd805):

```
SetRuntime(daemon.reapInterval, "-5s") ACCEPTED; Duration()=-5s
time.NewTicker(-5s) PANICS: non-positive interval for NewTicker
SetRuntime(daemon.reapInterval, "0s") ACCEPTED; Duration()=0s
time.NewTicker(0s) PANICS: non-positive interval for NewTicker
SetRuntime(daemon.saveInterval, "-1s") ACCEPTED; Duration()=-1s  -> NewTicker PANICS
SetRuntime(http.ssePing, "-1s") ACCEPTED; Duration()=-1s         -> NewTicker PANICS
SetRuntime(http.ssePing, "0s") ACCEPTED; Duration()=0s           -> NewTicker PANICS
Validate(<real registry decl>, "-5s") err=<nil>; Validate(..., "0s") err=<nil>  (all three decls)
```

## Why it matters

The settings system is the one choke point whose job is keeping an invalid value out of a running process (the #1697 reasoning). An interval of `-1s`/`0s` is an easy typo or generated-config artefact, and here it does not degrade anything — it crashes the daemon outright at startup (reap/save) or takes down an SSE request handler goroutine (ping). Other duration settings may legitimately mean something at zero (e.g. `daemon.idleExit` defaults to `0s` = disabled), so this cannot be fixed by a blanket "all durations must be > 0" rule; the interval/poll class needs its own pin.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Interval-class duration settings — at minimum `daemon.reapInterval`, `daemon.saveInterval`, `http.ssePing`, and any other setting a consumer spends as a `NewTicker`/`Tick` period (triage to enumerate: e.g. `proto.askPoll`, `protoTasks.pollInterval`, `transport.sseKeepAlive`, `autostart.pollInterval`) — refuse zero and negative values at `Validate`/`Normalize` time, with an error naming the value, at every layer (file/env/flag/preset/runtime).
- [ ] Duration settings where zero is a documented "disabled/never" meaning (e.g. `daemon.idleExit`) keep accepting `0s`; triage pins which class each duration setting belongs to rather than applying one global rule.
- [ ] No `NewTicker` call site reachable from a settings duration can panic on a validated value (either validation refuses it, or the site guards like `collectArtifacts` does).
- [ ] Regression tests cover `-5s` and `0s` for at least the three named settings plus one legitimate-zero setting staying accepted; existing `internal/settings` and `internal/daemon` tests keep passing.

## Notes for triage

- Where the positivity pin lives (a per-setting floor/class on the declaration vs a consumer-side guard) is the decision this filing leaves to triage — hence `task/triage`, not a self-solve.
- Distinct from: #1697 (KindBytes negatives/overflow, `make` cap panic — different kind, different consumer); #1758 (closed; adapter's own `parseDuration`, not the settings system); #2309 (plugin `goDurationMs` overflow → Infinity, a JS-side conversion).
- Found by new-issue-creator lane A, 2026-10-30.

title: mcpx testing: one deterministic-hypervisor (Antithesis) experiment on the pkgs/mcpx container image
body:
Filed from #1963 (approach C, step 4) during its close-out — queue task 3259, 2026-10-30.

## Summary

Run one deterministic-hypervisor experiment: execute the existing `pkgs/mcpx` container image under Antithesis (or an equivalent deterministic hypervisor) and record whether end-to-end determinism — including the deno/bun/node runtime subprocesses that no in-process seam can make deterministic — is achievable and worth pursuing.

## Evidence (from #1963's record)

- #1963's blockers table: runtime subprocesses and real MCP servers are "not feasible" for in-process determinism; a deterministic hypervisor running unmodified containers is the only realistic end-to-end path (approach C's endgame, explicitly "a prerequisite that is now met, not a plan").
- The container image exists: `pkgs/mcpx/Containerfile` (debian bookworm-slim runtime, bun, ~413 MB; `docs/container.md`), added by #182.

## Prerequisites / blockers (named, not hidden)

- The container image should have a CI job first — tracked by #1983 (environments as CI matrix entries, incl. container). Running the experiment before the image is CI-built risks experimenting on a stale image.
- Antithesis is a commercial external service: account access and cost need Drew's decision before any run. This issue records the experiment and its prerequisites; it does not authorize signing up or spending.

## Acceptance criteria

- A go/no-go note is recorded on this issue once both prerequisites are resolved (CI-built image available; access/cost decision made).
- If go: one experiment run is executed, and a short report is posted here — what was run, whether execution was deterministic across repeated runs from one seed, what broke the determinism if anything, and a recommendation (adopt / revisit / drop) for #1963's approach-C endgame.
- If no-go: the reason is recorded here and the issue is closed as dropped, so the question is not re-litigated ad hoc.

title: feat(pm-stack): dispatch service — launch/track OpenCode sessions from GitHub Actions
body:
New pm-stack service `pm-dispatch` (Drew's request, 2026-10-30): an HTTP service on the laptop with two authenticated endpoints.

- `POST /v1/sessions` — launch an OpenCode session on the laptop immediately: creates a GitHub issue (optional, default on), enqueues a repo-health queue task, launches the session with the prompt, and marks the task claimed immediately (worker `dispatch-opencode`, session id in progress) so no lane double-books it.
- `POST /v1/tasks` — enqueue-only: puts a repo-task/v1 packet into the Supabase queue (repo-health-*-pilot), optionally with a GitHub issue.
- Auth: GitHub Actions OIDC (aud `pm-dispatch`, token's repository claim must equal the request's repo) or a static bearer secret.
- `GET /health` unauthenticated, aggregator-style build version.

Deployed on the laptop like the aggregator (install.sh + user systemd unit, loopback + tailnet bind). Public reachability (a Cloudflare tunnel hostname on amd-6-pm-stack) is a separate later step.

title: antigravity-direct: a non-object JSON body is never a 400 — 'null' 500s at body.model, and scalar/array bodies fabricate an empty upstream request for model '-medium' and return 200
body:
# antigravity-direct: a non-object JSON body is never a 400 — `null` 500s at `body.model`, and scalar/array bodies fabricate an empty upstream request for model `-medium` and return 200

**Repo:** developing-today/code · **Main:** `df9381ff` · **File:** `bin/antigravity-direct.mjs` (landed today in `b0058ec7`, PR via `feat(antigravity-direct)`)

## Summary

`handleChatCompletions` (`bin/antigravity-direct.mjs:546-550`) parses the request body in a try/catch — malformed JSON correctly gets a 400 — but then dereferences the parsed value with no object-shape check:

```js
try { body = JSON.parse(await readBody(req) || '{}'); }
catch { return sendJson(res, 400, { error: { message: 'invalid JSON body', ... } }); }
const requestedModel = body.model || 'gemini-3.8-flash';   // :550 — first deref
```

Two failure modes, both verified this run:

1. **`null` body → HTTP 500, not 400.** `body.model` throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'model')` at `antigravity-direct.mjs:550`. The server-level catch (`:644+`) converts it to a 500 `internal_error` and logs a stack — a client error reported as a server fault.
2. **Scalar/array bodies (`42`, `"hello"`, `[]`) → fabricated upstream request, HTTP 200.** Nothing dereferences badly, so `buildV1Request` (`:294`) runs `resolveModelAndEffort(undefined, undefined)`, producing the model name **`-medium`** (empty base + `-medium`) and `contents: []`, and the proxy makes a **real upstream generate call** with that empty conversation, returning a successful `chat.completion` whose `model` field claims `gemini-3.8-flash` — a model the upstream was never asked for. Against the real upstream the `-medium` call presumably errors there instead, which is still wrong: a malformed client request becomes a wasted upstream round-trip and an `upstream_error` that blames Google, never a 400 that blames the request.

## Evidence (verified this run, real module)

Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-laneA-antigrav-body/`; `bin/antigravity-direct.mjs` md5 `de11cfa24df8200d66fd788422667ef8` identical on sandbox main `df9381ff` and the laptop). The proxy ran with `SECRET_TOOL_PATH` pointed at a stub `secret-tool` emitting a canned far-future credential and `ANTIGRAVITY_DIRECT_UPSTREAM` pointed at a local stub upstream that records every payload and answers a canned SSE — **no real keyring read and no real Google call**.

| Request body | Result |
|---|---|
| `{bad json` (control) | **HTTP 400** `invalid JSON body`, proxy alive |
| `null` | **HTTP 500** `{"error":{"message":"Cannot read properties of null (reading 'model')","type":"internal_error"}}`; proxy log: `handler error: TypeError … at handleChatCompletions (antigravity-direct.mjs:550:31)`; proxy alive (server catch) |
| `42` | **HTTP 200** chat completion (`stub-ok` from the stub upstream); upstream received `model: "-medium"`, `contents: []` |
| `"hello"` | **HTTP 200**; upstream received the same fabricated `-medium` / empty-contents payload |
| `[]` | **HTTP 200**; upstream received the same fabricated payload |
| `{"model":"gemini-3.8-flash","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}]}` (control) | **HTTP 200**; upstream received `model: "gemini-3.8-flash-medium"`, `contents: [{role:"user",parts:[{text:"hi"}]}]` — well-formed handling unchanged |
| `GET /healthz` after all cases | **HTTP 200** |

## Why it matters

This door was seated in opencode today as the replacement for the agy / antigravity-ls seats — it is about to become a long-lived shared fleet proxy. Its request-boundary contract is currently: the one body shape that should be the cheapest 400 either masquerades as a server fault (500 + stack in the log, misdirecting incident triage) or — worse for scalars/arrays — silently burns a real upstream call on an empty conversation under a nonsense model name and reports success under a model name that was never invoked. The in-repo oracle already exists: `bin/clef-proxy.mjs:211` and `bin/opencode-route-proxy.mjs:709` reject non-object bodies with a 400 before any dereference (see #2816).

## Dedup / relation to #2816

#2816 (filed earlier today) covers the seven `bin/*-proxy.mjs` handlers present at `c90fcbc7`, whose failure mode is a process exit 1. This file is not one of them: it is named `antigravity-direct.mjs` (outside #2816's `bin/*-proxy.mjs` acceptance glob), it landed in `b0058ec7` **after** #2816's snapshot, and its failure modes differ (no process exit — the server catch turns the null case into a 500; scalars/arrays fabricate a 200 instead of crashing or substituting a default model). Filing separately so the new door is actually covered; if triage prefers, it can be folded into #2816's fix pass as an eighth handler — the guard and tests are the same shape.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `POST /v1/chat/completions` with a parsed body that is not a plain object (`null`, array, string, number, boolean) returns HTTP 400 in this proxy's existing error shape (`{error:{message,type:"invalid_request_error"}}`), before any property dereference — mirroring `clef-proxy.mjs:211` / `opencode-route-proxy.mjs:709`.
- [ ] No upstream request is made for a non-object body (the stub-upstream oracle: zero `streamGenerateContent` calls for those cases).
- [ ] A new `bin/antigravity-direct.test.mjs` in the existing `bin/*.test.mjs` node-test style covers: malformed JSON → 400, `null`/array/string/number bodies → 400 with no upstream call, and the well-formed object control → 200 with the recorded upstream payload unchanged (model `gemini-3.8-flash-medium`, contents preserved).
- [ ] Well-formed object bodies and the `/v1/models` + `/healthz` routes are byte-for-byte unchanged.

title: fix(pm-dispatch): ensureWorker caches a rejected promise forever — one transient failure wedges every later launch
fix(pm-dispatch): POST /v1/sessions accepts an arbitrary directory — OIDC callers escape their repo clone
body:
## Finding

`POST /v1/sessions` in pm-dispatch accepts a caller-supplied `directory` with no validation, and launches the OpenCode session there. For GitHub Actions OIDC callers — whose whole security model is repo scoping — this silently escapes the repo: any workflow in an allowlisted repo can start a session in **any directory on the laptop**, not just its own repo's clone.

## Evidence

- PR #2650 (commit `19f12cb2e2`, MERGED) introduced the service and the field.
- The OIDC boundary, `pm-stack/dispatch/src/auth.ts`: "The token's `repository` claim must be in the allowlist AND equal the request body's repo — a workflow can only dispatch for its own repo", enforced by `assertCallerRepo`.
- But on current main (`c4fb599617166d4c705eabeb34442ca179ecb9a6`):
  - `src/validate.ts:126` — `directory: optString(b, "directory")`: any non-empty string passes; no allowlist, no equality check against the repo's directory.
  - `src/server.ts:175` — `const directory = body.directory ?? REPO_DIRS[body.repo]!;` used verbatim.
  - `src/opencode.ts:59` — the session is created with `location: { directory: opts.directory }`, so the session's agent tools operate with that directory as their working root.
- `REPO_DIRS` (`src/config.ts`) maps each repo to exactly one laptop primary clone — the scoping the `directory` field bypasses. The packet built for the task even records `scope.include` as just the repo, while the session itself runs elsewhere.

## Why it matters

The static bearer token is the operator's own credential and is trusted accordingly; the OIDC path exists specifically so a repo's workflows can dispatch *for that repo only*. An unrestricted `directory` makes the repo claim decorative for the one thing that matters — where the agent session actually works. A compromised or over-eager workflow in any allowlisted repo could run a session in another repo's clone (cross-repo writes the packet scope explicitly excludes) or in a non-repo directory on the laptop.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] For OIDC callers, `directory` must be absent or equal to `REPO_DIRS[repo]`; anything else is rejected (400/403) before any issue/task/session is created.
- [ ] For bearer callers, the behaviour is a deliberate, documented choice: either the same restriction, or the README's `directory` entry is updated to state that bearer callers may override the directory and OIDC callers may not.
- [ ] Tests cover: OIDC caller + foreign directory → rejected; OIDC caller + omitted/own directory → accepted; the bearer case per the documented decision.

Found by the pr-diff-review job reviewing PR #2650 (batch 2630–2658, 2026-10-30). Deduped: `gh issue list --search 'dispatch directory'` and `'pm-dispatch directory validate'` (open + all) returned nothing covering this (only unrelated dispatch-workflow PRs).

title: projector(webhook): a delivery whose apply failed is deduped as applied — GitHub redelivery returns 'duplicate' and the event is permanently dropped
body:
## Bug

The projector's webhook dedupe treats a delivery whose apply **failed** as
applied, so a GitHub redelivery of that delivery is answered `200
{"status":"duplicate"}` and the event is never applied. One transient
failure (a DB hiccup, a store error mid-apply) permanently and silently
drops the event from the read model; the only recovery is the periodic
reconcile poll happening to cover that repo/stream.

### Evidence (main `689e47c0`)

- `pm-stack/projector/src/server.ts` — the webhook handler checks
  `store.deliveryApplied(db, deliveryId)` **before** applying, and on an
  `applyEvent` throw it records the delivery and returns 500:

  ```ts
  const already = await store.deliveryApplied(db, deliveryId);
  if (already) return jsonResponse(200, { status: "duplicate" });
  ...
  } catch (e) {
    await store.recordDelivery(db, { deliveryId, event, outcome: "error", detail: ... });
    return jsonResponse(500, { error: "apply_failed" });
  }
  ```

  The `invalid_json` path records `outcome: "error"` the same way.

- `pm-stack/projector/src/store.ts:337` — `deliveryApplied` ignores the
  recorded outcome entirely:

  ```sql
  SELECT 1 AS x FROM pmp_deliveries WHERE delivery_id = ?
  ```

  Any row — `applied`, `ignored`, or `error` — makes every later
  delivery of that GUID a "duplicate".

- `pm-stack/projector/schema.sql:98` — `pmp_deliveries.delivery_id` is
  the PRIMARY KEY ("a redelivered webhook is applied at most once"), so
  a fix that retries on redelivery must also make the second
  `recordDelivery` an upsert/replace rather than a bare INSERT, or the
  retry succeeds and its bookkeeping insert throws.

### Reproduction (verified this run)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneA-projredeliver/`,
real `handleRequest` + `migrate` + HMAC-signed fixture
`fixtures/02-issue-opened.json`, projector sources copied from main
`689e47c0`):

1. `pmp_items` briefly renamed away → signed delivery
   `probe-delivery-1` returns `500 {"error":"apply_failed"}` and
   `pmp_deliveries` gains `{delivery_id: "probe-delivery-1",
   outcome: "error", detail: "SQLITE_ERROR: no such table:
   pmp_items"}`.
2. Table restored, the **same** delivery redelivered →
   `200 {"status":"duplicate"}` and `pmp_items` count stays **0** —
   the issue-opened event is lost.
3. Control: the same body under a fresh delivery id →
   `200 {"status":"applied","refs":["developing-today/code#754"]}`,
   item count 1.

### Why it matters

The projector is the PM stack's read model for issues/PRs/comments.
Webhook intake is supposed to be at-least-once-safe: GitHub redelivers
(automatically on 5xx in some paths, and manually from the App UI after
an incident) precisely so transient failures heal. Here the failure is
recorded in the very table that gates redelivery, converting a
transient error into permanent, silent data loss — the deliveries audit
even shows the delivery as present, so nothing looks missing until
someone notices a stale item. Distinct from #2982 (a missing
`X-GitHub-Delivery` header collapsing distinct deliveries onto the
empty-string key): this is about deliveries that *have* an id and
*failed*.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A delivery recorded with `outcome = 'error'` does **not** count
      as applied: redelivering it re-runs `applyEvent` and, on success,
      returns `applied`/`ignored` and the writes land.
- [ ] Recording the retried delivery's outcome does not violate the
      `pmp_deliveries` primary key (upsert/replace semantics), and the
      audit row reflects the final outcome.
- [ ] A delivery recorded `applied` or `ignored` still short-circuits
      as `duplicate` (existing e2e idempotency test keeps passing).
- [ ] Regression test beside the projector tests: fail an apply
      (transient store error), redeliver the same delivery id, assert
      it applies; and a redelivery after an `error` does not throw on
      the deliveries insert.
- [ ] Triage pins the `invalid_json` case: a malformed-body delivery
      can never succeed on redelivery — either it stays deduped
      deliberately (documented) or it is excluded from the deliveries
      table; either way the choice is explicit, not accidental.

title: id(cli): test_cli_parse_cat stack-overflows in the pkgs/id test binary (pre-existing, parse path)
body:
## Problem
In the `pkgs/id` test binary, `cli::tests::test_cli_parse_cat` aborts with a stack overflow, even run in isolation:

```
$ id-<hash> cli::tests::test_cli_parse_cat --exact --test-threads=1
thread 'cli::tests::test_cli_parse_cat' has overflowed its stack
fatal runtime error: stack overflow, aborting
```

Found 2026-11-01 by queue task 5262 (lane F) while running the full `pkgs/id` suite on the laptop from PR 3420's head (74c1a6e75). The PR's diff touches only `pkgs/id/src/commands/serve.rs` (`is_process_alive` + its test), which the CLI parse path does not call — so this failure is pre-existing relative to that change, not caused by it. All `commands::serve` tests pass (15/15).

## Acceptance
- Reproduce on clean `main` and confirm the overflow is in the parse path (likely clap derive recursion / large nested subcommand graph exceeding the test-thread stack).
- Fix so `test_cli_parse_cat` passes in the normal test-thread configuration (e.g. parse on a spawned thread with a larger stack in the test, or reduce parse recursion), or document the required `RUST_MIN_STACK` if that is the intended configuration.
- Full `pkgs/id` test binary run completes without aborting.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `test_cli_parse_cat` runs to completion in the pkgs/id test binary without a stack overflow (pass, or a normal assertion failure if the underlying parse behavior is separately wrong).
- [ ] The root cause is identified in the PR: either the recursive parse path gains a depth bound / iterative shape, or the test's input is shown to be invalid and corrected — not merely a larger test-thread stack.
- [ ] The rest of the pkgs/id test suite stays green in CI.
