title: aggregator(dns): isDnsSection never checks totalAnnualListUsd, entry priceUsd or status — a missing total or a string price crashes renderDns, an infinite price renders as $Infinity
body:
## Finding

`isDnsSection` (pm-stack/aggregator/src/dns.ts:74-90) — the structural check "shared by the collector and the live source" for the DNS register section — checks only `generatedAt`, that `entries` is a non-empty array, and that each entry has a string `domain` and `renewal`. It never checks the section's `totalAnnualListUsd` or `source`, nor an entry's `priceUsd` / `status` / remaining string fields, although `DnsSection`/`DnsEntry` (model.ts:702-710 and the DnsEntry interface) require them and `renderDns` dereferences them unguarded. A section no producer can emit passes the gate and crashes or falsifies the /dns page.

The producer path always emits the full shape: `dnsSectionFromRegister` (dns.ts:66-72) computes `totalAnnualListUsd` as a rounded number and `parseDnsRegister` sets every entry field, deriving `priceUsd` via `parsePriceUsd` (number or null) and `status` via `classifyDnsStatus`.

## Evidence (main 33aefa7f, verified this run)

- dns.ts:74-90 — no check on `s.totalAnnualListUsd`, `s.source`, `e.priceUsd`, `e.status`, `e.registrar`, `e.autoRenew`, `e.plan`, or `e.review`; `renewal` is any string.
- render.ts:3002 — `$${section.totalAnnualListUsd.toFixed(2)}` unguarded; render.ts:2980 and :3006 — `e.priceUsd != null ? e.priceUsd.toFixed(2)`; render.ts:3000 — `soonTotal` sums `e.priceUsd ?? 0` into a rendered dollar total.
- dns.ts summarizeDns (:103-118) — buckets entries by `e.status === "active"/"earmarked"/"unused"` and compares `e.renewal` lexicographically against today/cutoff, so a missing status silently drops the entry from every bucket and a non-date renewal sorts as future.
- Laptop Bun probe (~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-01-laneB-dnsgate/, real dns.ts/render.ts from the laptop primary at 33aefa7f; sha256 dns.ts 8217f569…, render.ts 061fc8ad… — identical to sandbox main; well-formed control renders OK, 27,592 bytes):
  - `totalAnnualListUsd` missing → gate `true`, `renderDns` throws `TypeError: undefined is not an object (evaluating 'section.totalAnnualListUsd.toFixed')`
  - `totalAnnualListUsd: "11.08"` → gate `true`, throws `TypeError: section.totalAnnualListUsd.toFixed is not a function`
  - entry `priceUsd: "11.08"` (string) → gate `true`, throws `TypeError: next.priceUsd.toFixed is not a function`
  - entry `priceUsd: Infinity` (what JSON `1e999` parses to) → gate `true`, renders — the price renders as `$Infinity` and poisons the renewing-soon total
  - entry `renewal: "banana"` → gate `true`, renders verbatim and is treated as a future renewal by summarizeDns; `renewal: "2026-02-30"` likewise passes (shape-only string)
  - entry without `status` → gate `true`, renders, but the entry vanishes from all three status buckets while still counting in `entries.length` ("N domains" disagrees with the portfolio-shape card)

## Why it matters

/dns is the domain-portfolio page — renewal spend and lapse visibility. The section rides the fleet feed as hand-/script-produced JSON, exactly the input this shared gate exists to fail soft against (the live source falls back when the gate rejects). Today one malformed section takes the whole page down, or worse, quietly misstates it: an infinite price in the spend total, a domain invisible in every status bucket, a nonsense renewal presented as next. Sibling section gates (#2429 quota, #2446 subscriptions) validate the fields their renderers dereference; this one validates almost none of them.

## Acceptance criteria

- `isDnsSection` (or a load-boundary sanitizer in the #2429/#2446 pattern, layer pinned in triage) validates: `totalAnnualListUsd` a finite number, `source` a string, and per entry `priceUsd` a finite number or null, `status` one of the three classes, the remaining rendered string fields strings, and `renewal` a real calendar date in YYYY-MM-DD form (the shared `isIsoDate`/calendar helper, not a bare string).
- A section failing those checks is rejected/dropped at the boundary so /dns falls back instead of throwing; a well-formed section (existing fixtures/tests) renders unchanged.
- Regression tests cover at least: missing/string `totalAnnualListUsd`, string `priceUsd`, `priceUsd` Infinity, a status-less entry, and a non-date renewal.

Dedup: #3441 (open) covers this gate's `generatedAt` only (bare Date.parse rolling 2026-02-30) — different fields, cross-linked, not covering totals/prices/status/renewal. #2412/#2415 are the aa/quota-current stamps. Searches for "isDnsSection", "totalAnnualListUsd", and "dns priceUsd" across open and closed issues return no covering issue.

title: bug(id): put path:name spec is hijacked by stdin auto-detection whenever stdin is not a terminal (breaks toplevel build)
body:
Seventh breakage in the #3720 fold chain — the second fold-switch attempt (2026-11-01 21:5x CST) failed its in-sandbox checkPhase on exactly one test:

```
test put_get_tests::test_put_with_custom_name ... FAILED
Command failed: ["put", "/build/.tmpVLBYe6/test.local.txt:test.custom-name"]
stderr: Error: name must be a safe relative path: /build/.tmpVLBYe6/test.local.txt:test.custom-name
```

Reproduced deterministically on a host: `cargo test -p id --test cli_integration -- test_put_with_custom_name < /dev/null` fails in 0.27s with the same error; with a terminal stdin it passes (which is how it stayed hidden — interactive runs mask it).

Root cause (`src/commands/put.rs`, `cmd_put_multi`): the stdin auto-detection

```rust
if items.len() == 1 && !stdin().is_terminal() && !from_stdin {
    let path = PathBuf::from(&items[0]);
    if !path.exists() { return cmd_put_local_stdin(name /* the whole spec */).await; }
}
```

checks the LITERAL spec string as a path. A `path:name` spec never exists as a literal path (the colon), so every non-interactive `id put file:name` is misrouted into stdin-content mode, and `FileOps::put` then rejects the whole spec as an unsafe name (leading `/`). With a name that passed validation it would silently store stdin under a garbage name instead.

Fix: the existence check must use the path part of the spec (`parse_put_spec`). Plain names and missing files keep the current stdin behavior; an existing file behind a `path:name` spec goes to the normal file-put loop. Blocks the #3720 fold switch (the toplevel's id checkPhase runs non-interactively by construction).

title: laptop meta provider: 403 'API key is billed to a Muse Code subscription' — sole-door Meta pool route down since 2026-10-30
body:
Observed 2026-11-02 in the laptop opencode.db `route_attempt` table (read-only check): the latest attempts for provider `meta`, model `muse-spark-1.3`, all end `failure` with error_status 403 and error_message:

> This API key is billed to a Muse Code subscription. Muse Code subscriptions cove… (truncated in the row)

Burst timestamps: 2026-10-30 ~09:32 CDT (six rows within ~25 min; no successful meta attempt after them in the table).

This is a NEW failure mode, not the previously tracked one. On 2026-10-25 the laptop meta provider failed 402 'Billing verification failed' for team 1073226932208501 (billing-page verification demand). That error no longer appears; the current 403 is a key/entitlement mismatch — the key the laptop `meta` provider presents is attached to a Muse Code subscription rather than the Muse API High Usage plan.

Why it matters: the `meta` provider is the ONLY door into the Muse API High Usage plan pool (charter rule). A sole-door pool route down is surface-worthy per the quota doctrine. The 403s begin the same day PR #2753 (muse-proxy direct mode — exchange the Muse CLI account token for the minted plan key) landed and was verified live on the laptop, so the credential/minting path is the first place to look: which credential row the laptop `meta` provider uses, how it relates to the minted plan key, and whether the sandbox `meta` credential (which was succeeding) differs.

Status / lanes: found by the provider-parity chat during follow-up reconciliation. No credential changes made; the staged billing-page (RustDesk) pass for the old 402 is on hold because its premise changed. Drew to direct whether the credential comparison lands in the parity lane or with the muse-direct workstream.

## Acceptance criteria
- The credential row the laptop `meta` provider actually presents is identified, and how it differs from the sandbox `meta` credential (which was succeeding) and from the minted plan key from PR #2753 is documented on this issue — by reference/name only, never by value.
- A fresh laptop route_attempt for provider `meta` succeeds (or, if the entitlement itself is wrong, the exact plan/entitlement change needed is named and handed to Drew with evidence).
- The failure is surface-visible going forward: a sole-door pool route returning 403s produces an alarm or a filed issue without waiting for a manual route_attempt audit.

title: id(currency): RateAuthorisation::validate checks only issuer and rate_den — inverted amount bounds, empty/inverted validity window, >100% fee_bps, zero rate and same-ledger bodies all fold Live, and a malformed higher version shadows a good one
body:
## Problem

In `pkgs/id/src/currency.rs`, `RateAuthorisation::validate` is the only validity gate the fold trusts — and it checks exactly two things (issuer match, `rate_den != 0`). Every other validity condition the type's own field docs state is never checked anywhere, `sign_authorisation` never calls `validate` at all, and the fold crowns the highest "valid" version — so a malformed authorisation signs, folds `Live`, and a malformed higher version permanently shadows a good lower one (the fold doc: no older version revives once a higher exists).

- `pkgs/id/src/currency.rs:152-163` — `validate()` checks only `issuer_id == author` and `rate_den == 0`. Its rustdoc (:146-151) names only those two errors, matching the one field with explicit validity language: `rate_den` is "non-zero in a valid authorisation" (:104-106).
- The unchecked documented conditions: `min_amount` is the "Smallest convertible amount" and `max_amount` the "Largest" (:108-112) — `min > max` is a contradiction no conversion can satisfy; `not_before` is "No conversions before this time" and `expires_at` the "Mandatory expiry: no conversions at or after" (:118-121) — `expires_at <= not_before` is an empty/inverted window; `fee_bps` is a "fee in basis points" (:124-126) — above 10,000 bps the fee exceeds 100% of the conversion; the module doc (:10-14) defines the object as one direction `source_ledger` → `dest_ledger` — identical ledgers are a degenerate self-conversion; `rate_num == 0` makes `apply_rate` return `Some(0)` for every amount (:169-175).
- `pkgs/id/src/currency.rs:279-311` — `fold_authorisation` filters candidates by `body.validate(author).is_ok()` (:291, under the doc at :262-277: "Among the expected issuer's valid versions the highest is the candidate") and crowns the highest version `Live`. An unchecked-malformed v2 therefore displaces a good v1, and since revocation/supersession never revives a lower version, the authorisation is bricked by its own malformed successor.
- `pkgs/id/src/currency.rs:313-336` — `sign_authorisation` serializes and signs any body without calling `validate`: even the two existing checks are sign-time unenforced, so an issuer can publish a zero-denominator authorisation the fold will silently drop (`fold` → `None`) while believing it live.

This is Phase 1 library code (#3800, closed), but the Phase 2/3 gateway (#3801/#3802, on #2290) will consume `fold_authorisation`'s `Live` state as its trust input — the gate should mean what the docs say before a gateway builds on it.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneB-currencyvalidate/` with `currency.rs` copied verbatim from `pkgs/id/src/currency.rs` (production code, md5 `291c105842289c856635a2b69ffd1d72`, identical in the sandbox clone at main `a0ff47b41` and the laptop checkout; only the `#[cfg(test)]` module was stripped and `crate::chain` stubbed to the surface `currency.rs` uses — `validate`/`fold_authorisation`/`apply_rate` are pure and unmodified), `cargo run --release`, using the #2290 worked example from the module's own tests as the baseline body:

- BASELINE (min 1 ≤ max 10,000, window 0 → 4102444800, no fee): `validate=Ok(())`, fold = `Live`.
- P1 `min_amount=10_001, max_amount=10_000`: `validate=Ok(())`, fold = `Live`.
- P2 `not_before=1000, expires_at=1000` (empty window): `validate=Ok(())`, fold = `Live`.
- P3 `not_before=2000, expires_at=1000` (inverted window): `validate=Ok(())`, fold = `Live`.
- P4 `fee_bps=Some(20_000)` (a 200% fee): `validate=Ok(())`, fold = `Live`.
- P5 `rate_num=0`: `validate=Ok(())`, `apply_rate(100)=Some(0)`, fold = `Live`.
- P6 `source_ledger == dest_ledger == "ABC"`: `validate=Ok(())`, fold = `Live`.
- CONTROL `rate_den=0`: `validate=Err(ZeroRateDenominator)`, fold = `None` — the one documented check beyond issuer works.
- P7 shadowing: good v1 + inverted-bounds v2 → fold = `Live` version 2 (min 10001, max 10000); the good v1 is unreachable.

Dedup: title/keyword searches for `RateAuthorisation`, currency-validate, fee_bps and min_amount across open and closed issues find only the #2290 design (open), the closed Phase 1 implementation #3800, and the gateway phases #3801/#3802 — none covers validation completeness.

## Why it matters

`Live` is the fold's promise that an authorisation is usable. Today it also covers authorisations that can never convert (inverted bounds, empty window), that charge more than the converted amount in fees, or that convert a ledger into itself — and because version selection trusts `validate`, one malformed successor silently retires every good earlier version. The issuer-side sign path compounds it: nothing stops publishing a body the fold will drop or crown wrongly. Fixing the gate now is cheap; after the #3801/#3802 gateway treats `Live` as authoritative, each unchecked case becomes a gateway bug instead of a library inconsistency.

## Acceptance criteria

- `RateAuthorisation::validate` rejects, with named `ValidateError` variants: `min_amount > max_amount`; `expires_at <= not_before`; `fee_bps > 10_000`. For `rate_num == 0` and `source_ledger == dest_ledger`, the fix either rejects them in `validate` too or documents explicitly at the field why they are intentionally valid — silence is not an accepted outcome.
- `sign_authorisation` refuses a body that `validate` rejects (sign/validate symmetry), or the asymmetry is documented as intentional at `sign_authorisation` with the reason.
- New unit tests cover each rejected case at both `validate` and the fold (a malformed higher version no longer crowns over a good lower version — it is skipped by the fold's validity filter, like the zero-denominator control), and the existing `currency` tests pass unchanged.
- The `validate` rustdoc lists every condition it checks, so the Phase 2 gateway (#3801/#3802) can rely on the doc as the contract.

title: id(references): resolve and insert_unambiguous ignore the tombstone — cleared targets still resolve, receive new commits, and contest live targets
body:
## Problem

In `pkgs/id/src/references.rs` (the friendly-name reference-resolution PoC, #2259), resolution never reads `IndexedObject.cleared`. The tombstone flag is written by `LocalIndex::clear` (:353-360) and read in exactly one place — `render` (:553) — while `resolve` (:383), `claimants` (:365), `best_match` (:408) and `insert_unambiguous` (:497) all treat a cleared target as fully live. Two consequences, both verified below:

- **A fresh reference can be committed to a tombstone.** When the only matching target is already cleared, `resolve` returns it as an ordinary candidate and `insert_unambiguous` returns `Ok` — the author's "unambiguous" commit succeeds, and the reference renders `Cleared` the first time it is shown. The `Cleared` render state exists for a target cleared *after* a reference was stored (module doc, four rendering states); nothing in the module's contract contemplates committing a new reference to a target the store already tombstoned.
- **A tombstone contests like a live rival.** `claimants` counts cleared objects, so when one live and one cleared object share a title/alias surface, the live target's exact match is marked `Contested` and `insert_unambiguous` refuses with `Ambiguous(2)` — byte-for-byte the same outcome as two live rivals (the by-design contested case). A dead claim blocks the live target's auto-commit indefinitely, because the tombstone never leaves the index.

Note: this module currently does not compile on main — that is tracked separately as #4454 (two errors, neither in the resolution path). This issue is about the resolution logic, which is independent of those errors; sequencing it after #4454 is fine.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Full-file read plus a laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-02-laneB-refcleared/` (`cargo run --release`, rustc 1.98, edition 2024) with `references.rs` copied from main `466cf98fb` (md5 `b939a8c3b71faa4fef2958834888ce1c`). The resolution code (`resolve`/`claimants`/`best_match`/`insert_unambiguous`/`render`/`clear`) is byte-identical to production; the probe carries only the surface the module uses — a stub `p2panda_core::Hash` (digest/to_hex/FromStr), `AuthorKey = [u8;32]` — plus two disclosed compile shims for the #4454 errors (a probe-local `Default for StoreId` impl, and owning the stripped hex `String` in `from_markdown`), neither of which touches the resolution path.

- CONTROL (one live object, title "Roadmap"): `candidates=1 contested=false`, `insert_unambiguous = Ok`, renders `Resolved`.
- P1 (the same object, cleared before resolution): `candidates=1 contested=false`, `insert_unambiguous = Ok` (reference committed), and rendering that just-committed reference gives `state=Cleared`.
- P2 (one live + one cleared object, both titled "Atlas"): `candidates=2 contested=true single=None`, `insert_unambiguous = Err(Ambiguous(2))`.
- CONTROL2 (two live objects titled "Atlas"): `candidates=2 contested=true` — P2 is indistinguishable from the by-design live-rival case.

Grep on current main confirms the mechanism: `cleared` occurs at :274 (field), :357 (set by `clear`), :553 (read by `render`) and in tests — nowhere in the resolution path.

Dedup: title/keyword searches for `references cleared resolve`, `LocalIndex`, `insert_unambiguous`, `friendly-name references` across open and closed issues find only the #2259 PoC epic and unrelated items — none covers cleared-target resolution. #4454 covers only the module's two compile errors.

## Why it matters

The module's core promise is "nothing is picked silently" — contested and ambiguous phrases are shown, never auto-committed. That promise is about *live* alternatives. Today a tombstone both (a) silently receives new commits as if it were the unambiguous live answer, producing citations that are dead on arrival, and (b) silently vetoes auto-commit for a genuinely unambiguous live target forever. As the PoC's index is fed from real store state (the v2 fan-out the spec plans), cleared documents/notes are common, so both failure modes would be routine, not exotic.

## Acceptance criteria

- `resolve` does not return cleared targets as candidates (or, if returning them is decided to be intentional, they are marked distinctly from live candidates and the module doc says so — silence is not an accepted outcome).
- `insert_unambiguous` never commits a reference whose only match is a cleared target: it returns `NoMatch` (or a dedicated error) in that case.
- `claimants` does not count cleared objects: a live target whose only surface rival is tombstoned resolves uncontested and `insert_unambiguous` succeeds for it.
- `render`'s `Cleared` state is unchanged (a target cleared *after* its reference was stored still degrades to its label).
- New unit tests cover: cleared-only match, live+cleared same-surface, and the existing live+live contested control; the existing `references` tests pass once the module compiles again (#4454).

title: ci(mcpx): restore the policy-listed PR test tier trigger
body:
## Problem

`.github/ci-policy.md` lists `mcpx test` as a PR-tier workflow (`init`, `unit`, `lint`, six static e2e shards, and `ci-ok`), but `.github/workflows/mcpx-test.yml` currently triggers only on pushes to `main` and `workflow_dispatch`; it has no `pull_request` trigger.

This was observed while verifying PR #4417, which changes `pkgs/mcpx/**`: the PR check rollup has only CodeRabbit (neutral/skipping), and `gh run list --branch queue/6157-4282-mcpx-mcpclient-bound-read` returns no GitHub Actions runs. The exact-head targeted test `go test ./internal/mcpclient/ -count=1` passed locally; that does not substitute for the policy-listed PR tier.

## Expected

Align the workflow trigger with the documented PR tier, then verify a non-draft mcpx PR receives the documented jobs. Until then, report the coverage gap rather than treating absent checks as green.

Related: #4282, PR #4417.

<!-- agent-note:v1 agent=repo-worker-code-openchamber-scheduled state=filed at=2026-11-02T18:49:00Z -->

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `.github/workflows/mcpx-test.yml` triggers on `pull_request` in addition to push-to-main and workflow_dispatch, matching the PR tier documented in `.github/ci-policy.md`.
- [ ] A non-draft PR touching `pkgs/mcpx/**` receives the documented jobs (init, unit, lint, six static e2e shards, ci-ok) — verified on a real PR after the change.
- [ ] Until the trigger lands, the coverage gap is reported rather than absent checks being treated as green.

title: Split charge-candidates producer: staged inputs staged on the sandbox, producer runs on the laptop
body:
## Problem

`pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/produce-charge-candidates.ts` (#1057, #2205) runs from a sandbox checkout of this repo solely because it shells out to the sandbox-only connector CLIs (`/opt/hatch/bin/plaid`, `/opt/hatch/bin/hatch_gws_cli`). Drew's 2026-11-02 rule removes ALL repo copies from the sandbox (work runs on the laptop via SSH), and the producer's standing trigger has already lapsed silently once (runs stopped 2026-11-02 09:18Z).

## Split (approved by Drew 2026-11-02)

- **Sandbox = thin fetcher, no repo.** A standalone script runs the exact CLI calls the producer makes today (one Plaid `transactions-get`, two Gmail `+triage` searches, plus `+read` for message bodies the producer requests) and stages the raw responses as JSON in the hatch-personal-synced hidden-files area: `plaid-transactions.json`, `gmail-triage.json`, `gmail-bodies.json`, `charge-inputs-manifest.json` (period + fetch times + per-source status).
- **Producer = laptop.** The producer gains a staged-input mode (`CHARGE_INPUTS_DIR`): it reads the staged raw responses instead of shelling out; the manifest's period governs. Gmail bodies it needs but staging lacks are written to `gmail-body-requests.json` and picked up on a later run once the fetcher stages them (each body fetched exactly once). Live CLI mode stays the default when the env is unset.
- Producer output (`charges-candidates.json`) is written directly at the laptop path the fleet-feed collector already reads. The cross-machine output ride and the sandbox clone both go away.

## Acceptance

- Parity: for a fixed historical window, staged-mode output candidates are identical to live-mode output candidates (verified before merge).
- Aggregator tests/typecheck green in the worktree.
- After cutover, one full cycle observed: fresh staged inputs -> fresh `charges-candidates.json` on the laptop -> collector consumes it.
- Old sandbox runner (`~/tools/produce-charge-candidates-scheduled.sh`) retired; no sandbox repo copy recreated.

title: bug(queue): claimed task 6700 rejected by lane/checkpoint/heartbeat/park RPCs; claim-response titles diverge from tasks table
body:
## Problem

On 2026-11-03 ~02:02–02:25Z, lane code-i (repo-queue-worker-shift-i) claimed task 6700 via `repo-queue.py claim --queue repo-health-code-pilot --worker repo-worker-code --lane code-i`. The claim returned success (status claimed, lease_until 2026-11-03T02:47:51Z), and a direct read of `agent.tasks` (id=eq.6700) confirms: status=claimed, worker_id=repo-worker-code, lane_id=code-i, attempts=1.

However every subsequent worker RPC for task 6700 rejects the claim:

- `repo-queue.py lane 6700` → HTTP 400 `assign_repo_task_lane: task 6700 does not exist`
- `repo-queue.py checkpoint 6700` → HTTP 400 `checkpoint_task: task 6700 is not claimed by repo-worker-code`
- `repo-queue.py heartbeat 6700` → HTTP 400 `heartbeat_task: task 6700 is not claimed by repo-worker-code`
- `repo-queue.py park 6700` → HTTP 400 `park_task: task 6700 is not claimed by repo-worker-code`

Repeated across ~20 minutes; not a transient single-call failure. The worker could not checkpoint, park, or work the task; its lease will expire and requeue it.

## Second observation: claim-returned titles vs tasks-table titles

For all three tasks claimed by this shift, the title in the claim RPC response did not match the title in a direct `agent.tasks` read minutes later:

- task 6562: claim returned `fix(id/world): track retained admin-history bytes incrementally (#4633)`; table title is `Reconcile merged PR #4655 into packets for sibling id P9 test issues #4643/#4644/#4645/#4646`
- task 6695: claim returned `Update all four repo-health lane instructions to pass remaining budget`; table title is `Promote the verified D2 finding in #3107 into an implementation packet for id P9a`
- task 6700: claim returned `Curate #2888: promote into a packet for id P9 lanes removing per-OS predicate duplication`; table title is `Curate #2955: stale review — no queue review artifact has ever covered merged PR #2955`

For task 6562 and task 6695 the checkpoint/park RPCs worked normally, so the divergence there is limited to the returned-vs-stored title (or titles are being rewritten after claim — also worth ruling out). For task 6700 the claim is unusable through the RPC surface at all.

## Impact

- A claimed task that no worker verb can touch is indistinguishable from a claim evaporation until its lease expires (the pattern §10 anti-evaporation discipline exists to prevent).
- If claim responses can describe a different task than the row actually claimed, a worker may do GitHub work (notes, labels, parks) against the wrong issue.

## Acceptance

- Reproduce or explain the task 6700 RPC rejections against a table row that reads claimed by the same worker.
- Explain the claim-response vs tasks-table title divergence for task 6562, task 6695, and task 6700 (response construction, post-claim title rewrite, or read-path difference).
- Add a check (helper self-test or fleet-monitor probe) that a fresh claim can immediately lane + checkpoint; alert when it cannot.

Filed by repo-queue-worker-shift-i (lane code-i) from its 2026-11-02 19:48 CST shift; related design surface: issue #3424.

title: queue: claim_repo_task rejects openchamber scheduled-lane UUIDs (P0001 unknown lane_id)
body:
OpenChamber scheduled lane 8ac61616 (repo-health-code-pilot, worker repo-worker-code) cannot claim with its lane id.

Evidence (2026-11-03 ~07:09Z, 3 attempts):
- \`claim --lane 8ac61616-3815-4e7b-b33d-840a3825154a\` -> HTTP 400 \`claim_repo_task: unknown lane_id 8ac61616-...\`
- \`agent.lanes\` HAS the row: lane_id=8ac61616, worker=repo-worker-code, queue=repo-health-code-pilot, surface=openchamber, enabled=true.
- Same command WITHOUT \`--lane\` succeeded immediately (claimed task 6303, parked-due).
- Pattern: with nothing due the RPC returns the null row without touching the lane check; once a candidate is due, lane validation fires and fails. So every openchamber lane hits this on every productive claim.

Impact: all 12 openchamber UUID lanes on the code queue (and likely the opencode-queue UUID lane) can only claim unattributed. Workaround used this run: claim as shared worker + \`"origin": "openchamber-scheduled-lane"\` in the first checkpoint for attribution. Lane ledger gets no execution row.

Ask: either fix the RPC lane validation to accept registered openchamber lanes, or bless no-lane claiming + origin-marker attribution for openchamber lanes and amend the scheduled-lane §8 instruction accordingly.

## Acceptance criteria

- A registered OpenChamber scheduled lane (e.g. lane 8ac61616-3815-4e7b-b33d-840a3825154a in agent.lanes, enabled=true) can claim a due task on repo-health-code-pilot with `claim --lane <uuid>` without the P0001 unknown lane_id error, and the claim writes its lane ledger execution row.
- The same check passes for the opencode-queue UUID lane.
- If the resolution is instead to bless no-lane claiming + origin-marker attribution, the scheduled-lane instruction (protocol §10 / lane §8) is amended to say so, and this issue records that decision.
- Unregistered/random lane ids still fail validation (the fix must not simply disable lane checking).

title: ci: nix-ci basic tier has no pull_request trigger — bin/-only PRs merge with zero basic checks
body:
## Problem

`.github/ci-policy.md` states the PR tier is the merge requirement and describes `basic: proxy port fallbacks` as the required context, and `.github/workflows/nix-ci.yml`'s own header comment says the job "runs on every PR". The workflow's `on:` block, however, is:

```yaml
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  schedule:
    - cron: "17 8 * * *"
  workflow_dispatch:
```

There is no `pull_request` trigger, so the basic tier never runs on a PR. A `bin/`-only PR therefore gets no basic-tier verification at all: the check rollup contains only CodeRabbit (neutral/skipping) and `gh run list --branch <branch>` returns no Actions runs.

## Evidence

While landing PR #3487 (`bin/provider-catalog-sync.mjs` shape validation, `bin/` + tests only):

- `gh run list --branch queue/5433-2827-catalogsync-shape` → only the two scheduled `jules-daily-*` push workflows, both failing in 0s; no `nix ci` run, before or after a fresh push to the branch.
- `gh pr checks 3487` → only `CodeRabbit skipping`.
- `gh pr view 3487 --json mergeable,mergeStateStatus` → `MERGEABLE CLEAN`, so the merge proceeded without the required context ever being reported.
- Local evidence stood in for CI: `node --test bin/provider-catalog-sync.test.mjs` → 35 pass / 0 fail.

This is the same class of gap as #4533 (mcpx PR test tier never triggers) and #3039 (host-eval not a required check), for the nix-ci basic tier.

## Impact

Any PR touching only `bin/`, docs, or other paths outside the PR-triggered workflows (id, mcpx*, mod-tidy, opencode-config-guard, production-line-guard, repo-sweeper) merges unverified by Actions. The proxy-port-fallback check is exactly the guard for `bin/*.mjs` port defaults, i.e. the one job that should have run here.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `nix-ci.yml` gains a `pull_request` trigger (with or without a paths filter that includes `bin/**`, `.opencode/opencode.jsonc`, `home/common/default.nix`, and the workflow itself).
- [ ] `basic: proxy port fallbacks` reports on a `bin/`-only PR (verify with a scratch PR, not just by reading the YAML).
- [ ] `ci-policy.md`, the workflow comment, and the actual trigger agree; if a path filter is deliberate, the policy says which paths each basic-tier job covers.
- [ ] Merge-queue behaviour is unchanged (the `merge_group` trigger, if required by the ruleset, is preserved).

title: aggregator(alerts): aggregator-wide auth/CSRF posture for mutating routes (#3702 disposition 2)
body:
Disposition 2 of design #3702 Phase 3 (audit task 5613, 2026-11-03). The aggregator has no auth model at all; the throat's mutating routes inherit that. Exact current exposure (all unauthenticated):

- `DELETE /api/push/subscriptions` (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/server.ts:1627`) — anyone who knows an endpoint can unsubscribe it. Endpoints are handed out by the page itself (`render.ts` `data-unsub` + the `SUBS` script constant), so "the endpoint is a secret" is not a boundary.
- `POST /api/alerts/<id>/(ack|close)` (`server.ts:1665`) — anyone can ack/close an incident, including a critical one, which suppresses its escalation. Route is UUID-gated but not authenticated.
- `POST /api/push/test` (`server.ts:1643`) — anyone can fan a push out to every subscription.

The intake route is the only authenticated one (`POST /api/alerts`, Bearer token via `alertsIntakeAuthorized`, `server.ts:322`).

The Phase 3 stance is: no partial auth on one route while the page that supplies the inputs is public — the aggregator-wide model is the decision, and the mitigation until then is the private origin the app is served on. This issue is that decision's implementation: a shared auth (or signed-page/CSRF) posture for the mutating routes, applied consistently, without breaking `assets/push-client.js` (POST/DELETE only).

Related open question in the design doc: "an aggregator-wide auth model". Filed from #3702 Phase 3 audit.

title: Fix #4887: id(hosted_binding): a pending delayed rebind does not reserv
body:
Implement GitHub issue #4887 in developing-today/code: id(hosted_binding): a pending delayed rebind does not reserve its target key

## Summary

The delayed-rebind protocol added in #4885 (slice 2 of #3809, `pkgs/id/src/hosted_binding.rs` at `9d1464c05`) never reserves the **target** key of a pending delayed rebind, and `effect_due_rebind` never re-checks it. During the 30-day wait, another account can bind that exact key by an ordinary ceremony; when the wait elapses, the delayed rebind still effects and `apply_rebind` silently overwrites the other binding's `binding_by_iroh` entry. Two `active` binding records then claim the same `iroh_id`, and the by-key index points at only one of them — breaking the §1.2 rule the ceremony itself enforces ("one `sub` per `iroh_id` at a time", `submit_proof` conflict check).

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe at origin/main `9d1464c05`)

Probe test appended in a throwaway laptop worktree (`probe-2026-11-03-laneB-scan20`, removed after the run; log `/tmp/probe-scan20.log` on the laptop):

1. Account A binds key21, then `request_delayed_rebind` to key22 → request `Pending`, binding `rebind_pending`.
2. A third account completes an ordinary `complete_browser_ceremony` with **key22** → succeeds. Nothing consulted the pending request: `request_delayed_rebind` checks only `binding_by_iroh` at request time (hosted_binding.rs:1269), the pending target key is inserted into no index, and `submit_proof`'s conflict check (hosted_binding.rs:~997) checks only `binding_by_iroh`.
3. Time advances past `effective_at`; `effect_due_rebind` with a valid new-key countersignature → succeeds. Unlike both other paths, it has **no** `NewKeyBoundElsewhere` recheck: `rebind_with_old_key_authorization` checks `binding_by_iroh.contains_key(&new_iroh_id)` at effect time (hosted_binding.rs:1414) and `request_delayed_rebind` checks it at request time (:1269); `effect_due_rebind` (hosted_binding.rs:1462) checks neither that nor pending requests.
4. `apply_rebind` (hosted_binding.rs:1538-1540) unconditionally does `binding_by_iroh.remove(old)` + `binding_by_iroh.insert(new, this binding)`, overwriting the third account's index entry.

Probe outcome (asserted in the probe, all true on current main): both A's and the third account's records are `Active` with `iroh_id` = key22; `binding_by_iroh[key22]` names A's binding only; the third account's record is silently unindexed for its own key.

The symmetric hole also exists at request time: two different accounts can both open pending delayed rebinds to the same target key, and whichever effects second overwrites the first's index entry the same way.

## Why it matters

The delayed path is the account-recovery path for a lost root key — exactly the path whose target-key ownership must be unambiguous. The 30-day wait is the security property (§4.2), but it also creates a 30-day window in which the target key is claimable by anyone: a squatter who binds the target key during the wait is not stopped at effect time, is not notified, and loses their by-key index entry without any error, while their binding record still says `active`. Any consumer resolving a binding by `iroh_id` (device authorization, grant references — §1) then reaches the wrong account's binding.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A pending delayed rebind reserves its target key: an ordinary ceremony (`submit_proof`) naming a key that is the target of a pending rebind fails with a conflict (e.g. `IrohIdBoundElsewhere` or a dedicated pending-rebind conflict), and a second `request_delayed_rebind` from another account naming the same target key fails with `NewKeyBoundElsewhere` (or equivalent).
- [ ] `effect_due_rebind` re-checks at effect time, before any mutation: if the target key is now bound to a different binding (or is the target of another pending request that was created earlier), it fails with `NewKeyBoundElsewhere` and leaves the binding, the request, and both indexes unchanged (the `RebindError` no-mutation contract).
- [ ] `apply_rebind` cannot silently overwrite a `binding_by_iroh` entry owned by a different binding: it refuses (or its callers guarantee the check) when the existing entry names another binding.
- [ ] Regression tests cover: ceremony-bind of a pending target key during the wait; two pending rebinds to one target key; effect after the target key was bound elsewhere (state unchanged on refusal); the existing 21 hosted_binding tests still pass (`cargo test -p id --lib hosted_binding`, laptop or CI).

Distinct from: #4868 / #4871 (the §3 ceremony's consumed-challenge and pairing-code findings in the same file — different functions and defects), #3809 (the delayed-rebind implementation epic this landed under; this is a defect in that new code, found by reading it against the §1.2 conflict rules).



Context: a Jules session began this issue on 2026-11-03 and was stopped mid-flight when the owner retired the Jules service (decommission, developing-today/code#5098). Before starting, check for any pull request or branch that attempt may have produced (search PRs referencing #4887) and treat the issue text above as the source of truth.

House rules from the repo owner: (1) Deliver the finished work as a pull request in this run; put "Fixes #4887" in the PR description so the issue closes on merge. (2) Cover the whole set in the one PR: every instance of the same problem, and any directly related dependency updates batched in — never one PR per item or per dependency. (3) Run the relevant tests and checks before opening the PR. (4) Merging is permitted only when you are reasonably certain the PR is correct and complete (checks green, tests run, low-risk); you never have to merge — when in doubt, leave the PR open and state your confidence and what a human should check. (5) If you hit a genuine blocker (missing credentials, a decision only the owner can make), stop and say exactly what is needed in your final summary.

title: Fix #4007: lab-ops-hub: Worker-fallback extractor — complete HTML character-referen
body:
Implement GitHub issue #4007 in developing-today/code: lab-ops-hub: Worker-fallback extractor — complete HTML character-reference decoding parity ## Problem The lab-ops-hub Worker-fallback extractor (pkgs/lab-ops-hub/src/lib.ts, decodeHtmlEntities) only decodes a small named-entity table and requires a trailing semicolon, so its output diverges from the container Extractor (Python html.parser + html.unescape) on standard references — stored titles/text then depend on which crawling path ran. Found by Codex review round 4 on PR #3918 (comment 4437512013), dispositioned there as a follow-up because the fix (complete HTML5 named-reference data + semicolon-omission rules) is larger than a review-fix round. Sibling of #569. ## Evidence (verified against the container Extractor, Python 3.13.13) Input: `Α &

→ A & B

` - Container: title `Α &`, text `→ A & B` - Worker fallback: every reference preserved literally ## Scope - Decode the complete HTML5 named character references (the data behind Python's html.entities.html5), including the legacy semicolon-less forms and the spec's semicolon-omission rules for text content (e.g. `A` -> `A`, `&` -> `&` in the cases html.unescape expands). - Keep the existing numeric-reference normalization (C1 remap, U+FFFD rules) intact. - Add shared parity fixtures (test/extractor-fixtures.json) pinning the cases above plus a spread of named references; expected values verified against the container suite before pinning. Both suites (node + python) must stay green. ## Acceptance - The example above produces identical {title, links, text} from the Worker fallback and the container Extractor. - New fixtures cover: a non-Latin-1 named reference (→), an uppercase legacy reference (&), a semicolon-less numeric reference, and a semicolon-less named reference. ## Acceptance criteria - The Worker-fallback extractor (`pkgs/lab-ops-hub/src/lib.ts`, `decodeHtmlEntities`) decodes the complete HTML5 named character references, including legacy semicolon-less forms, with the spec's semicolon-omission rules for text content matching Python `html.unescape`. - Filed evidence case: input `Α &

→ A & B

title: pm-stack(aggregator): dnsSectionFromRegisterJson accepts impossible renewal dates and negative prices — the Markdown parser and isDnsSection in the same file refuse both
body:
# pm-stack(aggregator): dnsSectionFromRegisterJson accepts impossible renewal dates (regex-only) and negative prices — the Markdown parser and isDnsSection in the same file refuse both

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe at main 5c53272ff)

`pm-stack/aggregator/src/dns.ts`:

- `:135` — the register.json parser gates `next_renewal` with only a format regex:
  `if (typeof renewal !== "string" || !/^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$/.test(renewal)) return null;`
  No `isIsoDate` re-check of the calendar components.
- `:57` (approx, `parseDnsRegister`) — the Markdown parser in the same file does it correctly, with the reason spelled out in its comment: an impossible calendar date (2026-02-30, 2026-13-01) "must be refused like a malformed row, or it string-sorts into the register, counts toward the annual total, and poisons nextRenewal / renewingSoon (#2199). isIsoDate re-checks the components, so leap dates (2024-02-29) still parse."
- `:161+` (`isDnsSection`, the shared gate) checks entry `renewal` only as `typeof string`, so a section built from an impossible date passes the gate too.
- `:136` — `renewal_price_usd` is gated finite-only, while `isDnsSection` (#4226) requires a present price and the total to be non-negative; the JSON parser can therefore build a section its own shared gate refuses.

Laptop bun probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-03-laneA-dns/probe.ts`, importing `dnsSectionFromRegisterJson` / `isDnsSection` / `summarizeDns` from main):

- `next_renewal: "2026-02-30"` → section ACCEPTED, `isDnsSection=true`, `summarizeDns(...).nextRenewal = "2026-02-30"`
- `"2026-04-31"` → ACCEPTED, `isDnsSection=true`, nextRenewal `2026-04-31`
- `"2026-13-01"` → ACCEPTED, `isDnsSection=true`, nextRenewal `2026-13-01`
- Controls `"2024-02-29"` (leap) and `"2026-03-15"` → ACCEPTED (correct)
- Two rows priced `20` and `-5` → section ACCEPTED with `totalAnnualListUsd=15`, prices `[20, -5]`, but `isDnsSection=false`

Production path: `pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/collect-fleet-feed.ts:697+` treats register.json as authoritative — when `dnsSectionFromRegisterJson` returns a section the collector marks the dns section "ok" and serves it; the Markdown fallback (which refuses these rows) runs only when the JSON parse returns null.

## Why it matters

register.json is the authoritative source for the DNS register (#902 slice 2). One impossible renewal date in it silently becomes the register's "next renewal", is rendered verbatim on /dns, and distorts `renewingSoon` (string comparisons in `summarizeDns`, dns.ts:242-248), exactly the poisoning #2199 fixed for the Markdown path. A negative list price produces a section that the shared `isDnsSection` gate refuses downstream, so the collector and the live source disagree about the same data.

## Acceptance criteria

- `dnsSectionFromRegisterJson` returns null for a row whose `next_renewal` is not a real calendar date (2026-02-30, 2026-04-31, 2026-13-01), mirroring `parseDnsRegister`'s `isIsoDate` rule; leap dates (2024-02-29) still parse.
- `dnsSectionFromRegisterJson` returns null for a negative `renewal_price_usd` (zero allowed), mirroring the #4226 non-negative rule in `isDnsSection`.
- New tests in `pm-stack/aggregator/test/slice3.test.ts` (or a dns test file) cover the refused shapes plus valid controls; every section the JSON parser returns satisfies `isDnsSection`.
- Aggregator bun test suite and typecheck pass.

title: pm-stack(aggregator): #4942 fix never landed — PR #5256 closed unmerged, applyCloudflareExport still accepts negative used on main
body:
# pm-stack(aggregator): #4942 fix never landed — PR #5256 closed unmerged, applyCloudflareExport still accepts negative used on main

## Summary

Issue #4942 (applyCloudflareExport accepts negative `used`) is CLOSED, but the bug is still live on `main`. Its fix was written and then lost: the implementing PR was closed without merging, and no equivalent change ever reached `main`.

## Evidence (verified this run, 2026-11-03, at origin/main 85c0e0b89)

- `pm-stack/aggregator/src/saas-extract.ts` — in `applyCloudflareExport`, the metrics filter is still finite-only:
  `.filter((m) => m && typeof m.id === "string" && typeof m.used === "number" && Number.isFinite(m.used))`
  The sibling `applySupabaseExport` in the same file drops `used < 0` / `limit < 0` metrics.
- Laptop bun probe at origin/main 85c0e0b89 (probe test mirroring `test/cloudflare-export.test.ts`'s freshDoc): a fresh Cloudflare export doc with `workers-requests used: -500` overlays as-is — stored `used = -500`, derived `percent = -0`, note stamped `Live via cloudflare-graphql-analytics`, card `sourceClass = "api"`. Control metric `kv-reads used: 1420` overlays normally.
- The fix exists but is stranded: commit `59c03cad6` ("fix(pm-stack/aggregator): drop negative Cloudflare export metrics", `Closes #4942`) is present only on branch `queue/8048-4942-cf-negative-used`; `git merge-base --is-ancestor 59c03cad6 origin/main` fails — it is NOT in main.
- PR #5256 from that branch is CLOSED with `mergedAt: null` (never merged), yet issue #4942 was closed at 2026-11-03T22:57Z. `test/cloudflare-export.test.ts` on main has no negative-used regression test.

## Why it matters

A broken/negative Cloudflare export measurement is stamped onto the live card as measured API data with a negative percent, instead of keeping the metric's prose/null fallback — the exact harm #4942 described. The closure of #4942 also makes the fleet believe this is handled, so nobody re-checks it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Land the negative-metric guard in `applyCloudflareExport` (the stranded commit `59c03cad6` on `queue/8048-4942-cf-negative-used` can be cherry-picked, or the one-filter change re-implemented): metrics with `used < 0` are dropped from the overlay, matching `applySupabaseExport`.
- [ ] The regression test from that commit (negative `workers-requests` keeps its fallback while a valid metric in the same doc still overlays) is present in `test/cloudflare-export.test.ts` and passes.
- [ ] Re-run the probe above against the fixed tree: `workers-requests` keeps its prose/null used value and no `Live via` note; `kv-reads` still overlays.
- [ ] Cross-link #4942 and PR #5256 in the fixing PR so the lost-fix path is traceable.

title: opencode-route-proxy: per-leg first-response timeout — shed transport-timeout legs inside the client window (#4370b)
body:
# opencode-route-proxy: per-leg first-response timeout — shed transport-timeout legs inside the client window (#4370 acceptance (b))

Implementation slice scoped by triage task 8950 (lane W, 2026-11-04) extending #3325 leg-shedding to the #4370 death classes. Findings and full evidence are on #3325 (task 8950 comment) and #4370.

## Problem (verified at main, blob 70f01618, bin/opencode-route-proxy.mjs, 1095 lines)

- `callLeaf`'s fetch passes only the shared walk signal — there is no per-leg timeout. A hung/slow leg holds the walk; the only cap is the whole-walk `TIMEOUT_MS` (line 62, default 1,200,000 ms).
- `runCompletion` does fall through on per-leaf transport errors, but only while the signal is not aborted; the OpenCode client's ~10 s no-output window (`provider.transport` "No response output within 10000ms", #4370) kills the session first, and a client abort is terminal in the walk.
- Net effect: a transport-timeout leg is never shed in time — ~30 fleet sessions died this way on 2026-11-01 (#4370).

## Scope

- Per-leaf first-response (headers) timeout in `bin/opencode-route-proxy.mjs`, configurable via env in the existing `OPENCODE_ROUTE_PROXY_*` pattern, sized well under the client no-output window; on timeout, record the attempt (outcome `timeout`, tag `Transport`, `failedOverTo` set) and continue the walk.
- Proxy tests: hung first leg sheds to a live second leg inside the timeout; ledger row written.
- Verify whether the client's ~10 s provider.transport window is configurable for proxied routes; if the proxy-side fix cannot beat it, record that on #4370 with the exact client setting named.

Out of scope: in-stream pre-content error shedding (task 8932, #3325), mid-stream fallthrough, route redesign.

## Acceptance criteria

- A transport-timeout leg is shed like a quota-exhausted leg: walk continues, session completes on a live leg.
- Per-leg timeout configurable + documented next to `TIMEOUT_MS`; responding legs unchanged.
- #4370 acceptance (b) satisfied by the merged fix, or closed out on #4370 with provider/client-side evidence.

Refs: #4370 (acceptance (b)), #3325, task 8950, task 7380.

title: id(artifact): home_declared accepts a duplicated (endpoint, world_id) server pair — parsed() has no duplicate check, artifact pushes go out twice
body:
## Problem

`SignedArtifact::parsed()` validates a `home_declared` body by count and by
per-server shape only — it never rejects a repeated server entry. A signed
declaration that names the same `(endpoint, world_id)` pair twice is accepted,
stored, and returned by `ArtifactLog::declared()`, and the push path then sends
one copy of every artifact per list entry, so the duplicated endpoint receives
every artifact push twice.

## Evidence (origin/main 1433b926f)

- `pkgs/id/src/artifact.rs:362-383` — the `HOME_DECLARED` arm of `parsed()`:
  checks the author matches the account (:365-369), the count is at most
  `MAX_HOME_SERVERS` (:370-374), and per server that `check_target(endpoint)`
  passes and `world_id` is non-empty (:375-382). No duplicate check anywhere.
- `pkgs/id/src/artifact.rs:296-301` — the same module's `check()` refuses a
  repeated hash in `after` (`"an artifact names {hash} twice in after"`), so
  list uniqueness is the module's own established rule; the `servers` list is
  the one list that escaped it. (Didit's `check_subjects` and the writer-body
  codecs filed as #5243/#5363 apply the same rule.)
- `pkgs/id/src/directory_view.rs:1445-1463` — `artifact_outbound` maps
  `declared.servers` verbatim to `Outbound` pushes, one per entry: a duplicated
  pair produces two identical artifact pushes to the same endpoint for every
  artifact the account publishes.
- Verified by a laptop cargo probe at origin/main `1433b926f` (probe test in
  `artifact.rs` tests, probe worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-04-laneA-homedecl`):
  a `HomeDeclared` whose `servers` is `[ (endpoint_of(7), "home"), (endpoint_of(7), "home") ]`
  signs and `ArtifactLog::insert` returns `Ok(Stored::New)`, with
  `declared(account).servers.len() == 2`. Controls in the same probe: two
  distinct endpoints insert Ok, and the same endpoint under two different
  `world_id`s inserts Ok (that shape is legitimate and must keep working).

## Why it matters

A home declaration is the account's published routing table for its artifacts.
Accepting a duplicated entry makes the stored declaration non-canonical (two
byte-different declarations describe the same routing) and makes every
downstream consumer pay for the duplication — today that is duplicate artifact
pushes to the same endpoint on every publish; any future consumer that counts,
prices, or health-checks servers inherits the double-count. The fix is cheapest
at the validation boundary every other list in this module already uses.

## Acceptance criteria

- `parsed()` for `home_declared` refuses a body whose `servers` list repeats an
  `(endpoint, world_id)` pair, with a `Refusal::Forbidden` error in the arm's
  existing style.
- The same endpoint under different `world_id`s, and distinct endpoints under
  the same `world_id`, remain accepted.
- New tests in `pkgs/id/src/artifact.rs` pin: duplicated pair refused; distinct
  endpoints accepted; same endpoint / two worlds accepted.
- Existing artifact and directory tests pass (`cargo test --lib artifact` and
  `cargo test --lib directory` from `pkgs/id`).

title: fleet-proxy: pool sized for the fleet's work — default 50 + bounded wait in pool_get
body:
## Order

Drew, 2026-11-04: "build something that supports all our work — that was always the goal — fix it." Both arms approved: the env raise now, and the code fix behind it.

## Evidence

The concurrency report on #5412 (comment 6634809392) isolated the defect in `crates/fleet-proxy/src/serve.rs`:

- The per-port tunnel pool is an idle cache capped by `LAPTOP_AGENT_POOL`, default **12**.
- `pool_get` never waits: no idle tunnel ⇒ open a brand-new tunnel immediately, which costs seconds under burst; only 12 are retained, so the next burst pays again.
- Benchmark (32 concurrent, production): queue-broker p50 **1001.7 ms** through the proxy vs 213.0 ms direct, ~1/6 the throughput; the cliff starts exactly at the cap (at 16 concurrent, p95 already 851 ms). The identical binary with the pool at 32 (scratch control) restored direct-class performance (p50 137.8 ms). Backends are exonerated; the cap + no-wait overflow is the cause.

## Scope

1. **Default idle cap 12 → 50.** Brokers are auto-spawned by `fleet proxy connect` (`ensure_broker`) from arbitrary consumers whose environments do not carry the knob — a production broker was observed respawned by a random consumer with no `LAPTOP_AGENT_POOL` in its environment, silently reverting an env-only raise. The right size must be the compiled default; the env var remains an override. (The immediate arm — `LAPTOP_AGENT_POOL=50` at the sandbox broker's owning launch surface, `init-ensure.sh` — lands with this issue and stays as an explicit override.)
2. **Bounded wait in `pool_get`.** When no idle tunnel exists and opening another would exceed the pool size in live tunnels, wait (condvar signalled by `pool_put`) up to a bounded budget (250–500 ms, justified from the benchmark's tunnel-return times) for a returned tunnel before opening a new one. Hard requirements: a request must never hard-fail because of the pool (timeout ⇒ open a new tunnel, as today); the existing failure path (discard dead pooled connection, retry once on a fresh tunnel, then 502) is preserved; the pool mutex is never held during network I/O; keepalive behavior unchanged (never resets idle-exit).
3. **Legibility.** Named constants, the overflow policy (idle → wait-bounded → grow) commented at `pool_get`, and the effective pool size rendered in the broker's startup line.
4. **Tests/smoke.** Unit coverage for the wait (a waiter is woken by `pool_put`; a waiter times out into a fresh tunnel; live-count accounting). The workspace smoke gains a 32-concurrent hermetic burst against a scratch broker on default config asserting no request hangs or fails, plus the startup-line pool rendering.

## Acceptance

- Workspace tests + full smoke suite green.
- Merged, and the production sandbox broker redeployed onto the merged build: health on all three ports, `repo-queue health`, framed secrets request, and a 32-concurrent burst spot-check at direct-class p50.
- A broker auto-spawned with no `LAPTOP_AGENT_POOL` in its environment verifiably runs the 50 default (startup line).

title: atlas-search: build-provenance hardening — Gate A parity must catch a divergent embedder build under the same FOD hash
body:
## Provenance of this issue — read first

This issue exists to examine a claim, not to report a confirmed defect.

During Atlas step 6 (#5356, Gate B + cutover), a mid-run relayed report claimed the embed builds are **bimodal under one FOD hash**: one machine's build embedding ~+0.88% uniformly "hot", another's ~−30% "cold", with both builds passing the startup assertion. That claim **does not appear in step 6's final report** and is **UNVERIFIED**. It may be a misread relay, a scratch-instance artifact, or real; nobody has reproduced it.

What IS verified, from step 6's completed work:

- Gate B's fresh paired run produced **byte-identical top-10 lists on 309/309 questions** (Rust packaged build vs the Python reference, production corpus).
- The cutover battery passed **cross-machine**: via-service ≡ standalone results, and the sensitivity-ceiling canary behaved correctly.
- Conclusion from evidence: the **currently deployed builds are consistent**. There is no known live defect.

## Why file it anyway

If the claim were true, it would be exactly the failure Gate A (embedder parity, #5351) exists to catch — and it would have slipped past it: two divergent embedder builds sharing one fixed-output-derivation hash, both green at startup, silently returning different rankings depending on which machine built or served the closure. Atlas step 7 should not dispatch on an unexamined provenance claim of that shape.

## Asks

1. **Verify or refute the bimodality claim** with a two-builder experiment: build the atlas-search closure on two machines, embed a fixed probe set with each build, and compare against the pinned reference embeddings within a tight cosine tolerance. Record the numbers either way.
2. **If real:** strengthen Gate A (the startup/reference parity check) so a divergent build fails loud instead of passing, and separate per-machine build outputs so divergent artifacts cannot share one FOD hash.
3. **Either way:** record the verdict on this issue and on epic #5350, so step 7's dispatch rests on an examined claim.

## Severity

Hardening / pre-step-7 gate. Not a live defect; no user-facing impact is known or claimed.

title: Scheduled Bolt — developing-today/code
body:
You are "Bolt" ⚡ - a performance-obsessed agent who makes the codebase faster, one optimization at a time.

Your mission is to identify and implement ONE small performance improvement that makes the application measurably faster or more efficient.


## Boundaries

✅ **Always do:**
- Run commands like `pnpm lint` and `pnpm test` (or associated equivalents) before creating PR
- Add comments explaining the optimization
- Measure and document expected performance impact

⚠️ **Ask first:**
- Adding any new dependencies
- Making architectural changes

🚫 **Never do:**
- Modify package.json or tsconfig.json without instruction
- Make breaking changes
- Optimize prematurely without actual bottleneck
- Sacrifice code readability for micro-optimizations

BOLT'S PHILOSOPHY:
- Speed is a feature
- Every millisecond counts
- Measure first, optimize second
- Don't sacrifice readability for micro-optimizations

BOLT'S JOURNAL - CRITICAL LEARNINGS ONLY:
Before starting, read .jules/bolt.md (create if missing).

Your journal is NOT a log - only add entries for CRITICAL learnings that will help you avoid mistakes or make better decisions.

⚠️ ONLY add journal entries when you discover:
- A performance bottleneck specific to this codebase's architecture
- An optimization that surprisingly DIDN'T work (and why)
- A rejected change with a valuable lesson
- A codebase-specific performance pattern or anti-pattern
- A surprising edge case in how this app handles performance

❌ DO NOT journal routine work like:
- "Optimized component X today" (unless there's a learning)
- Generic React performance tips
- Successful optimizations without surprises

Format: `## YYYY-MM-DD - [Title]
**Learning:** [Insight]
**Action:** [How to apply next time]`

BOLT'S DAILY PROCESS:

1. 🔍 PROFILE - Hunt for performance opportunities:

  FRONTEND PERFORMANCE:
  - Unnecessary re-renders in React/Vue/Angular components
  - Missing memoization for expensive computations
  - Large bundle sizes (opportunities for code splitting)
  - Unoptimized images (missing lazy loading, wrong formats)
  - Missing virtualization for long lists
  - Synchronous operations blocking the main thread
  - Missing debouncing/throttling on frequent events
  - Unused CSS or JavaScript being loaded
  - Missing resource preloading for critical assets
  - Inefficient DOM manipulations

  BACKEND PERFORMANCE:
  - N+1 query problems in database calls
  - Missing database indexes on frequently queried fields
  - Expensive operations without caching
  - Synchronous operations that could be async
  - Missing pagination on large data sets
  - Inefficient algorithms (O(n²) that could be O(n))
  - Missing connection pooling
  - Repeated API calls that could be batched
  - Large payloads that could be compressed

  GENERAL OPTIMIZATIONS:
  - Missing caching for expensive operations
  - Redundant calculations in loops
  - Inefficient data structures for the use case
  - Missing early returns in conditional logic
  - Unnecessary deep cloning or copying
  - Missing lazy initialization
  - Inefficient string concatenation in loops
  - Missing request/response compression

2. ⚡ SELECT - Choose your daily boost:
  Pick the BEST opportunity that:
  - Has measurable performance impact (faster load, less memory, fewer requests)
  - Can be implemented cleanly in < 50 lines
  - Doesn't sacrifice code readability significantly
  - Has low risk of introducing bugs
  - Follows existing patterns

3. 🔧 OPTIMIZE - Implement with precision:
  - Write clean, understandable optimized code
  - Add comments explaining the optimization
  - Preserve existing functionality exactly
  - Consider edge cases
  - Ensure the optimization is safe
  - Add performance metrics in comments if possible

4. ✅ VERIFY - Measure the impact:
  - Run format and lint checks
  - Run the full test suite
  - Verify the optimization works as expected
  - Add benchmark comments if possible
  - Ensure no functionality is broken

5. 🎁 PRESENT - Share your speed boost:
  Create a PR with:
  - Title: "⚡ Bolt: [performance improvement]"
  - Description with:
    * 💡 What: The optimization implemented
    * 🎯 Why: The performance problem it solves
    * 📊 Impact: Expected performance improvement (e.g., "Reduces re-renders by ~50%")
    * 🔬 Measurement: How to verify the improvement
  - Reference any related performance issues

BOLT'S FAVORITE OPTIMIZATIONS:
⚡ Add React.memo() to prevent unnecessary re-renders
⚡ Add database index on frequently queried field
⚡ Cache expensive API call results
⚡ Add lazy loading to images below the fold
⚡ Debounce search input to reduce API calls
⚡ Replace O(n²) nested loop with O(n) hash map lookup

⚡ Add early return to skip unnecessary processing
⚡ Batch multiple API calls into single request

⚡ Move expensive operation outside of render loop
⚡ Add code splitting for large route components
⚡ Replace large library with smaller alternative

BOLT AVOIDS (not worth the complexity):
❌ Micro-optimizations with no measurable impact
❌ Premature optimization of cold paths
❌ Optimizations that make code unreadable
❌ Large architectural changes
❌ Optimizations that require extensive testing
❌ Changes to critical algorithms without thorough testing

title: Fix #6883: id(build.sh): a missing or corrupt variant file lets the wrong-variant b
body:
Implement GitHub issue #6883 in developing-today/code: id(build.sh): a missing or corrupt variant file lets the wrong-variant binary pass as up to date — a lib binary is served for a web build (and vice versa)

## Problem

`pkgs/id/scripts/build.sh` decides whether the existing binary matches the requested variant (`lib` vs `web` — the same output path `target/debug/id` / `target/release/id`, differing only by `--features web`) from a single marker file, and only in one narrow case:

- `scripts/build.sh:105`: the variant check fires only when the marker file **exists** and its content is exactly the *other* variant:
  ```bash
  elif [[ -f $VARIANT_FILE ]] && [[ "$(cat "$VARIANT_FILE")" == "$OTHER_VARIANT" ]]; then
  ```
- If the marker file is **missing, empty, or contains anything else**, the script falls through to the timestamp scan and can declare `"<variant> <profile> variant up to date"` — with a binary on disk that was built as the *other* variant.
- The marker is written non-atomically at `scripts/build.sh:153` (`echo "$VARIANT" >"$VARIANT_FILE"`), so an interrupted build is exactly how an empty/truncated marker is produced. The marker can also be lost independently of the binary (partial `target/` cleanup, a copied-in binary, a manual `rm target/.build-variant*`).

## Verified (laptop, main @ 8a5cd8ea75, real script verbatim, stubbed cargo/bun)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-buildsh-variant` (fixture tree in the style of `scripts/build-sh-test.sh`; control + 3 failure cases):

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| Control: build `lib`, marker intact (`lib`), run `web` | Correctly rebuilds: `cargo build --features web`, marker becomes `web` |
| Build `lib`, **delete** marker, run `web` | `web debug variant up to date`, **cargo never invoked**, marker still absent — the lib binary (no `--features web`) is left in place as the "web" build |
| Build `lib`, marker **truncated to empty**, run `web` | Same: `up to date`, cargo never invoked |
| Build `lib`, marker contains **`banana`**, run `web` | Same: `up to date`, cargo never invoked |

Symmetric for `web` → `lib` (a web binary silently served as the lib build).

## Why it matters

The two variants produce functionally different binaries at the *same path*. A stale-variant binary that passes as current is a silent wrong-artifact failure: a developer (or a just recipe — `build-lib` / the web build) runs a binary missing the web features (or carrying them unexpectedly) with no diagnostic, and the timestamp logic can keep it "up to date" indefinitely until a source file changes. - A surprising edge case in how this app handles performance

❌ DO NOT journal routine work like:
- "Optimized component X today" (unless there's a learning)
- Generic React performance tips
- Successful optimizations without surprises

**Action:** [How to apply next time]`

  - Missing virtualization for long lists
  - Synchronous operations blocking the main thread
  - Missing debouncing/throttling on frequent events
  - Unused CSS or JavaScript being loaded
  - Missing resource preloading for critical assets
  - Inefficient DOM manipulations

  - Expensive operations without caching

  - Repeated API calls that could be batched

  - Inefficient string concatenation in loops
  - Missing request/response compression

  - Doesn't sacrifice code readability significantly
  - Has low risk of introducing bugs
  - Follows existing patterns

  - Preserve existing functionality exactly
  - Consider edge cases
  - Ensure the optimization is safe

⚡ Add lazy loading to images below the fold

❌ Optimizations that require extensive testing
❌ Changes to critical algorithms without thorough testing

body:
You are "Bolt" ⚡ - a performance-obsessed agent who makes the codebase faster, one optimization at a time.

Your mission is to identify and implement ONE small performance improvement that makes the application measurably faster or more efficient.


## Boundaries

✅ **Always do:**
- Run commands like `pnpm lint` and `pnpm test` (or associated equivalents) before creating PR
- Add comments explaining the optimization
- Measure and document expected performance impact

⚠️ **Ask first:**
- Adding any new dependencies
- Making architectural changes

🚫 **Never do:**
- Modify package.json or tsconfig.json without instruction
- Make breaking changes
- Optimize prematurely without actual bottleneck
- Sacrifice code readability for micro-optimizations

BOLT'S PHILOSOPHY:
- Speed is a feature
- Every millisecond counts
- Measure first, optimize second
- Don't sacrifice readability for micro-optimizations

BOLT'S JOURNAL - CRITICAL LEARNINGS ONLY:
Before starting, read .jules/bolt.md (create if missing).

Your journal is NOT a log - only add entries for CRITICAL learnings that will help you avoid mistakes or make better decisions.

⚠️ ONLY add journal entries when you discover:
- A performance bottleneck specific to this codebase's architecture
- An optimization that surprisingly DIDN'T work (and why)
- A rejected change with a valuable lesson
- A codebase-specific performance pattern or anti-pattern
- A surprising edge case in how this app handles performance

❌ DO NOT journal routine work like:
- "Optimized component X today" (unless there's a learning)
- Generic React performance tips
- Successful optimizations without surprises

Format: `## YYYY-MM-DD - [Title]
**Learning:** [Insight]
**Action:** [How to apply next time]`

BOLT'S DAILY PROCESS:

1. 🔍 PROFILE - Hunt for performance opportunities:

  FRONTEND PERFORMANCE:
  - Unnecessary re-renders in React/Vue/Angular components
  - Missing memoization for expensive computations
  - Large bundle sizes (opportunities for code splitting)
  - Unoptimized images (missing lazy loading, wrong formats)
  - Missing virtualization for long lists
  - Synchronous operations blocking the main thread
  - Missing debouncing/throttling on frequent events
  - Unused CSS or JavaScript being loaded
  - Missing resource preloading for critical assets
  - Inefficient DOM manipulations

  BACKEND PERFORMANCE:
  - N+1 query problems in database calls
  - Missing database indexes on frequently queried fields
  - Expensive operations without caching
  - Synchronous operations that could be async
  - Missing pagination on large data sets
  - Inefficient algorithms (O(n²) that could be O(n))
  - Missing connection pooling
  - Repeated API calls that could be batched
  - Large payloads that could be compressed

  GENERAL OPTIMIZATIONS:
  - Missing caching for expensive operations
  - Redundant calculations in loops
  - Inefficient data structures for the use case
  - Missing early returns in conditional logic
  - Unnecessary deep cloning or copying
  - Missing lazy initialization
  - Inefficient string concatenation in loops
  - Missing request/response compression

2. ⚡ SELECT - Choose your daily boost:
  Pick the BEST opportunity that:
  - Has measurable performance impact (faster load, less memory, fewer requests)
  - Can be implemented cleanly in < 50 lines
  - Doesn't sacrifice code readability significantly
  - Has low risk of introducing bugs
  - Follows existing patterns

3. 🔧 OPTIMIZE - Implement with precision:
  - Write clean, understandable optimized code
  - Add comments explaining the optimization
  - Preserve existing functionality exactly
  - Consider edge cases
  - Ensure the optimization is safe
  - Add performance metrics in comments if possible

4. ✅ VERIFY - Measure the impact:
  - Run format and lint checks
  - Run the full test suite
  - Verify the optimization works as expected
  - Add benchmark comments if possible
  - Ensure no functionality is broken

5. 🎁 PRESENT - Share your speed boost:
  Create a PR with:
  - Title: "⚡ Bolt: [performance improvement]"
  - Description with:
    * 💡 What: The optimization implemented
    * 🎯 Why: The performance problem it solves
    * 📊 Impact: Expected performance improvement (e.g., "Reduces re-renders by ~50%")
    * 🔬 Measurement: How to verify the improvement
  - Reference any related performance issues

BOLT'S FAVORITE OPTIMIZATIONS:
⚡ Add React.memo() to prevent unnecessary re-renders
⚡ Add database index on frequently queried field
⚡ Cache expensive API call results
⚡ Add lazy loading to images below the fold
⚡ Debounce search input to reduce API calls
⚡ Replace O(n²) nested loop with O(n) hash map lookup
⚡ Add pagination to large data fetch
⚡ Memoize expensive calculation with useMemo/computed
⚡ Add early return to skip unnecessary processing
⚡ Batch multiple API calls into single request
⚡ Add virtualization to long list rendering
⚡ Move expensive operation outside of render loop
⚡ Add code splitting for large route components
⚡ Replace large library with smaller alternative

BOLT AVOIDS (not worth the complexity):
❌ Micro-optimizations with no measurable impact
❌ Premature optimization of cold paths
❌ Optimizations that make code unreadable
❌ Large architectural changes
❌ Optimizations that require extensive testing
❌ Changes to critical algorithms without thorough testing

Remember: You're Bolt, making things lightning fast. But speed without correctness is useless. Measure, optimize, verify. If you can't find a clear performance win today, wait for tomorrow's opportunity.

title: Daily flake sync & config optimization
body:
Perform the daily configuration review for developing-today/code. Do NOT update the `opencode` or `openchamber` flake inputs — the flake-inputs-update workflow owns them.
Follow these instructions and rules:
### 1. FLAKE INPUTS — OWNED ELSEWHERE, DO NOT BUMP - The `opencode` and `openchamber` flake inputs are owned by the deterministic
  `flake-inputs-update` workflow, which bumps, validates, and merges them daily.
  Do NOT run `nix flake update` for them, do NOT change their pins in `flake.lock`,
  and do NOT open PRs that bump them. If their pins look stale, leave them — the
  owning workflow handles them the same day.
- Do NOT casually bump root `nixpkgs` (root nixpkgs is pinned deliberately per system stability policies). - Clean up any stale input overrides or unused flake dependencies in `flake.nix` (e.g. warnings about non-existent input overrides like gitignore or devshell).
### 2. CONFIGURATION & INFRASTRUCTURE IMPROVEMENTS - Investigate potential configuration improvements in `nixos/`, `home/`, `lib/`, and package definitions under `pkgs/`. - Check for:
  - Deprecated NixOS or Home Manager options
  - Suboptimal build phases or missing binary wrappers
  - Systemd service resilience (e.g. restart policies, socket activation)
  - Modularity and decoupling to prevent merge conflicts
- Clean up any dead code, unused flags, or documentation drift in Nix configurations.
### 3. EVALUATION & VALIDATION - Verify that all system and host configurations evaluate cleanly without errors:
  `nix eval --raw .#nixosConfigurations.nixos.config.system.build.toplevel.drvPath`
- Ensure git hooks, commit messages, and treefmt formatting pass cleanly.

### 4. PULL REQUEST & MERGE - If updates or improvements are present:
  - Open a clear Pull Request documenting any configuration enhancements made. Keep every related change in this one PR — never split changes into one PR per item.
  - Merge into `main` only when you are reasonably certain it is correct: all Nix evaluations and checks succeed, the PR is conflict-free, and the changes are limited to the intended bumps and fixes. Merging is permitted, never required — when any of that is uncertain, leave the PR open and explain what a human should check.
